subject: DOC
question: The Christian faith affirms that Jesus Christ is truly human and truly divine. Discuss five (5) proofs that Jesus was indeed divine and human.
idealAnswer: The story of the birth of Jesus is not just a beautiful idea or an abstract theological truth; it is historical, and the syllabus sets out several facts about the Incarnation which show that Jesus is truly God and truly man. First, Christ was Son of God from eternity: the New Testament teaches that Jesus existed long before he was born and did not come into being at the time of his birth, but has always existed as the Son of God; it was through him that God created the universe, and in him all things hold together. Secondly, it was by supernatural conception: the circumstances of Christ’s birth help us to understand that he was born without sin, for the human inclination to sin is inherited from our parents, and though his birth was as normal as any human’s, his conception occurred through the intervention of the Holy Spirit, so that Jesus was both God and man. Thirdly, it upholds Christ’s full deity: as the New Testament unfolds, the fact that Christ is God is increasingly revealed in his character, for he lived his life without a taint of sin; in his claims, to be the centre of all truth, the world’s judge and to have a unique relationship to the Father; and in his conduct, in performing miracles, forgiving sins and accepting worship. Fourthly, it establishes Christ’s full humanity: the New Testament shows that Christ was fully human, born into a Hebrew family and subject to the Hebrew law, experiencing all the problems people face – hunger and thirst, fatigue and sorrow – and facing the full force of temptation; although still fully God, he shared completely the weaknesses of all humankind except sin, and so was perfectly qualified to be the unique go-between bringing humankind and God together. Fifthly, it explains Christ’s unique personality: he is both God and man, in two distinct natures and one person for ever – the same Jesus who declared that he was thirsty also referred in prayer to the glory which he shared eternally with the Father. Sixthly, it validates Christ’s saving ministry: we know enough to realize that Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, is the one Saviour humankind needs, for by laying aside his eternal splendour and involving himself in humankind’s burdens, even to death on the cross, he becomes the reconciler between God and humankind. The Bible thus presents Christ as altogether God and altogether man – the perfect mediator between God and humankind because he partakes fully of the nature of both.
keyPoints: Christ was Son of God from eternity – he did not come into being at his birth
It was by supernatural conception – through the intervention of the Holy Spirit, so he was both God and man
It upholds Christ’s full deity – his character, his claims and his conduct
It establishes Christ’s full humanity – hunger, thirst, fatigue, sorrow and temptation
It explains Christ’s unique personality – two distinct natures, one person for ever
It validates Christ’s saving ministry – truly God and truly man, the one Saviour we need
He shared the weaknesses of humankind except sin, and so is the unique go-between
The Bible presents Christ as altogether God and altogether man

markingRubric.label: Supernatural conception
markingRubric.description: Shows that his conception occurred through the intervention of the Holy Spirit, so that he was born without sin and was both God and man.

markingRubric.label: Full deity
markingRubric.description: Shows Christ’s full deity from his character, his claims and his conduct – sinlessness, unique relation to the Father, miracles, forgiving sins, accepting worship.

markingRubric.label: Full humanity

subject: DOC
question: Write short notes on five facts about the Resurrection of Jesus Christ that Christians need to bear in mind.
idealAnswer: The resurrection is the central doctrine of Christianity, affirming that God raised Jesus from the dead on the third day; without it, Paul declared, Christian preaching and belief are meaningless, there would be no church and we would still be in our sins. Five things Christians need to know about it are these. First, it is the foundation of the Christian faith: it lifts Christianity from the level of philosophy or a mere code of conduct to the stature of God’s good news for the human race, for in the resurrection God set his seal of approval upon Christ as Son of God and underlined the value of his death; it transformed the followers of Jesus and sent them out to preach, and it is the non-negotiable pivot of the faith. Second, it is an event supported by evidence: there is factual evidence – the empty tomb with only the abandoned grave clothes, the failure of every other explanation, and the numerous reported appearances of the risen Jesus at different times and before different people – and psychological evidence – the transformed disciples, the conviction of the early church under persecution, and the change of the day of worship from Saturday to Sunday. Third, it is a promise of ultimate victory: had Christ not been raised, his death would have been evidence enough of the failure of his mission, but the resurrection assures the believer that he has not believed in vain and that all things, even the last enemy, death, must submit to the victory and rule of Jesus. Fourth, it is the power of Christian experience: the resurrection is far more than a past event, for it plays a vital part in Christian living now and colours the outlook, hopes and motives of every believer, who lives and works in the very power by which God raised Jesus from the dead. Fifth, it is the assurance of eternal security: the finality has been taken out of death, for all who die know that Christ has been through the experience before them and will bring them through it to be with him, and because Christ’s body was raised the Christian is guaranteed a resurrection body of beauty and strength, related to the old but without weakness or decay.
keyPoints: It is the foundation of the Christian faith – the non-negotiable pivot
God set his seal of approval upon Christ as Son of God
It is an event supported by evidence – empty tomb, grave clothes, appearances
Psychological evidence – transformed disciples, the persecuted church, Saturday changed to Sunday
It is a promise of ultimate victory – death, the last enemy, must submit to Jesus
It is the power of Christian experience
It is the assurance of eternal security
The Christian is guaranteed a resurrection body without weakness or decay

subject: DOC
chapter: THE DOCTRINE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT
topic: Hallmark of the Gifts of the Spirit
question: What is/are the difference(s) between the Fruit of the Holy Spirit and the Gifts of the Holy Spirit?
idealAnswer: The fruit of the Spirit and the gifts of the Spirit are both the work of the one Holy Spirit, but they differ. The fruit of the Spirit is concerned with character, while the gifts of the Spirit relate to abilities and functions distributed among believers. All the fruit should be exhibited in every Christian, but the gifts differ widely from person to person. The fruit is singular, not plural: Paul writes in Galatians 5:22-23 that “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control,” so there are not nine fruits but one fruit composed of nine elements, and the one kind of fruit the Spirit produces is Christ-likeness. Unlike the gifts, only some of which are given to a Christian, each believer is to have all nine virtues composing the fruit; and as fruit on a tree takes time to grow and mature, so the Spirit does not cultivate these virtues in a believer’s life overnight. The fruit is not produced by human effort but as Christians live in communion with the Lord, and it is the evidence of salvation and of the genuine work of the Spirit. The gifts, by contrast, began to be given when the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples at Pentecost and will continue until Christ comes again. They are not restricted to outstanding individuals or leaders: each believer has at least one gift, no one believer possesses all the gifts, and so the members of the Church need one another. Their hallmarks are that they glorify Christ, they involve all, they should unite all, they lay foundations, they edify the Church and they promote its mission; and they can be abused – by not using them in love, by neglecting the gifts imparted to us, or by attempting to use gifts not imparted to us.
keyPoints: The fruit is concerned with character; the gifts relate to abilities and functions
All the fruit should be exhibited in every Christian; the gifts differ widely from person to person
The fruit is singular – one fruit of nine elements (Gal. 5:22-23) – and its kind is Christ-likeness
The fruit takes time to mature and is not produced by human effort
The gifts began at Pentecost and continue until Christ comes again
Each believer has at least one gift; no believer has all the gifts
Hallmarks of the gifts: they glorify Christ, involve all, unite all, lay foundations, edify the Church, promote mission
The gifts can be abused

topic: The Apostle's Creed and its Explanation
question: How would you explain the fact that the church is holy and therefore different from other organizations or groups of people?
idealAnswer: The basic meaning of the word holy is “different” or “separate”. Since the Church is the body of Christ, and Christ is pure and blameless and was set apart for a purpose, so is the Church. When we confess that the church is holy we do not mean that its members know better or are morally superior to other people; the church is holy because its members are called by God to live unselfish, pure and consecrated lives. There are three ways in which we can say that the church is holy, or different and distinguished from other organizations or groups of people. First, it is a community of people who know they are sinners and freely admit that they are not good or superior. From the time of the prophets to the apostles, individual and social sinfulness have been identified among the people of God and addressed. As Charles C. Morrison aptly put it, the church is not a society of good people; it is a society of sinners, the only organization in human society that takes sinners into its membership just because they are sinners, and the only one that keeps on saying, week after week and age after age, “We have left undone those things which we ought to have done, and we have done those things which we ought not to have done.” Secondly, it is a community of people who are not satisfied with themselves or with the way things are in the world around them: they gather not to justify their present way of life or to publicize their holiness, but to admit publicly that they need to be forgiven for what they are, that they want to change and that they need help. Thirdly, it is a community which is gathered in the name of Jesus Christ, who is its Head. As Guthrie says, holiness is not found in the church and its members as such, but in him from whom they seek forgiveness, change, help and new direction; the church which is the body is holy only because the Head is the “Holy One”.
keyPoints: The basic meaning of holy is “different” or “separate”
The Church is the body of Christ, who is pure and blameless and set apart
Holiness does not mean the members are morally superior
The church is holy because its members are called by God to live unselfish, pure and consecrated lives
It is a community of people who know they are sinners – Morrison: a society of sinners
It is a community not satisfied with itself or the world, gathered to admit its need of forgiveness and change
It is a community gathered in the name of Jesus Christ, its Head
Guthrie: holiness is found in him from whom they seek forgiveness and new direction

subject: DOC
question: Write short notes on the following Christological titles: (a) Messiah (b) God (c) Lord (d) Son of Man.
idealAnswer: The many different names of Jesus Christ reveal the distinctive characteristics of his person and the work that he came to do. Messiah: for hundreds of years the Jews had been looking for a future King who would be a descendant of David when Jesus came into the world; this person they called the Messiah, which in Greek is Christos, from which we get Christ, and both words mean “the anointed one” or “one who has been anointed”. He would have God’s authority and power to bring in the end of the age and establish the kingdom of God. It was Simon Peter who made the first clear declaration that Jesus was the Christ, but Jesus totally rejected the popular idea of the Messiah as a political deliverer from the Roman Empire and saw his messianic role as one of suffering and death for the salvation of humankind; the Jews, looking for a king who would lead their nation to political victory over Rome, did not believe the Messiah would be God himself come to earth as a man or that he would die on a cross. God: Jesus is called God in the New Testament. Thomas, convinced that the risen Christ stood before him, abandoned his doubts with the confession, “My Lord and my God!”, and the classic text is John 1:1, where John declared that the Word existed not only “in the beginning”, where he was “with God”, but also actually “was God”. Lord: several words denoting lordship were used of Jesus in the New Testament. This title is somewhat different from the other titles, because whilst the others are descriptive terms, “Lord” expresses rank or worth. To acknowledge Jesus Christ as Lord appears to have been one of the earliest Christian confessions of faith, and “Jesus is Lord” is the ultimate Christian creed; when we call Jesus “Lord” we are certainly saying something about him as well as expressing our devotion and allegiance to him, recognizing him as an exalted being. As Graham Stanton puts it, the kyrios Christology expresses the authority of the Lord over the individual and the Christian community, and is often related to ethical statements. Son of Man: the expression, ben adam in Hebrew and bar nasha in Aramaic, was commonly used as a periphrasis for “man”. Jesus used this title more than any other to describe himself; although it seems to speak of his humanity, in reality it is a pointer to his deity, and it usually emphasizes his messianic role, for in the Old Testament the Messiah was called the Son of Man in Daniel 7:13-14. He used the title in three ways: when speaking of his earthly ministry, of his death and of his coming glory. The terms “Son of God” and “Son of Man” are used interchangeably in Matthew 26:63-65.
keyPoints: The many names of Jesus reveal the characteristics of his person and work
Messiah/Christ means “the anointed one”; Peter made the first clear declaration
Jesus rejected the political idea of the Messiah and saw his role as suffering and death
God – Thomas’s confession “My Lord and my God”; the classic text John 1:1
Lord – expresses rank or worth, unlike the descriptive titles
“Jesus is Lord” is the ultimate Christian creed and an early confession of faith
Son of Man – ben adam / bar nasha; Jesus’ favourite self-designation
Son of Man points to his deity and his messianic role (Dan. 7:13-14), used of his ministry, death and coming glory

subject: DOC
topic: The Work of Jesus can be discussed in terms of past, present, and future:
question: Discuss the work of Christ in terms of past, present and future.
idealAnswer: The work of Jesus can be discussed in terms of past, present and future. By the “finished” work of Christ is meant the work of atonement or redemption for the human race which he completed by his death on the Cross. This work is so perfect in itself that it requires neither repetition nor addition, and because of it he is called “Saviour of the world”. His finished work broke hell’s powers: Colossians 2:15 speaks of the “principalities and powers” as the evil powers which have controlled humanity, against which there was no hope of successful resistance, and when it looked as if death and hell had conquered him too, he conquered them on the cross. The saving work of Christ therefore includes the reconciliation of sinners to God and also brings them together as human beings, so that hostile divisions of humanity have peace with one another through him. The present work of Christ begins with his exaltation by God, after the completion of his finished work in his death and resurrection. Its first aspect was the sending of the Holy Spirit to dwell in his people, the fulfilment of which Peter announced. The aspect of his present work which receives the main emphasis in the New Testament is his intercession: Jesus’ presence with God as his people’s representative provides the assurance that their requests for spiritual help are heard and granted, and to know that he is there is a powerful incentive to his followers, since no good thing that Jesus seeks for them is withheld by the Father. His exaltation is repeatedly presented in the New Testament as the fulfilment of Psalm 110:1, “Sit at My right hand, till I make your enemies your footstool,” which means that Christ reigns from his present place of exaltation and must do so until all his enemies are overthrown. The future work of Christ is the raising of the dead and the passing of final judgment. To raise the dead and to judge the world are prerogatives of God, but he delegated these works to his Son to discharge at the time of the end, and they are associated with the Second Coming of Christ; Paul viewed Christ’s appearing in glory as the occasion when his people would share his glory and be displayed to the universe as the sons and daughters of God. Both the present work of Christ and his future work depend upon his finished work, which was the beginning of God’s good work in his people – a work that will not be completed until “the day of Jesus Christ”, when the entire universe will be united in Christ.
keyPoints: The finished work – atonement and redemption completed on the Cross, needing neither repetition nor addition
He is called “Saviour of the world”; his finished work broke hell’s powers
The saving work includes the reconciliation of sinners to God and to one another
The present work begins with his exaltation after death and resurrection
Its first aspect was the sending of the Holy Spirit to dwell in his people
Its main emphasis in the New Testament is his intercession as his people’s representative
The future work – the raising of the dead and the passing of final judgment, delegated by the Father
Present and future work both depend on the finished work, completed at “the day of Jesus Christ”

markingRubric.label: The finished work
markingRubric.description: Explains the atonement completed on the Cross, needing neither repetition nor addition, breaking hell’s powers and reconciling sinners to God and to one another.

markingRubric.label: The present work
markingRubric.description: Explains the exaltation, the sending of the Holy Spirit, and above all his intercession as his people’s representative, with the fulfilment of Psalm 110:1.

markingRubric.label: The future work
markingRubric.description: Explains the raising of the dead and the passing of final judgment, delegated to the Son and associated with the Second Coming, and the dependence of present and future work on the finished work.

chapter: THE DOCTRINE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT
topic: The Work of the Holy Spirit
question: Write a sermon to your congregation explaining how the Holy Spirit works in the life of a Christian.
idealAnswer: The Holy Spirit is mainly featured in the Bible for his work in the lives of men and women. In his general activity he convinces of sin, for as Spirit of truth his work is to convince the unbeliever of being wrong – something achieved not by human means but as he makes the message of the Bible plain; he illuminates truth, for as he inspired the writing of God’s word so he shows us what it means, and without his enlightening work the truth of God’s message remains misty and can even seem nonsensical and offensive; he reveals Christ, for his task is to focus the spotlight not on himself but on Christ, so that in having the Holy Spirit we have Christ; he lives in believers, making Christ real to the Christian, for no one who belongs to Christ is without him; he inspires prayer, helping us because he understands our weaknesses and preventing prayer from degenerating into mechanical drudgery or powerless routine; and he prepares us for heaven, for the whole Christian life is a life directed by the Spirit, who helps the Christian in the battle with sin and prepares him or her for glory. From the beginning of Christian discipleship the Holy Spirit lives within the Christian, giving the power to follow Christ, confidence in believing, and unity with other believers. He gives life – the new birth, for without the power of God a person is spiritually dead, and this new birth is brought about by the Spirit in one who responds to the good news of Christ, and is not earned by personal achievement but is God’s free gift. He gives assurance – the witness of the Spirit – confirming the reality of the believer’s new relationship with Christ, that he or she is a child of God, and that the Bible’s promise of eternal life is to be believed. He gives unity – fellowship in the Spirit. He gives ownership – the seal of the Spirit, the invisible yet permanent stamp of God’s ownership, so that we belong to God and cannot be separated from his love. He gives power – the fullness of the Spirit, which Christians are commanded to know as a continuous and regular experience. And he gives confidence – the pledge of the Spirit, a foretaste of all that God has prepared for his people. He also produces in the believer the fruit of the Spirit, which is Christ-likeness, and distributes gifts for the building up and mission of the Church.
keyPoints: He convinces of sin and illuminates truth
He reveals Christ – in having the Spirit we have Christ
He lives in believers and inspires prayer
He prepares the Christian for heaven
Life – the new birth, God’s free gift, not earned by achievement
Assurance – the witness of the Spirit; unity – fellowship in the Spirit
Ownership – the seal; power – the fullness; confidence – the pledge of the Spirit
He produces the fruit of the Spirit, which is Christ-likeness, and distributes gifts

subject: DOC
topic: The Apostle's Creed and its Explanation
question: How will you explain to a non-Christian friend the fact that the church is holy and therefore different from other organizations or groups of people?
idealAnswer: The basic meaning of the word holy is “different” or “separate”. Since the Church is the body of Christ, and Christ is pure and blameless and was set apart for a purpose, so is the Church. When we confess that the church is holy we do not mean that its members know better or are morally superior to other people; the church is holy because its members are called by God to live unselfish, pure and consecrated lives. There are three ways in which we can say that the church is holy, or different and distinguished from other organizations or groups of people. First, it is a community of people who know they are sinners and freely admit that they are not good or superior. From the time of the prophets to the apostles, individual and social sinfulness have been identified among the people of God and addressed. As Charles C. Morrison aptly put it, the church is not a society of good people; it is a society of sinners, the only organization in human society that takes sinners into its membership just because they are sinners, and the only one that keeps on saying, week after week and age after age, “We have left undone those things which we ought to have done, and we have done those things which we ought not to have done.” Secondly, it is a community of people who are not satisfied with themselves or with the way things are in the world around them: they gather not to justify their present way of life or to publicize their holiness, but to admit publicly that they need to be forgiven for what they are, that they want to change and that they need help. Thirdly, it is a community which is gathered in the name of Jesus Christ, who is its Head. As Guthrie says, holiness is not found in the church and its members as such, but in him from whom they seek forgiveness, change, help and new direction; the church which is the body is holy only because the Head is the “Holy One”.
keyPoints: The basic meaning of holy is “different” or “separate”
The Church is the body of Christ, who is pure and blameless and set apart
Holiness does not mean the members are morally superior
Its members are called by God to live unselfish, pure and consecrated lives
A community of people who know they are sinners – Morrison: a society of sinners
A community not satisfied with itself or the world, admitting its need of forgiveness and change
A community gathered in the name of Jesus Christ, its Head
Guthrie: holiness is found in him from whom they seek forgiveness and new direction

markingRubric.label: The meaning of holiness
markingRubric.description: Explains that holy basically means “different” or “separate”, and that the church is holy because it is the body of the pure and blameless Christ.

markingRubric.label: What holiness does not mean
markingRubric.description: States that holiness does not mean moral superiority, but that the members are called by God to live unselfish, pure and consecrated lives.

markingRubric.label: A community of admitted sinners
markingRubric.description: Explains that the church is a community of people who know and admit they are sinners, citing Morrison.

markingRubric.label: A community seeking change
markingRubric.description: Explains that the church gathers to admit publicly its need of forgiveness, change and help.

markingRubric.label: A community gathered in Christ’s name
markingRubric.description: Explains that the church is gathered in the name of Jesus Christ its Head, in whom its holiness is found.

explanation: Tests whether the candidate can explain the holiness of the Church to someone outside it.

options.text: The work of atonement or redemption for the human race which He completed by His death on the Cross
The raising of the dead and the passing of final judgment
options.rationale: These are the future work of Christ.

options.text: His intercession at the right hand of God
options.rationale: Intercession is the present work of Christ, not the finished work.

options.text: The sending of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost
options.rationale: The sending of the Spirit is named as the first aspect of Christ's present work.

explanation: The syllabus defines the finished work as the atonement completed on the Cross, so perfect that it requires neither repetition nor addition.

manualReference.topicTitle: The Work of Jesus can be discussed in terms of past, present, and future:
manualReference.excerpt: By the "finished" work of Christ is meant the work of atonement or redemption for the human race which He completed by His death on the Cross. This work is so perfect in itself that it requires neither repetition nor addition.
manualReference.citation: Christian Doctrine — THE DOCTRINE OF CHRIST — The Work of Jesus can be discussed in terms of past, present, and future:

subject: DOC
topic: The Work of Jesus can be discussed in terms of past, present, and future:
question: Which aspect of the present work of Christ receives the main emphasis in the New Testament?

options.rationale: Judgment is part of the future work of Christ.
The baptism of Jesus is treated among the critical events in the Gospels.
Teaching belongs to Christ's earthly ministry, not his present work.

explanation: The syllabus says intercession is the aspect of Christ's present work that receives the main emphasis in the New Testament.

manualReference.topicTitle: The Work of Jesus can be discussed in terms of past, present, and future:
manualReference.excerpt:
The present work of Christ that receives the main emphasis in the New Testament is His 
intercession.

subject: DOC
question: The apostle Paul declared that without the resurrection Christian preaching and belief are meaningless.
explanation: The syllabus cites 1 Corinthians 15:14 to this effect, and adds that without the resurrection there would be no church or Christianity.

manualReference.excerpt: Without the resurrection, the apostle Paul declared, Christian preaching and belief are meaningless (1 Cor. 15:14).
manualReference.citation: Christian Doctrine — THE DOCTRINE OF CHRIST — The Resurrection of Jesus Christ

subject: DOC
question: Which of the following does the syllabus classify as psychological evidence for the resurrection?

options.text: The numerous reported appearances of the risen Jesus
options.rationale: The appearances are listed under the factual evidence.

options.text: The failure of all explanations other than that Christ had risen
options.rationale: This too belongs to the factual evidence.

options.text: The empty tomb containing only the abandoned grave clothes
options.rationale: The empty tomb is listed under the factual evidence.

options.text: The change from Saturday to Sunday as the Christian day of worship

explanation: The syllabus divides the evidence into factual and psychological; the change of the day of worship is psychological evidence, along with the transformed disciples and the conviction of the early church.

manualReference.excerpt: There is also the psychological evidence. For example, there are the transformed disciples, the conviction of the early church in the face of persecution, and the change from Saturday to Sunday as the Christian day of worship (after centuries of Sabbath worship) (John 20:1-29; 1 Cor. 15:1-8).
manualReference.citation: Christian Doctrine — THE DOCTRINE OF CHRIST — The Resurrection of Jesus Christ

subject: DOC
question: What guarantee does the syllabus say the Christian has because Christ's body was raised from death?

options.text: That the millennium will begin immediately
options.rationale: The syllabus notes that Christians disagree about the millennium and does not teach this.

options.text: That he or she will not experience physical death
options.rationale: The syllabus says death is still an enemy, though a defeated one.

options.text: That he or she too will receive in eternity a resurrection body of beauty and strength
That the old body will be restored unchanged
options.rationale: The syllabus says the new body will be related to the old, but without weakness or decay.

explanation: Under 'It is the Assurance of Eternal Security' the syllabus grounds the believer's resurrection body in Christ's own bodily resurrection.

manualReference.excerpt: Furthermore, because Christ's body was raised from death, the Christian has the guarantee that he or she too will receive in eternity a resurrection body of beauty and strength. This new body will be related to the old, but without weakness or decay (John 11:25, 26; 1 Cor. 15:20, 42-57).
manualReference.citation: Christian Doctrine — THE DOCTRINE OF CHRIST — The Resurrection of Jesus Christ

manualReference.citation: Christian Doctrine — THE DOCTRINE OF CHRIST — Main Aspects of Christ's Ministry

question: At what point in Jesus' public ministry were the twelve disciples chosen?

options.rationale: The syllabus places the temptation immediately after the baptism.

Towards the end of his public ministry

The syllabus places the choosing of the Twelve within the public ministry.

question: Over which issues does the syllabus say Jesus clashed with the Jewish leaders? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: That he denied the resurrection of the body
options.rationale: The syllabus nowhere attributes such a denial to Jesus.

options.text: That he claimed to be God
That he refused to teach in parables

manualReference.excerpt: Jesus clashed with the Jewish leaders over the following issues: that he mixed with sinners, challenged traditions, liberated the Sabbath, and that he claimed to be God (Mark 2:5-7, 15, 16; Matt. 23:13-36; 26:62-66).
manualReference.citation: Christian Doctrine — THE DOCTRINE OF CHRIST — Main Aspects of Christ's Ministry

subject: DOC
question: During the reign of which Roman emperor was Jesus born?

Pilate was the governor under whom Jesus suffered, not an emperor.
Constantine convened the First Council of Nicaea in AD 325.

manualReference.excerpt: Jesus was born during the reign of the Roman emperor Caesar Augustus, into an extremely poor family. He was born in alien surroundings during a Roman census, and he was born into immediate danger - as King Herod searched to kill him.
manualReference.citation: Christian Doctrine — THE DOCTRINE OF CHRIST — Critical Events in the Gospels

The syllabus gives the figure as thirty-six hours.

Thirty-six hours after the burial, Jesus' tomb was found empty, except for the discarded 
grave clothes.
manualReference.citation: Christian Doctrine — THE DOCTRINE OF CHRIST — Critical Events in the Gospels

chapter: THE DOCTRINE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT
question: Whom did Jesus promise to send to his disciples after he had departed this world, and when was the promise fulfilled?

options.text: The Counsellor (Comforter); the promise was fulfilled on the Day of Pentecost
The Counsellor (Comforter); the promise was fulfilled at his baptism
options.rationale: The descent of the Spirit at the baptism was God's approval of Jesus' own ministry.

options.text: The Son of Man; the promise will be fulfilled at his Second Coming
options.rationale: 'Son of Man' is a title of Jesus himself, not of the promised Counsellor.

manualReference.chapterTitle: THE DOCTRINE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT
manualReference.excerpt:
During the latter period of his earthly life Jesus promised his disciples that after he had departed this world he would send the Counsellor (Comforter) to them (John 16:7). After 
the Lord had ascended into heaven the promise was fulfilled on the Day of Pentecost.
manualReference.citation: Christian Doctrine — THE DOCTRINE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT — INTRODUCTION

chapter: THE DOCTRINE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT
topic: The Deity of the Holy Spirit
question: How does the syllabus describe the place of the Holy Spirit within the Godhead?

options.text: He is an attribute of God rather than God himself
options.rationale: Under 'The Spirit of God' the syllabus says he is not an attribute of God, but God himself.

options.text: He is the third person of the Trinity, presented in the Bible as a person fully worthy of worship
He is the impersonal power or influence of God at work in the world
options.rationale: The syllabus insists the Spirit is not just an influence or power and may not be called 'It'.

options.rationale: That is precisely what Arius taught, which the syllabus identifies as heresy.

subject: DOC
question: Explain the doctrine of the Incarnation of Jesus Christ, setting out the facts about it which the syllabus notes.
idealAnswer:
The word Incarnation comes from the Latin incarnare, which means "to make flesh", or in a general sense the bodily manifestation of a supernatural being. The idea that God or the gods have made themselves present among humankind in human form is widespread in the history of religions, but in Christianity the doctrine states that God, in one of the modes of his triune being and without in any way ceasing to be God, has revealed himself to mankind for their salvation by coming among them as a man. Livingstone K. Buama says that the word incarnation directs our attention to the bringing together in one person, Jesus Christ our Lord, of both Godhood and manhood, and that it has to do with how the eternal word became flesh. St. Augustine explains that the meaning of the Word being made flesh is not that the divine nature was changed into flesh, but that the divine nature assumed our flesh except without sin. The story of Jesus' birth is recorded only in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke; it emphasises the belief that God is with us, and it is historical.

The syllabus notes six facts about the Incarnation. First, Christ was Son of God from eternity: he did not come into being at his birth but has always existed as the Son of God, and it was through him that God created the universe. Second, it was by supernatural conception: though his birth was as normal as any human's, his conception occurred through the intervention of the Holy Spirit, so that he was born without the inherited human inclination to sin. Third, it upholds Christ's full deity, seen in his character, his claims and his conduct in performing miracles, forgiving sins and accepting worship. Fourth, it establishes Christ's full humanity: he was born into a Hebrew family, subject to the Hebrew law, and exposed to hunger, thirst, fatigue, sorrow and temptation, sharing the weaknesses of humankind except sin, and so qualified to be the unique go-between. Fifth, it explains Christ's unique personality: he is both God and man, in two distinct natures and one person for ever. Sixth, it validates Christ's saving ministry: truly God and truly man, he is the one Saviour humankind needs, and by laying aside his eternal splendour and dying on the cross he becomes the reconciler between God and humankind.
keyPoints: Incarnation comes from the Latin incarnare, 'to make flesh'
God, without ceasing to be God, came among humankind as a man for their salvation
Augustine: the divine nature assumed our flesh, it was not changed into flesh
The birth story is recorded only in Matthew and Luke
Christ was Son of God from eternity; the universe was created through him
Supernatural conception by the Holy Spirit, so that he was born without sin
It upholds Christ's full deity and establishes his full humanity
It explains his unique personality (two natures, one person) and validates his saving ministry

subject: DOC
topic: The Necessity of the Virgin Birth
question: Discuss the reasons why the virgin birth was a necessity.
idealAnswer:
The Virgin Birth, or Parthenogenesis, is the biblical doctrine that Jesus was miraculously begotten by God and born of Mary, who was a virgin. The term explains the way in which the Son of God entered human existence: it means that Mary had not had sexual relations with any man when she conceived Jesus. The syllabus gives three reasons why this was a necessity.

The first is Christ's pre-existence. The Bible teaches that the Word who became flesh was with God from the very beginning, and the pre-existence of Christ is testified many times in the New Testament. When Jesus came into the world he was not a newly-created individual such as we are, but was rather the eternal Son of God. To be born into this world of the Virgin Mary required divine intervention, and this is exactly what the Gospels record.

The second reason is the transmission of original sin. Jesus needed to be virgin-born because of his sinless nature. According to Ambrose and Augustine, both Early Church Fathers, the transmission of original sin is bound up with the sexual nature of propagation and the carnal desires aroused by procreation. That Jesus was conceived without any sexual relations explains how he was free of original sin. A basic New Testament teaching is that from the day he was born until the day he died, Jesus was without sin. To be a perfect sacrifice he must himself be perfect, without sin; and since our race is contaminated with sin, a miraculous entrance into the world was required, hence the virgin birth.

The third reason is Jesus' inheritance of the throne of David. If Jesus had been fathered by Joseph he would not have been able to assume the throne of David. According to the prophecy of Jeremiah 22:28-30 there could be no king in Israel who was a descendant of King Jeconiah, and Matthew 1:12 relates that Joseph was from the line of Jeconiah. Had Joseph been his father, Jesus could not rightly have inherited the throne, since he would have been a relative of the cursed line. The syllabus concludes that there are possibly other ways God could have chosen to send his Son into the world, but the way he chose was through the virgin birth.
keyPoints: The virgin birth (Parthenogenesis) means Mary had not had sexual relations when she conceived Jesus
Reason 1: Christ's pre-existence - he was the eternal Son of God, not a newly-created individual
His entry into the world therefore required divine intervention
Reason 2: the transmission of original sin - Ambrose and Augustine bound it up with sexual propagation
A perfect sacrifice must be sinless, so a miraculous entrance was required
Reason 3: Jesus' inheritance of the throne of David
Jeremiah 22:28-30 barred descendants of Jeconiah, and Joseph was of that line
God could possibly have chosen other ways, but he chose the virgin birth

subject: DOC
question: Give an account of the Christological titles (the names) of Christ.
idealAnswer:
The many different names of Jesus Christ reveal the distinctive characteristics of his person and the work he came to do. The name Jesus itself means "the one who saves".

Messiah is the title the Jews gave to the future King who would descend from David; in Greek Christos, whence Christ; both mean "the anointed one". Simon Peter made the first clear declaration that Jesus was the Christ, but Jesus rejected the popular idea of the Messiah as a political deliverer from Rome, seeing his messianic role as one of suffering and death for the salvation of humankind.

The Holy One of God, given by Peter, belonged to him as the Messiah, especially set apart for God. Son of God occurs most frequently in John's Gospel and usually emphasises Jesus' deity; he was acclaimed Son of God at his baptism and given the title by the angel Gabriel at the annunciation. Jesus expressed his special sense of the fatherhood of God in the word abba.

Son of Man, in Hebrew ben adam and in Aramaic bar nasha, was a periphrasis for "man". Jesus used this title of himself more than any other. Though it seems to speak of his humanity, it points to his deity, for it is drawn from the book of Daniel, where the Son of Man rules an everlasting kingdom. Jesus used it when speaking of his earthly ministry, his death and his coming glory, and is thought to have favoured it because it carried no nationalistic associations, implied identification with humans, and had overtones of divinity and undertones of humanity.

Word and Wisdom: Jesus is designated the Word, or Logos, through whom God created all things and who is the perfect expression of God to humankind; he is also portrayed as the personal wisdom of God. High Priest, given to Christ in Hebrews, is drawn from the Old Testament sacrificial system, Christ's unrepeatable death making him the perfect mediator. Lord translates the Greek kurios; to call Jesus Lord was the mark of a true Christian and invited opposition from the Jewish authorities for blasphemy and from the Romans for treason. Unlike the other, descriptive titles, "Lord" expresses rank or worth, and "Jesus is Lord" is the ultimate Christian creed. Finally, Jesus is called God, as in Thomas's confession and in the classic text John 1:1. The Bible thus presents Christ as altogether God and altogether man.
keyPoints: The names of Christ reveal the characteristics of his person and work
Messiah / Christ means 'the anointed one'; Peter made the first clear declaration
Jesus rejected the political idea of Messiahship (Macquarrie: a victor, not a sufferer)
The Holy One of God - given by Peter, set apart for God
Son of God - most frequent in John, emphasises deity; abba
Son of Man - ben adam / bar nasha; used by Jesus more than any other; drawn from Daniel
Word (Logos) and Wisdom; High Priest from the Old Testament sacrificial system
Lord (kurios) expresses rank or worth; and Jesus is called God (John 1:1; Hebrews 1:8)

subject: DOC
question: Outline the main aspects of Christ's ministry which distinguish him from any religious leader who ever lived.
idealAnswer:
Christ was unlike any prophet or religious teacher that ever lived. By his authority and deeds, and by the power of his teaching and example, he challenged his hearers to believe in him as the unique Son of God. The syllabus sets out six aspects of his ministry.

First, authority that convinced. The authority with which Jesus taught astonished those who heard him. The prophets of old repeatedly declared "The Lord says...", but Jesus directed his hearers towards himself, saying "But I tell you...". The Jewish leaders of his day took their authority from the great teachers of the past, but Christ taught in his own name and authority.

Second, parables that provoked. His teaching was given in terms and images understood in daily life, and this is particularly true of his unforgettable parables, which both concealed and revealed truth.

Third, miracles that confirmed. Christ's authority was further demonstrated by his miracles: the wind and the waves obeyed his command and even the dead were brought back to life. Most of his miracles were acts of healing that formed part of his mission of love, and they pointed to his identity as the Son of God and to the coming of God's kingdom.

Fourth, compassion that attracted. His deep concern for people was born of his understanding that human beings are created in God's own image but are also fallen and live in a fallen world. He showed care for the individual in his encounters with the bereaved, the sick and the demon-possessed.

Fifth, training that prepared. Towards the beginning of the second year of his public ministry the twelve disciples were chosen to share in his work of teaching, preaching and healing. They learned from his example and from private instruction, and were sent out, with some seventy others, to do his work. They did not understand all that was taught them at the time, but their training was vitally important for the future development of the Church.

Sixth, controversy that challenged. From the outset the words and actions of Jesus had a controversial cutting edge that finally provoked a collision with the Jewish authorities: he mixed with sinners, challenged traditions, liberated the Sabbath, and claimed to be God. Yet it is remarkable that while he directed his hearers towards himself he never gave the impression of being conceited, arrogant or selfish.

Authority that convinced - 'But I tell you' rather than 'The Lord says'
Parables that provoked - concealed and revealed truth; the hearers found the parable was about themselves
Miracles that confirmed - mostly healings, pointing to his identity and the kingdom
Compassion that attracted - care for the individual, the bereaved, sick and demon-possessed
Training that prepared - the Twelve chosen towards the beginning of the second year
Controversy that challenged - mixing with sinners, challenging traditions, liberating the Sabbath, claiming to be God
He never gave the impression of being conceited, arrogant or selfish

subject: DOC
question: Explain the importance of the atoning death of Jesus Christ.
idealAnswer:
The syllabus sets aside the many theories of atonement and treats instead the importance of the death of Jesus Christ.

It initiated a new relationship. Man's sin has created a barrier of guilt between him and his creator, but Jesus accepted the responsibility for human sin and willingly took its penalty on the cross. A new relationship is now available for those who respond to the good news that their sins can be forgiven; hostility has been replaced by friendship.

It fulfilled Old Testament scripture. The Old Testament showed that God and man could not be reconciled unless a sacrifice was made, for only then could the guilt of sin be removed. The Old Testament animal sacrifices could not in themselves take away sin, nor be a final solution to the problem of sin; the New Testament sees them as illustrations of the perfect sacrifice Jesus was to make.

It destroyed Satan's kingdom. The power of Satan's kingdom was broken through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ. The final destruction of the Devil is yet to be, but the Christian is confident of victory through the power of the cross.

It reversed sin's dominion. The idea of redeeming, or buying back, a person who is enslaved is very strong in the Bible. Christ is presented as the one who by his death redeems his people from the penalty of God's moral law, and because he has taken our guilt upon himself, sin no longer has the power to dominate the life of the Christian.

It provided a way of victory. With the power of the Devil limited and the guilt of sin removed, the cross has set the Christian free - not free from the fight for moral purity but free for the fight. The tenses of salvation are these: we have been saved from the penalty of sin by a crucified Saviour; we are being saved from the power of sin by a living Saviour; we shall be saved from the presence of sin by a coming Saviour.

It guaranteed an eternity with God. The cross is the guarantee that God has set his eternal love upon his people. Death is still an enemy, but a defeated one, and like the Devil it will face ultimate annihilation. The work of Christ has often been stated in relation to his threefold office as prophet, priest and king.
keyPoints: The syllabus sets aside theories of atonement and treats the importance of Christ's death
It initiated a new relationship: hostility replaced by friendship; the Christian is a new person
It fulfilled Old Testament scripture: animal sacrifices were illustrations of the perfect sacrifice
It destroyed Satan's kingdom, though the final destruction of the Devil is yet to be
It reversed sin's dominion through redemption, buying back the enslaved
It provided a way of victory - the three tenses of salvation
It guaranteed an eternity with God; death is a defeated enemy
The work of Christ is stated in his threefold office as prophet, priest and king

subject: DOC
chapter: THE DOCTRINE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT
topic: The Deity of the Holy Spirit
question: Discuss the evidence which the syllabus gives for the deity of the Holy Spirit.
idealAnswer:
The syllabus asks directly whether the Holy Spirit is God, and answers with several lines of evidence. The Spirit was associated with the work of creation; he gives the Christian new life; he is the source of all knowledge, the guide and helper of the Church in all ages; and he makes salvation a real experience to individuals. The apostle Peter equated lying to the Holy Spirit with lying to God. The Holy Spirit is the third person of the Trinity, and he is presented in the Bible as a person fully worthy of worship.

First, the Spirit possesses divine attributes. He is holy - and the syllabus notes that in the title "Holy Spirit" the word holy is not a noun but an adjective describing his character. He is eternal, omnipotent, omniscient, omnipresent, and he is truth. Each of these attributes is supported from Scripture: eternity from Hebrews 9:14, omnipotence from Genesis 1:2 and Job 26:13, omniscience from 1 Corinthians 2:10-11 and John 14:26, omnipresence from Psalm 139:7-10, and truth from 1 John 5:6.

Secondly, the Holy Spirit does things that only God can do. He was associated with the work of creation; he makes salvation a real experience to individuals; he gives the Christian new life; he is the author of the new birth; he makes prophecy possible; and he convinces people of righteousness and of judgment to come.

Thirdly, there is the descent of the Holy Spirit. One of the clearest indications of the full divinity of the Holy Spirit is given by Jesus himself when he promised to send the Spirit to the disciples. The Spirit is included in the Christian formula of baptism and in the apostolic blessing, and Peter equated lying to him with lying to God. When Christ had left the world, the Spirit was given his most specific work, and the book of Acts, which is the account of the early Church, portrays the Spirit as directing and controlling the new Christian movement. Taken together this evidence establishes that the Holy Spirit is God, the third person of the Trinity.

subject: DOC
chapter: THE DOCTRINE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT
topic: The Emblems of the Holy Spirit
question: Describe the emblems of the Holy Spirit and state what each teaches about his nature and mission.
idealAnswer:
The emblems of the Holy Spirit throw light upon both his nature and his mission. The syllabus treats six of them.

Wind indicates unseen power, and the main ideas conveyed are mystery, sovereignty and energy. This vivid description of the Spirit's activity is used in Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones being given new life, in Christ's words to Nicodemus, and in the sound of rushing wind at Pentecost.

Water indicates life and cleansing. The key reference to the Spirit's work as water comes from words Christ spoke about streams of life-giving water flowing from those who believe in him; he was clearly talking about the life-giving activity of the Holy Spirit.

Fire indicates five things: the presence of the Lord, the protection of the Lord, the approval of the Lord, the purifying from the Lord, and the judgment of the Lord. The prophet Malachi predicts the coming of God's messenger in terms of refining fire, and this picture is reiterated in the New Testament when John the Baptist said that Jesus would baptize with the Holy Spirit and with fire. It is possible that the tongues of flame at Pentecost were meant to show the Spirit's refining activity.

Oil indicates light, healing, and anointing for service. In the Old Testament, anointing with oil was a sign that God had chosen someone for a particular task, and in this way priests or kings were set apart for God's service. The Bible tells us that Jesus was anointed by the Spirit, and this is also true for his followers.

The Dove indicates purity, peace, and modesty. The Spirit, in the form of a dove, descended upon Jesus at his baptism. Without doubt Jesus possessed the Spirit already, but this event pictures the gentleness associated with the dove, a gentleness which would characterise Christ's work.

A Seal indicates ownership, finished transaction, identification, security, value, authority and genuineness.

The syllabus adds an important caution: these images are nothing more than pictures meant to help us appropriately describe the work of the Spirit.
keyPoints: The emblems throw light upon both the Spirit's nature and his mission
Wind - unseen power; mystery, sovereignty and energy (Ezekiel's dry bones, Nicodemus, Pentecost)

Fire - the presence, protection, approval, purifying and judgment of the Lord
Oil - light, healing and anointing for service; priests and kings set apart
The Dove - purity, peace and modesty; descended on Jesus at his baptism
A Seal - ownership, finished transaction, identification, security, value, authority, genuineness
These images are only pictures to help us describe the work of the Spirit

subject: DOC
chapter: THE DOCTRINE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT
topic: The Work of the Holy Spirit
question: What is meant by the fruit of the Spirit? Explain the significance of the word "fruit" and outline the nine elements of which it is composed.
idealAnswer:
In Galatians chapter 5 Paul states the principle of fruit bearing: the fruit is produced by yielding to the sweet influences that are about us. "The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such, there is no law." It is important to notice that the word is singular - is, not are - and it happens to be singular in the Greek. There are not nine fruits, but one fruit composed of nine elements; the Holy Spirit produces one kind of fruit, that is, Christ-likeness.

The word fruit is significant for three reasons. It means the result, product, outcome or effect produced by the Spirit in the believer's life. Unlike the gifts of the Spirit, which are plural and only some of which are given to a Christian, each believer is to have all nine virtues composing the fruit of the Spirit. And as fruit on a tree takes time to grow and mature, so the Spirit does not cultivate these virtues in the believer's life overnight.

Love is what God is and what we ought to be, a selfless, sacrificial and practical love modelled on Christ's own. Joy is contentment and satisfaction with God and with his dealings, totally independent of circumstances, and differing from happiness. Peace includes the peace of God and harmonious relations with others; it is tranquility of soul and does not mean the absence of trouble. Longsuffering means patience in affliction, annoyance and persecution - patient endurance under provocation with no thought of retaliation, its supreme example being Luke 23:34. Kindness is graciousness and kindly disposition, best explained in the Lord's attitude toward little children. Goodness is kindness shown to others: kind but firm, ready to do good; it is love in action, expecting no rewards. Faith here means fidelity or faithfulness, which makes one true to one's promise and faithful to one's task. Gentleness is taking the lowly place, as Jesus did when he washed his disciples' feet; it is not weakness but controlled strength. Self-control is rational restraint of the natural impulses, a sign of strength and growth in character.

The fruit of the Spirit is not produced by human effort but as Christians live in communion with the Lord. It is the evidence of salvation and the genuine work of the Holy Spirit.

Unlike the gifts, every believer is to have all nine virtues
As fruit takes time to grow, the Spirit does not cultivate these virtues overnight

The fruit is not produced by human effort but by communion with the Lord, and is the evidence of salvation

subject: DOC
topic: Some Heresies (False Views about the Trinity)
question: Explain the heresies of Modalism and Tri-theism, and state what the doctrine of the Trinity affirms in place of them.
idealAnswer:
The Church slowly formulated the doctrine of the Trinity in opposition to false interpretations of the faith, specifically over the deity of Jesus Christ. Two ancient trinitarian heresies are set out in the syllabus.

Modalism teaches that the one God assumes different forms, or plays different roles. In the beginning God acted as Creator and Law-giver; later in history, when things went wrong, he revealed himself as the Redeemer; and later still he revealed himself as the Holy Spirit who is the Enlightener and Sanctifier. Against this the syllabus insists that God did not as a matter of urgency become threefold for the purpose of creation, redemption and sanctification. As William Barclay emphasizes, God is always, from eternity, through time, and when time shall end, Creator, Redeemer, Sustainer and Enlightener.

Tri-theism pictures and presents the three persons of the Godhead - Father, Son and Holy Spirit - as consisting of three separate but co-operating Gods. Its emphasis is upon the Three-ness of God, but it overlooks the Oneness, the indivisible unity of God.

The early Church rejected both false solutions and worked out its own statement. Its alternative was not really a solution to the problem of how God is one and yet three; all it really did was to affirm both God's oneness and his genuine presence and work in Christ and in the Spirit. The one God makes himself known to us and works in our world and our individual lives in three different ways, but in each of these ways we have to do with the one God himself - not with three gods, nor with a hierarchy of divine beings, nor with masks which hide who the one behind them really is. The Westminster Confession puts it thus: "In the unity of the Godhead there are three persons of one substance, power, and eternity"; and the Belgic Confession says, "God is one in essence, yet distinguished in three persons." One essence or one substance originally meant that Father, Son and Holy Spirit are the same in being. It is very important to note that there are not three persons or personalities in God: God is only one person, and "one God in three persons" means one God who has at the same time three distinct ways of existence, exercised not in temporal succession but simultaneously.
keyPoints: The Church formulated the doctrine in opposition to false interpretations, over the deity of Christ
Modalism: the one God assumes different forms or plays different roles in succession
Barclay: God is always Creator, Redeemer, Sustainer and Enlightener
Tri-theism: three separate but co-operating Gods; it emphasises Three-ness and overlooks Oneness
The early Church rejected both and affirmed God's oneness together with his presence in Christ and the Spirit

subject: DOC
topic: The Relevance of the Doctrine of the Trinity
question: Discuss the relevance of the doctrine of the Trinity for Christian life and relationships.
idealAnswer:
The doctrine of the Trinity is ultimately a practical doctrine with radical consequences for Christian experience and life. God lives as the mystery of love among persons; and since we are created in his image and likeness, the question of what forms of life best enable us to live as Christ lived becomes urgent.

In our relationship with God, the doctrine is a way of contemplating the mystery of God and of ourselves in relation to him. The truth about both God and ourselves is that we are meant to exist as persons in communion in a common household, living as persons from and for others, not persons in isolation, withdrawal or self-centeredness. Christians are baptized into the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit; to live in the name of another is to appropriate their personal history and relational identity, so that our identity is linked intimately with theirs.

In our relationship with others, the Godhead reveals that God is truly a living one, personal and not impersonal, who deals with us at one and the same time as loving Father, self-giving Saviour and sanctifying Spirit. This helps us to affirm our own personhood and that of others, a moral obligation. The Triune God is Love: according to St. Augustine, without the Trinity there can be no fellowship as love in God; and Dr. Livingstone K. Buama says that love is the distinguishing characteristic of a true Christian, so that the practical demand is to abide in God's love and propagate it in word and in deed. The Trinity also teaches that God is indivisibly one, with unity of purpose and action, so that as we worship the God of unity we must pursue unity in our relationships. The three persons live in mutual co-existence, solidarity, fellowship and harmony, with no power struggle or personality conflict within the Godhead; those who embrace this are obliged to promote fellowship, solidarity and harmonious communal existence, and so freedom, justice, peace and prosperity.

The doctrine is also relevant to prayer. St. Augustine acknowledged the presence of the Triune God in Christian prayer, each Person playing a distinct role: we pray to the Father, who gives us power to become children of God; prayers are addressed to Christ, through him and in his name; and the Holy Spirit animates the prayer and enables us to discover God as our Father.
keyPoints: The doctrine is practical, with radical consequences for Christian experience and life
God lives as the mystery of love among persons; we are created in his image
We are meant to exist as persons in communion, not in isolation or self-centeredness
Baptism into the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit links our identity with theirs
God is personal, relating to us as loving Father, self-giving Saviour and sanctifying Spirit
Augustine: without the Trinity there can be no fellowship as love in God; Buama: love is the distinguishing characteristic of a true Christian
God is indivisibly one, so we must pursue unity; the Godhead has no power struggle or personality conflict
The Trinity and prayer: Father, Son and Holy Spirit each play a distinct role

subject: DOC
topic: History of the Formulation of the Nicene Creed
question: Give an account of the history of the formulation of the Nicene Creed.
idealAnswer:
The formulation of the creed began with questions about the person of Christ: was he God or man? By the beginning of the fourth century the answer was not clear. One who attempted an answer was Arius, a presbyter from Alexandria. He said the Son, Jesus Christ, was a creature and not God; for him only the Father is unbegotten and self-subsistent, while the Son is begotten, so that there must have been a time when he was not. His main reason was that there is only one God: if the Son is also God, we have two Gods.

This view was strongly opposed by Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria, who suspended Arius from office. But Arius stuck to his opinions and gained support, so that the dispute threatened the unity of the church and of the empire. Emperor Constantine therefore summoned the first great ecumenical council of bishops at Nicaea in 325. The council condemned Arianism and drafted a creed to which all bishops had to assent. This was not the creed we now call the Nicene Creed, but it stated the essentials of belief so as to exclude any Arian interpretation. Its most noteworthy feature was its assertion that Christ is "of one substance as the Father", or of the same being as the Father.

In 328 Athanasius became bishop of Alexandria; earlier, in his treatise De Incarnatione, usually dated 318, he had already contributed to Christology, a "Christology of the Word, which took a body of the virgin": Christ the Word became man that we might become God, for only God, the Uncreated and giver of life, can save us.

The views of Athanasius triumphed some years after his death, at an ecumenical council at Constantinople in 381. It was this council which agreed what we now call the Nicene Creed, more accurately the Niceno-Constantinopolitan creed. It enshrined homoousios, "of the same being" or "consubstantial", as the most accurate term for the relation of Christ to the Father. At Nicaea the divinity of the Holy Spirit had been discussed but denied; at Constantinople it was officially accepted and affirmed, the Spirit being confessed as "The Lord and giver of life, who proceeds from the Father". Later, in the West and under the influence of St. Augustine of Hippo, the words "and the Son" were added, the Latin Filioque; the Eastern Church preferred "from the Father through the Son".

Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria, opposed him and suspended him from office
Emperor Constantine summoned the first great ecumenical council at Nicaea in 325
The council condemned Arianism; the creed of 325 asserted Christ is 'of one substance as the Father'
Athanasius became bishop of Alexandria in 328; his De Incarnatione is usually dated 318
The council of Constantinople in 381 agreed what we now call the Nicene Creed (Niceno-Constantinopolitan)
It enshrined homoousios, 'of the same being' or 'consubstantial', and affirmed the divinity of the Holy Spirit
The Filioque was added later in the West under the influence of Augustine; the East preferred 'from the Father through the Son'

subject: DOC
topic: The Apostle's Creed and its Explanation
question: What are the marks of a true church? Explain also what is meant by the holiness and the catholicity of the church.
idealAnswer:
The church of the New Testament was richly diverse; but despite all the local differences certain common elements stood out, and these are described as the marks of a true church. It accepts the full teachings of the Christian faith as spelt out in the Bible, that is, faith in Jesus as Messiah and Lord. It maintains continuity with the experience of Christians in the past - their unity and oneness of purpose, their love and joy, their devotion and purity of life. It celebrates the sacraments commanded by our Lord, that is, Baptism and Holy Communion. Its members follow the standard of life set by Christ, which is different from that of other people. It follows the apostolic preaching and instruction. And its members live in constant expectation of the coming kingdom of God.

The holiness of the church must be rightly understood. The basic meaning of holy is "different" or "separate". Since the Church is the body of Christ, and Christ is pure and blameless and was set apart for a purpose, so is the Church. To confess that the church is holy does not mean that its members are morally superior to other people; the church is holy because its members are called by God to live unselfish, pure and consecrated lives. The syllabus gives three ways in which the church is holy. It is a community of people who know they are sinners and freely admit that they are not good or superior - as Charles C. Morrison says, the church is not a society of good people but a society of sinners. It is a community of people not satisfied with themselves or with the way things are around them, gathered to admit that they need forgiveness and want to change. And it is a community gathered in the name of Jesus Christ who is its Head; the body is holy only because the Head is the Holy One.

The word catholic is probably derived from the Greek adverbial phrase kath' holou, which means "on the whole". Hence the Catholic Church means the Universal Church: it consists of all people throughout the world - races, nationalities, cultures, ethnic groups, social status and gender - who believe in Jesus Christ as Saviour and Lord. Though the word is not used in the New Testament, its meaning is expressed in Galatians 3:28 and Ephesians 4:4-6.
keyPoints: The New Testament church was richly diverse, but common elements are the marks of a true church
It accepts the full teachings of the faith - faith in Jesus as Messiah and Lord
It maintains continuity with Christians of the past and follows the apostolic preaching and instruction
It celebrates Baptism and Holy Communion, and its members follow the standard of life set by Christ
Its members live in constant expectation of the coming kingdom of God
Holy means 'different' or 'separate'; the church is not morally superior but called to consecrated lives
Three ways the church is holy: a society of sinners (Morrison), a community dissatisfied with itself, a community gathered in the name of Christ its Head
Catholic derives from kath' holou, 'on the whole'; the Catholic Church is the Universal Church of all who believe

subject: DOC
chapter: THE DOCTRINE OF THE LAST THINGS (ESCHATOLOGY)
question: Explain why the return of Christ is described as a practical doctrine and not merely an escape route for wishful thoughts.
idealAnswer:
The return of Christ occupies a prominent place in the Old Testament, in that most Old Testament prophecies concerning the coming of Christ deal not with the first advent, in which he died as our sin-bearer, but with his Second Advent, in which he is to rule as king. In the New Testament one verse in twenty-five deals with the Lord's return; the subject is mentioned 318 times in the 260 chapters, and it appears in every New Testament book except Galatians and the very short books such as 2 and 3 John and Philemon. Paul called the return of Jesus Christ "our blessed hope", and Peter called it our "living hope".

The syllabus insists that this is a practical doctrine and not merely an escape route for wishful thoughts. The early Christians expressed their belief in Jesus' personal return, a return closely associated with a period of great wickedness on earth, with the resurrection and transformation of their own bodies, with an earthly rule of the glorified Jesus, and with a final judgment of individuals and nations.

First, the early Christians acknowledged that their lives should be lived differently because of the return of Jesus. If we are expecting the Lord's return, that conviction ought to be seen in how we deal with social, political, economic, cultural and all other issues of concern. If we are motivated by prejudice, injustice, hatred, corruption, sexual immorality, abuse in all its forms, tearing down other people or wasting our gifts, then the return of Jesus has not made its proper impression on our thinking.

Secondly, it comforts those who are suffering. It helped the early Christians: as they suffered persecution and imprisonment, entered the arena to face the lions, or faced their executioner, they looked for Christ's coming and thought that perhaps in an instant Jesus would appear and call them home. Believers today have also lost children, parents and friends, and belief in the return of Jesus comforts them; the people of Paul's day had lost friends through death, and he reminded them of this blessed hope, saying "Therefore comfort one another with these words". The return of Christ is thus a practical doctrine because it is an encouragement to godly living and, at times, even to go on living, so that it bears upon present history as well as upon history's end.
keyPoints: Most Old Testament prophecies of Christ's coming deal with his Second Advent, in which he rules as king
One verse in twenty-five in the New Testament deals with the Lord's return; 318 times in 260 chapters
It is mentioned in every New Testament book except Galatians and the very short books
Paul called it 'our blessed hope'; Peter called it our 'living hope'
The early Church associated the return with great wickedness, resurrection and transformation of bodies, an earthly rule of the glorified Jesus, and a final judgment
It is an encouragement to godly living: our conviction should be seen in our social, political, economic and cultural dealings
It comforts those who are suffering, as it comforted the persecuted early Christians
It comforts the bereaved: 'Therefore comfort one another with these words'

subject: LIT
question: What is an Expository sermon? Examine the advantages of an Expository sermon.
idealAnswer: Preachers who preach expository sermons select a paragraph of Scripture, discover the theme from the passage and develop it point by point using evidence from the chosen paragraphs. Here the preacher uses the sermon to expose what the meaning of the Scripture is. When preaching expository sermons one needs to study the passage until its insight is clear to him or her, and allow the content of the passage, and the background surrounding it, to determine its treatment. The expository sermon, like the textual sermon, takes its subject and main points from a particular text, but unlike the textual sermon it also takes its sub-points from the immediate text; references to other texts may occur, but they are used only to support, elaborate or confirm what is already evident in the immediate text. A sermon is not expository merely because it addresses a subject in the Bible or because it cites numerous Scriptures: the true expository sermon discloses the thoughts of the author, covers the range of the passage, and applies its truths to the lives of the listeners. The advantages of expository preaching are several. The main advantage is that it gives the hope of possibly covering the entire Bible, for an expositor who does not pick and choose favourite passages but expounds the Bible bit by bit in a sequential order may hopefully cover the whole Bible in a given period of time, no matter how long it takes. Secondly, the preacher will always have a sermon subject to preach on; very few preachers have preached through the entire Bible in their lifetime or with one congregation, and those who finish with the same congregation will find many new faces have come in, so they can start all over again. Thirdly, expository preaching focuses the hearer's attention on the Scripture as the source of authority and teaching. Fourthly, the preacher does not expound just a great book, a poem, a political passage, or his personal opinion; rather he or she concentrates on the authoritative word of God. Finally, the expository sermon demands integrity on the part of the preacher.

subject: LIT
question: Define a sermon and explain what the following words mean when used to describe a sermon: prophetic, kerygmatic, didactic, and therapeutic.
idealAnswer: Preaching the sermon is essentially telling the Good News to people; this Good News is about God, or from God. A sermon is therefore not a personal view about current events, whether social or political, nor even about current theological issues, but the word of God as contained in the Scriptures, delivered with the aim of bringing home its saving and liberating truth to the hearers and enabling them to understand that truth in relation to their lives. This is not accomplished by the preacher but by the Holy Spirit, who uses the preacher as an agent to bring the truth to the people. Bernard Manning sees preaching the sermon as a “manifestation of the Incarnate Word, from the written word, by the spoken word”, while Bultmann defines preaching as “the communication of Biblical truth by man to man with the explicit purpose of eliciting behavioural change”. Unlike an address, a sermon is geared towards eliciting behavioural change and is thus aligned with decision-making. Four words are used to describe the sermon. It is prophetic in that preaching should point out what things are wrong and how to remedy them, and is further aimed at teaching those who do not know the way of God to know it. It is kerygmatic in that its purpose is the proclaiming of the Gospel. It is didactic in that its purpose is teaching. And it is therapeutic in that it is aimed at healing the broken spirit and the broken society. These purposes together show why the uniqueness of sermons calls for a distinctive way of preparation, and why the preacher, who preaches best with his lifestyle, must be an imitator of Christ, a person of deep piety and affection for others.
