subject: LIT
question: What is prayer? Discuss the content of a prayer.
idealAnswer: Prayer is a conversation or communication with God. It is the means by which we link up our souls with the Spirit of God and convey our heart's desires and concerns to Him. Real prayer is expressing our devotion to our heavenly Father and inviting Him to talk to us as we talk to Him. It is the intercourse of the soul with God, not only in contemplation or meditation but also in direct address to Him, and it may be oral or mental, occasional or constant, extempore or formal. Throughout the Bible prayer is described variously as calling upon the name of the Lord, beseeching the Lord, pouring out the soul before the Lord, crying to heaven, seeking unto God and making supplication, drawing near to God and approaching God's throne of grace. Although prayer cannot be reduced to a mere formula, there are certain basic elements that should be included in our communication with God; this formula is popularly known as CATS or ACTS — Adoration, Confession, Thanksgiving and Supplication. To adore God is to worship and praise Him, to honour and exalt Him in our heart and mind and with our lips; we need not begin our prayer by placing a tall list of requests before God, for prayer is interaction with God and not a presentation of requests, and adoration should be the entry point of our prayer. When our discipline of prayer begins with adoration, the Holy Spirit has opportunity to reveal any sin in our life that needs to be confessed; confession of sins must be sincere and specific, and must culminate in repentance and change. Thanksgiving is the expression of gratitude or appreciation to God, for who He is and for the benefits we enjoy because we belong to Him; it enables us to recognise that He controls all things, not just the blessings but the problems and adversities as well. Supplication includes petition for our own needs and intercession for others. Petition is asking God for personal things in prayer, while intercession is prayer for others — for our families, neighbours, those in authority and the nation, and for the salvation of souls. For the preacher, intercession is an integral part of the ministry, for a preacher who does not pray for those he or she preaches to has an incomplete and unfulfilled ministry.

Supplication: petition for our own needs and intercession for others
Intercession is an integral part of the preacher's ministry

subject: LIT
chapter: THE METHODIST SUNDAY MORNING ORDER OF SERVICE
question: Outline the new order for Sunday Morning Worship of the Methodist Church Ghana and examine its relevance.
idealAnswer: The outline of the new order for Sunday Morning Worship of the Methodist Church Ghana runs as follows: Call to Worship; Introit; Hymn; Prayer; Hymn or Lyric; The Ministry of the Word; The Old Testament; The Epistle; Te Deum; The Gospel Reading; Affirmation of Faith; Hymn; Sermon; Invitation to Christian Discipleship; Announcements; Tithes and Offertory; Hymn; and Benediction and Dismissal. Its relevance may be examined item by item. The Call to Worship is a way of calling the congregation's attention to the fact that the service is about to begin, after which the Choir, Singing Band and Clergy process; where the procession comes first, the liturgist may join the call to worship and welcome as one item after the introit. The Introit is sung in preparation for the continuation of the worship service after the procession by the choir. The Affirmation of Faith acts as a yardstick of correct belief, the Apostles' Creed being said on ordinary occasions and the Nicene Creed on Communion Sundays, Christmas, Easter and other special days, and by it Methodists affirm the doctrine of the Trinity. The place given to Lyrics helps to control the spontaneous singing of lyrics, while still allowing the preacher to accept those that are relevant to the sermon. The Response and Dedication, or altar call, is where people give or rededicate their lives to Christ, or seek corporate assistance in prayer, in response to the Word preached, and is the appropriate time for ministry in healing, deliverance or the gifts of the Spirit, and for testimony sharing. The Dismissal with Blessing belongs to the clergy, and whenever a minister is present the local preacher must give him or her the first option to pronounce the benediction. Above all, the order of service is mainly a guideline: it is there to guide us in the conduct of worship but not to pin us down, and there should always be reasonable and cautious flexibility. The Te Deum, for instance, may be varied with other canticles, a shorter canticle being sung where time must be saved, though some canticles are occasion specific — it is always appropriate to sing the Magnificat during Christmas.

subject: LIT
question: What is Pentecost? Examine the importance of Pentecost Sunday on the Church's Calendar.
idealAnswer: In Judaism, Pentecost was a harvest festival which was also known as the Feast of Weeks and the Feast of First Fruits. The descent of the Holy Spirit recorded in the Book of Acts took place at the Jewish Pentecost, and this made Christians fix their celebration of the pouring down of the Holy Spirit on the fiftieth day after Easter, that is, the seventh Sunday after Easter. It was a day of universal rejoicing, and as Tertullian records, “we spent our time in all exaltation”. The importance of Pentecost Sunday on the Church's calendar may be seen in several ways. St. Athanasius calls it “Magna Dominica”, the “Great Sunday”, and consequently neither fasting nor kneeling was allowed during its celebration. Pentecost Sunday is also called White Sunday or Whitsunday, possibly in reference to the white robes worn by catechumens and others who were baptised on that day; an alternative derivation is from the word “wit” or “wisdom”, which implies that it was the day the Apostles were filled with wisdom from God by the Holy Spirit. The sanctuary colour of Pentecost Sunday is red, the colour of the Church. The red symbolises the Fire of Pentecost as well as that of the Apostles and other disciples of Jesus who were gathered in the Upper Room for the empowerment from God to preach the gospel to other nations.

subject: LIT
question: Discuss a Textual Sermon and its advantages.
idealAnswer: In textual sermons the preacher takes a few verses, a verse, or even a part of a verse from the Bible. The preacher discovers the theme of the verse in context and preaches on it in his own words. In the textual sermon both the subject and the main points are based on ideas in the text, but, unlike the expository sermon, the development of the main ideas comes from sources outside of the immediate text. This sermon looks to the text to bring out the meaning, and uses the “hook-book-look-and-took” method: something is used to hook the audience, such as an interesting story that would bring people to think about the sermon; the book is turning to the Scripture; look discusses what that Scripture is saying; and the took is what each person should take away from the sermon. It is almost a combination of the narrative and expository sermons. A textual sermon is generally good for preaching to audiences with short attention spans such as children and the elderly, for preaching at occasions other than church services such as banquets and funerals, and for preaching series on “Great Bible Texts” or “Favourite Bible Verses”. Its advantages are these. First, a textual sermon is a great technique for bringing the actual words of the Bible before the hearers, giving Divine authority to the message. Secondly, since the text is short it will be easier to remember or memorise, so the preacher can easily make constant reference to the text many times during the sermon. Thirdly, the preacher who employs the textual method deals with distinctively Scriptural themes that come right out of the text, so that a well-constructed textual sermon is much more intimately in contact with the text, drawing from it not only the subject treated but all the leading thoughts of the treatment. Finally, it gives ample opportunity for variety, freshness and originality.

The theme of the verse is discovered in context and preached in the preacher's own words
Subject and main points come from ideas in the text, but development of the main ideas comes from sources outside the immediate text
It uses the hook-book-look-and-took method and is almost a combination of narrative and expository sermons
Good for audiences with short attention spans, for occasions other than church services, and for “Great Bible Texts” series

subject: LIT
question: What is an Expository sermon? Examine the advantages of an Expository Sermon.
idealAnswer: Preachers who preach expository sermons select a paragraph of Scripture, discover the theme from the passage and develop it point by point using evidence from the chosen paragraphs. Here the preacher uses the sermon to expose what the meaning of the Scripture is. When preaching expository sermons one needs to study the passage until its insight is clear to him or her, and allow the content of the passage, and the background surrounding it, to determine its treatment. The expository sermon, like the textual sermon, takes its subject and main points from a particular text, but unlike the textual sermon it also takes its sub-points from the immediate text; references to other texts may occur, but they are used only to support, elaborate or confirm what is already evident in the immediate text. A sermon is not expository merely because it addresses a subject in the Bible or because it cites numerous Scriptures: the true expository sermon discloses the thoughts of the author, covers the range of the passage, and applies its truths to the lives of the listeners. The advantages of expository preaching are several. The main advantage is that it gives the hope of possibly covering the entire Bible, for an expositor who does not pick and choose favourite passages but expounds the Bible bit by bit in a sequential order may hopefully cover the whole Bible in a given period of time, no matter how long it takes. Secondly, the preacher will always have a sermon subject to preach on; very few preachers have preached through the entire Bible in their lifetime or with one congregation, and those who finish with the same congregation will find many new faces have come in, so they can start all over again. Thirdly, expository preaching focuses the hearer's attention on the Scripture as the source of authority and teaching. Fourthly, the preacher does not expound just a great book, a poem, a political passage, or his personal opinion; rather he or she concentrates on the authoritative word of God. Finally, the expository sermon demands integrity on the part of the preacher.

Advantage: the expository sermon demands integrity on the part of the preacher

question: What is a creed? Write short notes on the Apostle's Creed.
idealAnswer: A creed is a statement of faith. The purpose of a creed is to act as a yardstick of correct belief. The creeds of Christianity have been drawn up at times of conflict about doctrine, and the acceptance or rejection of a creed serves to distinguish believers and deniers of a particular doctrine or set of doctrines. For that reason a creed was called in Greek a sumbolon, meaning half of a broken object which, when placed together with the other half, verified the bearer's identity; the Greek word passed through the Latin symbolum into the English symbol, which later took on the meaning of an outward sign of something. Creeds, as statements of faith, confirm the faithful in their faith, thus strengthening their corporate unity, and they should endorse what is at the core of the Christian faith as well as of the life of the wider community whose vicissitudes raise questions for the believer. The Apostles' Creed and the Nicene Creed are the ones commonly used among Ghanaian Methodists in affirming our faith, the Apostles' Creed being said on ordinary occasions and the Nicene Creed on Communion Sundays, Christmas, Easter and other special days. The Apostles' Creed is the basic creed of the Reformed churches. It is a statement of Christian belief and is widely used by a number of Christian denominations for both liturgical and catechetical purposes. It appears to have been originally formulated as a refutation of Gnosticism, an early heresy, and this can be seen in almost every phrase: for example, the creed states that Christ Jesus was born, suffered and died on the cross, which is a statement directly against the heretical teaching that Christ only appeared to become man and did not truly suffer and die but only appeared to do so. The Apostles' Creed, as well as other baptismal creeds, is esteemed as an example of the apostles' teachings and a defence of the Gospel of Christ. It does not, however, address some Christological issues defined in the Nicene and other Christian creeds; it thus says nothing explicitly about the divinity of either Jesus or of the Holy Spirit.

subject: LIT
question: What is prayer? Discuss the content of a prayer.
idealAnswer: Prayer is a conversation or communication with God. It is the means by which we link up our souls with the Spirit of God and convey our heart's desires and concerns to Him. Real prayer is expressing our devotion to our heavenly Father and inviting Him to talk to us as we talk to Him. It is the intercourse of the soul with God, not only in contemplation or meditation but also in direct address to Him, and it may be oral or mental, occasional or constant, extempore or formal. Throughout the Bible prayer is described variously as calling upon the name of the Lord, beseeching the Lord, pouring out the soul before the Lord, crying to heaven, seeking unto God and making supplication, drawing near to God and approaching God's throne of grace. Although prayer cannot be reduced to a mere formula, there are certain basic elements that should be included in our communication with God; this formula is popularly known as CATS or ACTS — Adoration, Confession, Thanksgiving and Supplication. To adore God is to worship and praise Him, to honour and exalt Him in our heart and mind and with our lips; we need not begin our prayer by placing a tall list of requests before God, for prayer is interaction with God and not a presentation of requests, and adoration should be the entry point of our prayer. When our discipline of prayer begins with adoration, the Holy Spirit has opportunity to reveal any sin in our life that needs to be confessed; confession of sins must be sincere and specific, and must culminate in repentance and change. Thanksgiving is the expression of gratitude or appreciation to God, for who He is and for the benefits we enjoy because we belong to Him; it enables us to recognise that He controls all things, not just the blessings but the problems and adversities as well. Supplication includes petition for our own needs and intercession for others. Petition is asking God for personal things in prayer, while intercession is prayer for others — for our families, neighbours, those in authority and the nation, and for the salvation of souls. For the preacher, intercession is an integral part of the ministry, for a preacher who does not pray for those he or she preaches to has an incomplete and unfulfilled ministry.

question: Outline the new order for Sunday Morning Worship of the Methodist Church Ghana and mention three relevance of the order.
idealAnswer: The outline of the new order for Sunday Morning Worship of the Methodist Church Ghana runs as follows: Call to Worship; Introit; Hymn; Prayer; Hymn or Lyric; The Ministry of the Word; The Old Testament; The Epistle; Te Deum; The Gospel Reading; Affirmation of Faith; Hymn; Sermon; Invitation to Christian Discipleship; Announcements; Tithes and Offertory; Hymn; and Benediction and Dismissal. Three points of relevance may be mentioned. First, the order is mainly a guideline: it is there to guide us in the conduct of worship but not to pin us down, so that there should always be reasonable and cautious flexibility — the Te Deum, for instance, may be varied with other canticles, and where time must be saved a shorter canticle such as Canticle 6 may be sung, though some canticles are occasion specific and it is always appropriate to sing the Magnificat during Christmas. Secondly, particular items carry a particular purpose: the Call to Worship calls the congregation's attention to the fact that the service is about to begin, after which the Choir, Singing Band and Clergy process, while the Introit is sung in preparation for the continuation of the worship service after the procession; and the Affirmation of Faith acts as a yardstick of correct belief, the Apostles' Creed being said on ordinary occasions and the Nicene Creed on Communion Sundays, Christmas, Easter and other special days. Thirdly, the new order gives a specific place to items which had previously been spontaneous or neglected: it provides a specific place for lyrics, which helps to control the spontaneous ones while allowing those relevant to the sermon; and it makes room for the Response and Dedication, the altar call at which people give or rededicate their lives to Christ or seek corporate assistance in prayer in response to the Word preached, and the appropriate time for ministry in healing, deliverance and the gifts of the Spirit and for testimony sharing. Finally, the Dismissal with Blessing belongs to the clergy, and whenever a minister is present the local preacher must give him or her the first option to pronounce the benediction.

subject: LIT
question: What is Pentecost? Examine the importance of Pentecost Sunday on the Church's Calendar.
idealAnswer: In Judaism, Pentecost was a harvest festival which was also known as the Feast of Weeks and the Feast of First Fruits. The descent of the Holy Spirit recorded in the Book of Acts took place at the Jewish Pentecost, and this made Christians fix their celebration of the pouring down of the Holy Spirit on the fiftieth day after Easter, that is, the seventh Sunday after Easter. It was a day of universal rejoicing, and as Tertullian records, “we spent our time in all exaltation”. The importance of Pentecost Sunday on the Church's calendar may be seen in several ways. St. Athanasius calls it “Magna Dominica”, the “Great Sunday”, and consequently neither fasting nor kneeling was allowed during its celebration. Pentecost Sunday is also called White Sunday or Whitsunday, possibly in reference to the white robes worn by catechumens and others who were baptised on that day; an alternative derivation is from the word “wit” or “wisdom”, which implies that it was the day the Apostles were filled with wisdom from God by the Holy Spirit. The sanctuary colour of Pentecost Sunday is red, the colour of the Church. The red symbolises the Fire of Pentecost as well as that of the Apostles and other disciples of Jesus who were gathered in the Upper Room for the empowerment from God to preach the gospel to other nations.

subject: LIT
question: Discuss the Manners that affect sermon delivery.
idealAnswer: After all the spiritual and physical preparation needed in the work of the preacher, one of the important tasks is how to deliver the sermon, for a preacher may write a very good sermon while the effectiveness or the achievement of the desired end of changing lives is largely determined by the delivery. The issues that affect sermon delivery include the appearance of the preacher and his or her body language, and other manners such as the tone of the preacher and his eye contact. As to appearance, the preacher's appearance has a major impact on the congregation, and the dressing must be decent; while modesty is necessary, it is not good to go to the pulpit shabbily dressed in the name of modesty, and depending on the social status of the congregation the dressing should be generally acceptable and neither offensive nor expensive. The preacher must avoid dresses that draw attention to the preacher rather than the message, and must look cheerful, healthy and fit. As to posture, the preacher must be mindful of how he or she carries himself in the pulpit: be yourself and imitate no one except Christ, be natural in voice and style, and do not put your hands in your pocket or on your waist, for it carries a wrong impression; the preacher should preach with passion, since a passionate preacher is more likely to make a positive impact than one emotionally detached from the message. As to gesture, the preacher may motion the hands, the head and other parts of the body to express or stress points, but this should be done with care; a microphone should be held in the left hand so that the right may be used to stress points, remembering that in some cultural settings using the left hand to talk to people is not acceptable, and the preacher should not be glued to words like Praise the Lord, Halleluiah and Amen just for the sake of it. As to tone, the preacher must check the tone of the voice and of the message; the gospel is a message of joy and happiness and the preacher must not sound too gloomy even when preaching on sin and repentance, and while some points may need a loud voice, it should not be the preacher's habit to shout — one should be heard without shouting, speaking clearly and confidently. The preacher must also involve the congregation, chiefly by calculated eye contact, consciously looking round to all corners of the chapel, and by verbally involving the people, leaving the ends of some quotations to be completed by them; notes may be consulted but staying too glued to them detaches the preacher from the people, and since the average listening capacity spans between ten and twenty-five minutes the preacher must be mindful of time. Finally, the preacher must know how to end the sermon: ending does not necessarily mean reaching the written conclusion or saying everything in the notes, and the preacher should be sensitive to the Holy Spirit, the time spent, the mood of the listeners and whether the peak of delivery has been reached — the peak being the point where anything more said brings down the excitement and joy of the listeners — and when these signs show, raise a song, repeat the text or theme, say a prayer and end there.

subject: LIT
question: What is an Expository sermon? Examine the advantages and disadvantages of expository sermon.
idealAnswer: Preachers who preach expository sermons select a paragraph of Scripture, discover the theme from the passage and develop it point by point using evidence from the chosen paragraphs. Here the preacher uses the sermon to expose what the meaning of the Scripture is, studying the passage until its insight is clear and allowing the content of the passage, and the background surrounding it, to determine its treatment. Like the textual sermon it takes its subject and main points from a particular text, but unlike the textual sermon it also takes its sub-points from the immediate text; references to other texts are used only to support, elaborate or confirm what is already evident there. The advantages are these. The main advantage is that it gives the hope of possibly covering the entire Bible, for an expositor who does not pick and choose favourite passages but expounds the Bible bit by bit in sequential order may hopefully cover the whole Bible in a given period of time. Secondly, the preacher will always have a sermon subject to preach on. Thirdly, expository preaching focuses the hearer's attention on the Scripture as the source of authority and teaching. Fourthly, the preacher does not expound just a great book, a poem, a political passage or his personal opinion, but concentrates on the authoritative word of God. Finally, the expository sermon demands integrity on the part of the preacher. The disadvantages are equally clear. The main disadvantage is that expository preaching covers many topics and necessitates often lengthy diversions into other passages for clarification; it does not allow for detailed coverage of a particular topic when only a specific text is covered, so that in order to address the context and content properly the preacher does become topical. Secondly, the expository sermon is a time-consuming task, and most expository preachers will never cover the entire Bible in their lifetime. Thirdly, Exegesis — the art of critically analysing or interpreting the passage, which must be done honestly — may give way to Eisegesis, the “art” of reading preconceived opinions into the text, so that the preacher forces out of the passage what he already wants to say. Finally, the expositor may wander from the text, departing from true exposition, stretching and straining it to draw lessons it was never intended to teach; thus, instead of exposing the passage, the preacher may rather exploit it. A further danger is that the expositor may fail to proceed from interpretation to application and so end up producing an expository lesson, which aims only at the mind, instead of an expository sermon, which also seeks to change the behaviour of the listeners.

Sub-points as well as subject and main points come from the immediate text
Advantage: hope of possibly covering the entire Bible by expounding it bit by bit in sequential order

Advantage: the preacher will always have a sermon subject; it focuses attention on Scripture as the source of authority; it concentrates on the authoritative word of God; it demands integrity of the preacher
Disadvantage: it covers many topics and necessitates lengthy diversions into other passages, without detailed coverage of a topic
Disadvantage: it is time-consuming, and most expository preachers never cover the entire Bible in a lifetime
Disadvantage: Exegesis may give way to Eisegesis, reading preconceived opinions into the text
Disadvantage: the expositor may wander from the text and exploit rather than expose the passage, or produce an expository lesson instead of a sermon

subject: LIT
question: Define a sermon and explain what the following words mean when used to describe a sermon: prophetic, kerygmatic, didactic, and therapeutic.
idealAnswer: Preaching the sermon is essentially telling the Good News to people; this Good News is about God, or from God. A sermon is therefore not a personal view about current events, whether social or political, nor even about current theological issues, but the word of God as contained in the Scriptures, delivered with the aim of bringing home its saving and liberating truth to the hearers and enabling them to understand that truth in relation to their lives. This is not accomplished by the preacher but by the Holy Spirit, who uses the preacher as an agent to bring the truth to the people. Bernard Manning sees preaching the sermon as a “manifestation of the Incarnate Word, from the written word, by the spoken word”, while Bultmann defines preaching as “the communication of Biblical truth by man to man with the explicit purpose of eliciting behavioural change”. Unlike an address, a sermon is geared towards eliciting behavioural change and is thus aligned with decision-making. Four words describe the sermon. It is prophetic in that preaching should point out what things are wrong and how to remedy them, and is further aimed at teaching those who do not know the way of God to know it. It is kerygmatic in that its purpose is the proclaiming of the Gospel. It is didactic in that its purpose is teaching. And it is therapeutic in that it is aimed at healing the broken spirit and the broken society. These purposes together show why the uniqueness of sermons calls for a distinctive way of preparation, and why the preacher, who preaches best with his lifestyle, must be an imitator of Christ.

Unlike an address, a sermon is geared towards eliciting behavioural change and is aligned with decision-making

Therapeutic: aimed at healing the broken spirit and the broken society

subject: LIT
question: What is prayer? Discuss the content of a prayer.
idealAnswer: Prayer is a conversation or communication with God. It is the means by which we link up our souls with the Spirit of God and convey our heart's desires and concerns to Him. Real prayer is expressing our devotion to our heavenly Father and inviting Him to talk to us as we talk to Him. It is the intercourse of the soul with God, not only in contemplation or meditation but also in direct address to Him, and it may be oral or mental, occasional or constant, extempore or formal. Throughout the Bible prayer is described variously as calling upon the name of the Lord, beseeching the Lord, pouring out the soul before the Lord, crying to heaven, seeking unto God and making supplication, and approaching God's throne of grace. Although prayer cannot be reduced to a mere formula, there are certain basic elements that should be included in our communication with God; this formula is popularly known as CATS or ACTS — Adoration, Confession, Thanksgiving and Supplication. To adore God is to worship and praise Him, to honour and exalt Him in our heart and mind and with our lips; we need not begin our prayer by placing a tall list of requests before God, for prayer is interaction with God and not a presentation of requests, and adoration should be the entry point of our prayer. When our discipline of prayer begins with adoration, the Holy Spirit has opportunity to reveal any sin in our life that needs to be confessed; confession of sins must be sincere and specific, and must culminate in repentance and change. Thanksgiving is the expression of gratitude or appreciation to God for who He is and for the benefits we enjoy because we belong to Him; Psalm 136 makes a tall list of what we must thank God for, because His mercy endures forever. Supplication includes petition for our own needs and intercession for others: petition is asking God for personal things in prayer, while intercession is prayer for others — for family, neighbours, those in authority and the nation, and for the salvation of souls. For the preacher, intercession is an integral part of the ministry, for a preacher who does not pray for those he or she preaches to has an incomplete and unfulfilled ministry.

subject: LIT
chapter: THE METHODIST SUNDAY MORNING ORDER OF SERVICE
question: Outline the new order for Sunday Morning Worship of the Methodist Church Ghana and examine its relevance.
idealAnswer: The outline of the new order for Sunday Morning Worship of the Methodist Church Ghana runs as follows: Call to Worship; Introit; Hymn; Prayer; Hymn or Lyric; The Ministry of the Word; The Old Testament; The Epistle; Te Deum; The Gospel Reading; Affirmation of Faith; Hymn; Sermon; Invitation to Christian Discipleship; Announcements; Tithes and Offertory; Hymn; and Benediction and Dismissal. Its relevance may be examined item by item. The Call to Worship is a way of calling the congregation's attention to the fact that the service is about to begin, after which the Choir, Singing Band and Clergy process; where the procession comes first, the liturgist may join the call to worship and welcome as one item after the introit. The Introit is sung in preparation for the continuation of the worship service after the procession by the choir. The Affirmation of Faith acts as a yardstick of correct belief, the Apostles' Creed being said on ordinary occasions and the Nicene Creed on Communion Sundays, Christmas, Easter and other special days, and by it Methodists affirm the doctrine of the Trinity. The place given to Lyrics helps to control the spontaneous singing of lyrics, while still allowing the preacher to accept those that are relevant to the sermon. The Response and Dedication, or altar call, is where people give or rededicate their lives to Christ, or seek corporate assistance in prayer, in response to the Word that has been preached, and is the appropriate time for ministry in healing, deliverance or the gifts of the Spirit, and for testimony sharing. The Dismissal with Blessing belongs to the clergy, and whenever a minister is present the local preacher must give him or her the first option to pronounce the benediction. Above all, the order of service is mainly a guideline: it is there to guide us in the conduct of worship but not to pin us down, and there should always be reasonable and cautious flexibility. The Te Deum, for instance, may be varied with other canticles, and a shorter canticle such as Canticle 6 may be sung where time must be saved, though some canticles are occasion specific — it is always appropriate to sing the Magnificat during Christmas.

subject: LIT
question: What is Pentecost? Examine the importance of Pentecost Sunday on the Church's Calendar.
idealAnswer: In Judaism, Pentecost was a harvest festival which was also known as the Feast of Weeks and the Feast of First Fruits. The descent of the Holy Spirit recorded in the Book of Acts took place at the Jewish Pentecost, and this made Christians fix their celebration of the pouring down of the Holy Spirit on the fiftieth day after Easter, that is, the seventh Sunday after Easter. It was a day of universal rejoicing, and as Tertullian records, “we spent our time in all exaltation”. The importance of Pentecost Sunday on the Church's calendar may be seen in several ways. St. Athanasius calls it “Magna Dominica”, the “Great Sunday”, and consequently neither fasting nor kneeling was allowed during its celebration. Pentecost Sunday is also called White Sunday or Whitsunday, possibly in reference to the white robes worn by catechumens and others who were baptised on that day; an alternative derivation is from the word “wit” or “wisdom”, which implies that it was the day the Apostles were filled with wisdom from God by the Holy Spirit. The sanctuary colour of Pentecost Sunday is red, the colour of the Church. The red symbolises the Fire of Pentecost as well as that of the Apostles and other disciples of Jesus who were gathered in the Upper Room for the empowerment from God to preach the gospel to other nations.
keyPoints: In Judaism Pentecost was a harvest festival, also known as the Feast of Weeks and the Feast of First Fruits
The descent of the Holy Spirit in Acts took place at the Jewish Pentecost

subject: LIT
question: Discuss a Textual Sermon and its advantages.
idealAnswer: In textual sermons the preacher takes a few verses, a verse, or even a part of a verse from the Bible. The preacher discovers the theme of the verse in context and preaches on it in his own words. In the textual sermon both the subject and the main points are based on ideas in the text, but, unlike the expository sermon, the development of the main ideas comes from sources outside of the immediate text. This sermon looks to the text to bring out the meaning, and uses the “hook-book-look-and-took” method: something is used to hook the audience, such as an interesting story; the book is turning to the Scripture; look discusses what that Scripture is saying; and the took is what each person should take away from the sermon. It is almost a combination of the narrative and expository sermons. A textual sermon is generally good for preaching to audiences with short attention spans such as children and the elderly, for preaching at occasions other than church services such as banquets and funerals, and for preaching series on “Great Bible Texts” or “Favourite Bible Verses”. Its advantages are these. First, a textual sermon is a great technique for bringing the actual words of the Bible before the hearers, giving Divine authority to the message. Secondly, since the text is short it will be easier to remember or memorise, so the preacher can easily make constant reference to the text many times during the sermon. Thirdly, the preacher who employs the textual method deals with distinctively Scriptural themes that come right out of the text, so that a well-constructed textual sermon is much more intimately in contact with the text, drawing from it not only the subject treated but all the leading thoughts of the treatment. Finally, it gives ample opportunity for variety, freshness and originality.
keyPoints: The preacher takes a few verses, a verse, or even part of a verse from the Bible
The theme of the verse is discovered in context and preached in the preacher's own words
Subject and main points come from ideas in the text, but development of the main ideas comes from outside the immediate text
It uses the hook-book-look-and-took method and is almost a combination of narrative and expository sermons
Good for audiences with short attention spans, occasions other than church services, and “Great Bible Texts” series
Advantage: it brings the actual words of the Bible before the hearers, giving Divine authority to the message
Advantage: the short text is easier to remember or memorise and can be constantly referred to
Advantage: it deals with distinctively Scriptural themes drawn from the text, and gives ample opportunity for variety, freshness and originality

subject: LIT
question: Which of the following is given as an advantage of topical sermons?

question: Which of the following is listed as a disadvantage of topical sermons?

subject: LIT
question: Which three elements should the preacher attend to when studying a passage for an expository sermon?

question: What does the syllabus give as the main advantage of expository preaching?

question: What is eisegesis, which the syllabus warns may displace exegesis in expository preaching?

Exegesis (the art of critically analyzing or interpreting the passage, which must be done honestly) may give way to Eisegesis (the "art" of reading preconceived

the

manualReference.citation: Liturgics — SERMON PREPARATION AND DELIVERY — Tone (syllabus ¶3875)

question: What does the syllabus give as the average listening capacity of any human being?

options.text: Between ten and twenty five minutes

The syllabus gives a shorter span.

question: When does the syllabus say is the most appropriate time to select the hymns for a service?

subject: LIT
chapter: GENERAL INTRODUCTION TO THE LITURGY OF THE WORD
question: Explain the term "the preliminaries" and describe the four items of which they consist in the liturgy of the word.
idealAnswer: The sentences are scriptural passages selected to be read to the congregation at worship services. Apart from preparing the congregation for a take off in the service, they remind the worshipper of the sins which need to be confessed and of God's readiness to forgive them, and so they are not to be read for the sake of it but in a manner that appeals to the heart of the listener. Dating from the late seventh century, the readings were preceded by four distinct items, and it is these four which are known as the preliminaries: the Introit, the Kyries, the Gloria and the Collect. The Introit takes its name from the Latin introitus, meaning entry or entrance. It is a hymn or psalm sung when the ministers enter at the opening of a service, a chant which accompanied the advance of the priest to the altar. It was originally a psalm sung alternately with its antiphon, and it dates, according to older liturgists, from the fifth century and Pope Celestine 1. Sung by the choir, it announces the mystery and feast solemnized, and it also covered the entrance of the ministers, which at a solemn papal mass in a large basilica would take some time. The Kyries stand for Invocation in Greek and mean 'Lord have mercy'. Found in the Old Testament and the Gospels, they entered the liturgy late, first in the East, then in Rome in the fifth century and in Gaul in the sixth. They were the reply of the people to the litany of the deacon; Christe, eleison was later added, and in the ninth century a third series addressed to the Holy Spirit, so that the invocations became fixed at three of the Divine Person. The Gloria is an ancient hymn of praise to the Trinity, in use since the second century, whose opening line comes from Luke 2:14; it was introduced to the West by St. Hilary of Poitiers. Methodists sing it in its short form as a conclusion to canticles and psalms, in recognition of the tradition to which we belong and of the doctrine of the Trinity. The Collect, believed to have been introduced by Leo 1 or his immediate predecessor, is the prayer which gathers together the aspirations of the assembly and which the people make their own by the final Amen. Its form is an address to God, a clause referring to some attribute or saving act of God, the petition, the purpose for which we ask, and the conclusion.
keyPoints: The sentences are scriptural passages selected to be read to the congregation at worship

The Introit: from Latin introitus, entry or entrance; a hymn or psalm sung as the ministers enter
The Kyries: Invocation in Greek, "Lord have mercy", fixed at three invocations by the ninth century
The Gloria: an ancient hymn of praise to the Trinity, opening line from Luke 2:14
The Collect: introduced by Leo 1 or his predecessor; gathers the aspirations of the assembly
The five-fold form of the Collect: address, clause on an attribute of God, petition, purpose, conclusion

chapter: THE METHODIST SUNDAY MORNING ORDER OF SERVICE
topic: Outline Of The New Order For Sunday Morning Worship
question: Outline, in their proper sequence, the items of the New Order for Sunday Morning Worship of the Methodist Church Ghana.
idealAnswer: The New Order for Sunday Morning Worship begins with the Call to Worship, which calls the congregation's attention to the fact that the service is about to begin, and after which the choir, singing band and clergy process. This is followed by the Introit, then a Hymn, then Prayer, then a Hymn or Lyric. There follows the Ministry of the Word, which consists of the Old Testament reading, the Epistle, the Te Deum and the Gospel Reading. After the Gospel Reading comes the Affirmation of Faith, in which the Apostles' Creed is generally said on ordinary occasions and the Nicene Creed on Communion Sundays, Christmas, Easter and other special days. A Hymn follows, and then the Sermon. After the Sermon comes the Invitation to Christian Discipleship, then the Announcements, then the Tithes and Offertory, then a Hymn, and finally the Benediction and Dismissal. It should be noted that the order of service is mainly a guideline; it is there to guide us in the conduct of worship but not to pin us down, and there should always be reasonable and cautious flexibility. The Te Deum, for instance, can be varied with other canticles, and where time must be saved a shorter canticle such as Canticle 6 may be sung; some canticles are occasion specific, and it is always appropriate to sing the Magnificat during Christmas. Choruses and canticles play the same role of singing God's praise, and one may be used in place of the other for the sake of time. The Dismissal with Blessing belongs to the clergy, so that whenever a minister is present the local preacher must give him or her the first option to pronounce the benediction.

question: Discuss the place of the Affirmation of Faith in Methodist worship, distinguishing between the Apostles' Creed and the Nicene Creed.
idealAnswer: The purpose of a creed is to act as a yardstick of correct belief. The creeds of Christianity have been drawn up at times of conflict about doctrine, and the acceptance or rejection of a creed serves to distinguish believers and deniers of a particular doctrine or set of doctrines. For that reason a creed was called in Greek a sumbolon, meaning half of a broken object which, when placed together with the other half, verified the bearer's identity; the Greek word passed through the Latin symbolum into the English symbol, which later took on the meaning of an outward sign of something. In the Methodist Church Ghana the Apostles' Creed is generally said on ordinary occasions and the Nicene Creed on Communion Sundays, Christmas, Easter and other special days, and preachers and liturgists should also know the other new creeds that have been added and when they are appropriate. The Apostles' Creed is the basic creed of Reformed churches and a statement of Christian belief, widely used for both liturgical and catechetical purposes. It appears to have been originally formulated as a refutation of Gnosticism, an early heresy, as can be seen in almost every phrase: it states that Christ Jesus was born, suffered and died on the cross, against the heretical teaching that Christ only appeared to become man and did not truly suffer and die. It is esteemed as an example of the apostles' teachings and a defence of the Gospel of Christ, but it does not address some Christological issues defined in the Nicene and other creeds, and says nothing explicitly about the divinity of either Jesus or the Holy Spirit. The Nicene Creed is the profession of faith most widely used in Christian liturgy. It is called Nicene because in its original form it was adopted in the city of Nicaea in 325, in the face of the Arian controversy. Arius, a Libyan preacher, had declared that although Jesus Christ was divine, God had actually created him and there was a time when he was not, which made Jesus less than the Father and contradicted the doctrine of the Trinity. The Nicene Creed therefore explicitly affirms the divinity of Jesus, applying to him the term God, and speaks of the Holy Spirit as worshipped and glorified with the Father and the Son. As Methodists we recite the Nicene Creed to affirm that the doctrine of the Trinity, which makes the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit equally divine, is true. Creeds, as statements of faith, confirm the faithful in their faith and thus strengthen their corporate unity.

The Greek sumbolon: half of a broken object verifying identity

The Nicene Creed affirms the divinity of Jesus and of the Holy Spirit, and so the Trinity

subject: LIT
question: Outline the steps a Methodist preacher should follow in linking the three lessons to the theme in sermon preparation.
idealAnswer: The Methodist preacher normally has to deal with three lessons and a theme as given in the Almanac, and it is the task of the preacher to link these passages to the theme. Sermon preparation has different styles that call for different steps and procedures, and the steps recommended are not exhaustive but are deemed helpful. Step 1 is to read the passages over and over again, in different versions of the Bible including the local language, noting any translational differences that may enhance explanation and interpretation, and to meditate on the passages and the theme for some time. Step 2 is to write down your understanding of the three passages and the lessons in them, narrowing down to those lessons related to the theme. Step 3 is to select your text based on your understanding of the theme, delimiting the aspect of the theme you intend treating if the theme is broad; the text can be chosen from any of the three lessons. Step 4 is to read other parallels of your text in other books of the Bible, since the Gospels, especially the Synoptics, report almost all the events in Jesus' life but with differences which enhance interpretation, inference and implications, and the Old Testament and the Epistles also have parallels. Step 5 is to consult other materials such as Bible dictionaries, commentaries, concordances and other writings, not in order to copy other people's opinions but to help shape your own and to be relevant. Step 6 is to look critically at the background of the text and its implications for the theme and its treatment, remembering that the background of the other passages can also enhance the linkage. Step 7 is to look at the text in line with the theme and the other lessons, asking how the text treats the theme and what part of the theme the text treats. Step 8 is to consider the hows, the whys, the becauses, the therefores, the notwithstandings and the in additions. In some cases only one of the three lessons may be needed to treat the theme properly, and where the situation calls for that the preacher should not hesitate; but this is not an opportunity for lazy work. There is always a link among the three lessons in treating the theme: some links are obvious and others obscure, and the preacher must strive to unearth the link.

subject: LIT
question: Explain the terms "exegesis" and "hermeneutics" and outline the steps which help the preacher to undertake a proper exegesis.
idealAnswer: In The Foundations of Preaching, Rev. Prof. Emmanuel Asante states that the task of the preacher is to expose the world of the Bible to his or her audience, and that this task involves the interpretation of the text, which must be considered as a process involving two approaches, namely exegesis and hermeneutics. Quoting Daniel Parte in What is Structural Exegesis, Asante defines the two terms thus: exegesis aims at understanding the text in itself, while hermeneutics attempts to elucidate what the text means for the modern interpreter and the people of his culture. Exegesis is therefore the art of critically analysing or interpreting the passage, which must be done honestly, and it must not be allowed to give way to eisegesis, the art of reading preconceived opinions into the text. The syllabus sets out points which help the preacher in sermon preparation to undertake a proper exegesis. The first is the text: the passage from which the text is chosen, and the full passage must be read. The second is the context: an overview of how the text was used in the Bible. The third is the historical setting: the historical background surrounding the text. The fourth is the geography of the land of the Bible, which may be very helpful for sermons on the baptism, transfiguration, temptation and death of Christ, since these events involve certain landmarks which, when understood, can aid in the interpretation of the events. The fifth is culture: the preacher should explain the customs and practices of the people to whom the word was originally spoken, which will help in applying the text to our modern culture. The sixth is the circumstances peculiar to the writer, that is the occasion and the target audience. Attention to these points ensures that the preacher first understands the text in itself before attempting to say what it means for the hearers of today.

Exegesis aims at understanding the text in itself
Hermeneutics elucidates what the text means for the modern interpreter and his culture

subject: LIT
question: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of the topical sermon.
idealAnswer: A topical sermon is preaching on a subject: one chooses the subject, then finds all the Scripture that relates to that subject and forms that material into a sermon. It is the most oratorical type of sermon, taking only its subject from the text, and its organization is based on the subject rather than on the distinctions of the text. It requires the preacher to have an overall knowledge of the Bible and the ability to pull together related passages from different parts of the Bible, and in preparing one the preacher must make effective use of a concordance, a dictionary or a topical Bible. Its advantages are several. First, topical sermons allow the preacher to get a grasp of a Bible subject completely, since everything about a particular subject is not found in one place in the Bible, so that the material must be collected together on purpose, analysed and preached, and in such a task the knowledge of the preacher about the whole Bible is broadened. Secondly, if there is too much Scripture to cover in one sermon, a series of sermons can be developed to cover all the passages that relate to that topic, the preacher dividing the topic into sub-topics and dealing with them in a series to ensure full coverage. Thirdly, topical sermons acknowledge and preserve the unity of the Bible, impressing on preacher and hearer alike that even though the Bible is made up of sixty-six books written by many human authors of varied backgrounds, it is one volume in unity, because the ultimate author is God Himself. Fourthly, and because of these benefits, many writers believe that topical sermons constitute the best way to preach about and completely cover the great doctrines of the Bible, each passage relating to the chosen doctrine being expounded so as to cover every aspect of it. The disadvantages are two. First, topical sermons give too much room for oratory and argumentative preaching rather than concentration on the import of the Bible. Secondly, a preacher may choose and develop a topic with passages from the Bible to support it when a careful study will show that the Bible does not intend that teaching; in other words there is the danger of misapplication of Bible passages to support the topic.

subject: LIT
question: Explain what an expository sermon is and discuss its advantages and disadvantages.
idealAnswer: Preachers who preach expository sermons select a paragraph of Scripture, discover the theme from the passage and develop it point by point using evidence from the chosen paragraphs; the preacher uses the sermon to expose what the meaning of the Scripture is. He must study the passage until its insight is clear to him and allow the content of the passage, and the background surrounding it, to determine its treatment, paying attention to three elements: statements, which are sentences that report facts; expressions, which demonstrate emotion; and prescriptive sentences, which describe what is to be done. Like the textual sermon it takes its subject and main points from a particular text, but unlike the textual sermon it also takes its sub-points from the immediate text, and references to other texts are used only to support, elaborate or confirm what is already evident in the immediate text. The difference between expository and topical preaching is that the former concentrates on a specific text and discusses topics covered in it, while the latter concentrates on a specific topic and finds texts covering that topic. The advantages are these: the main advantage is that it gives the hope of possibly covering the entire Bible, since an expositor who does not pick and choose favourite passages but expounds the Bible bit by bit in sequential order may hopefully cover the whole Bible in a given period; the preacher will always have a sermon subject to preach on; expository preaching focuses the hearer's attention on the Scripture as the source of authority and teaching; the preacher expounds not a great book, a poem, a political passage or his personal opinion but the authoritative word of God; and the expository sermon demands integrity on the part of the preacher. The disadvantages are these: the main disadvantage is that it covers many topics and necessitates often lengthy diversions into other passages for clarification, and does not allow detailed coverage of a particular topic; it is a time-consuming task, and most expository preachers will never cover the entire Bible in their lifetime; exegesis may give way to eisegesis, the art of reading preconceived opinions into the text; and the expositor may wander from the text, stretching and straining it to draw lessons it was never intended to teach, so that instead of expositing the passage the preacher exploits it. The greatest danger of all is that the expositor may fail to proceed from interpretation to application, producing an expository lesson which aims only at the mind instead of an expository sermon which addresses both the mind and the will.

subject: LIT
question: Describe the factors a preacher should observe in the delivery of a sermon.
idealAnswer: After all the spiritual and physical preparation needed in the work of the preacher, one of the important tasks is how to deliver the sermon, for a preacher may write a very good sermon but the effectiveness or the achievement of the desired end of changing lives is largely determined by the delivery. The issues that affect sermon delivery include the appearance of the preacher and his body language, and other manners such as his tone and eye contact. As to appearance, the preacher's appearance has a major impact on the congregation, and the dressing must be decent; while modesty is necessary, it is not good to go to the pulpit shabbily dressed in the name of modesty, and depending on the social status of the congregation the dressing should be generally acceptable and neither offensive nor expensive. The preacher must avoid dresses that draw attention to the preacher rather than the message, and must look cheerful, healthy and fit. As to posture, the preacher must be mindful of how he carries himself, be himself and imitate no one except Christ, be natural in voice and style, and not put his hands in his pockets or on his waist, which carries a wrong impression; he must preach with passion, for a passionate preacher is more likely to make a positive impact than one emotionally detached from the message. As to gesture, the preacher may motion the hands, head and other parts of the body to express or stress points, but this should be done with care; a microphone should be held in the left hand so that the right hand is free for stressing points, remembering that in some cultural settings using the left hand to talk to people is not acceptable, and words like Praise the Lord, halleluiah and Amen should not be used just for the sake of it. As to tone, the preacher must check the tone of his voice and of the message; the gospel is a message of joy, so he must not sound too gloomy even when preaching on sin and repentance, and while some points need a loud voice, it should not be his habit to shout, for he should be heard without shouting and must speak clearly and confidently. The preacher must also involve the congregation by calculated eye contact, looking round to all corners of the chapel, and by verbally involving them, leaving the ends of some quotations to be completed by them, though this must not be abused; he may consult his notes, but staying too glued to them detaches him from the people, and since the average listening capacity spans between ten and twenty five minutes he must be mindful of his time.

subject: LIT
question: Discuss the common problems preachers face in the selection of hymns for service, and suggest how they may be overcome.
idealAnswer: One major problem preachers commonly face is the time to get settled and prepare sermons. Some preachers have always seen sermon preparation as part time or even secondary, and many prepare their sermons on Saturday night or even Sunday morning. Once enough time is not allowed for the sermon preparation, hymn selection will suffer, for the most appropriate time to select hymns is when the sermon has been prepared, or at least when the first draft, outline or sketch is done. A simple suggestion is offered: read the passages latest by Monday evening, keep reflecting on them and on the theme, write points down as they come and gather them by Wednesday night, by which time the preacher may have enough points or ideas to help him select his hymns. Another problem is that most preachers are not familiar with the hymns. We may not know the hymns by their numbers, but at least certain lines should be remembered; the preacher may consult the contents of the Methodist Hymn Book to get an idea of the range of hymns that fit various subjects, and it pays to ask for help from fellow Lay Preachers and Ministers. A third problem is that a number of preachers do not find it easy to understand the theme and find it difficult to link the theme to the passages, let alone to select the appropriate hymns. The remedy is to spend a little more time to reflect and to consult other literature and the help of other preachers, so that we can contribute to a lively and spirit-led worship, but above all to pray for guidance and the Holy Spirit's enlightenment. These problems show themselves in practice when a preacher relies on the same favourite hymns for every appointment without recourse to the theme and lessons, or falls back on 'Tell me the old old story' and 'Lord thy word abideth' as sermon hymns, and on 'Forth in thy name O Lord I go' and 'Now thank we all our God' as closing hymns, because he is not able to select fitting hymns. Since hymns enhance inspirational worship, make participation by all possible and unify the congregation, preachers must approach sermon preparation and hymn selection with all the attention and inspiration they deserve.

subject: LIT
question: Explain the role of each of the four hymns in a Methodist Sunday morning service, and state the factors to consider in choosing the sermon hymn and the closing hymn.
idealAnswer: The first hymn in our services always serves as the hymn of praise and adoration. It is the part of the service that sings the praise of our Maker, and we use it to show our appreciation to God for who He is and what He does; it is therefore amazing to hear people singing 'Faith of our Fathers' or 'Stand up stand up for Jesus' as the first hymn unless the service is a special one that demands it. There is a whole range of hymns that qualify as hymns of praise, the common ones being MHB 1 to MHB 35 and MHB 82 to MHB 116. The second hymn is a hymn of invocation, serving to inspire the worshippers to immerse themselves in the worship and to encourage them to pray; preachers have often chosen from MHB 273 to MHB 301. The third hymn is usually the sermon hymn, sung to prepare the congregation for the day's sermon, and it is expected to be relevant to the sermon by touching on the core or at least an important point of it. Preachers who cannot find a relevant hymn too often fall back on 'Tell me the old old story' or 'Lord thy word abideth', which is not good enough. A hymn wholly expressing the core of the message does not always exist; just a stanza or two, or even a few lines, may be what is needed, and it is the duty of the preacher to show the congregation, during the delivery, that minute part of the hymn which is relevant, by referring to it at the appropriate time. The closing hymn is the hymn of response; it should state the desired response to the sermon and answer the question, what should we do after hearing this sermon? Here again 'Forth in thy name O Lord I go' and the so-called Methodist closing anthem 'Now thank we all our God' have been misused by preachers unable to select fitting hymns of response. Three factors help in choosing the sermon and closing hymns. The first is the theme, which serves as the first point of reflection and, when well understood, gives clues to the hymns, the preacher delimiting which aspect of the theme he will handle. The second is the text, whether the verse or two on which the sermon is anchored or the main passage, or even all three lessons, which when read in the light of the theme give a clue. The third is the proposition, the central thought of the sermon containing the main message and the desired response; it is even thought that the proposition does the best job as an aid to hymn selection. Finally, the preacher must know the special occasion or season on which he is preaching, so that hymns are not sung out of season.

subject: LIT
question: What is prayer? Discuss the four elements which make up the content of prayer.
idealAnswer: Prayer is a conversation or communication with God. It is the means by which we link up our souls with the Spirit of God and convey our heart's desires and concerns to Him; real prayer is expressing our devotion to our heavenly Father and inviting Him to talk to us as we talk to Him. It is the intercourse of the soul with God, not only in contemplation or meditation but also in direct address to Him, and it may be oral or mental, occasional or constant, extempore or formal. Although prayer cannot be reduced to a mere formula, there are certain basic elements that should be included in our communication with God, and this formula is popularly known as CATS, that is Confession, Adoration, Thanksgiving and Supplication, or ACTS, that is Adoration, Confession, Thanksgiving and Supplication. To adore God is to worship and praise Him, to honour and exalt Him in our heart and mind and with our lips. We need not begin our prayer by placing a tall list of requests before God, for prayer is interaction with God and not a presentation of requests; to adore God is to display our awareness of His majesty and capability, and as the Psalmist praised God in Psalm 95 for who He is and what He does, this should be the entry point of our prayer. When our discipline of prayer begins with adoration, the Holy Spirit has opportunity to reveal any sin in our life that needs to be confessed, as Isaiah saw how awful his sins were when he entered the awesome glory of God and confessed them and was purged. Confession of sins must be sincere and specific; it is not a time to tell God hypocritically to forgive unknown sins, but to tell Him also the known and intentional ones, and it must culminate in repentance and change. Thanksgiving is the expression of gratitude or appreciation to God for who He is and for the benefits we enjoy because we belong to Him, and it enables us to recognize that He controls all things, not just the blessings but the problems and adversities as well; in it the Christian sees God as the creator of a world that was good, the provider of salvation and the giver of every good and perfect thing. Supplication includes petition for our own needs and intercession for others. Petition is asking God for personal things, since we have varied needs and God has promised to supply them all; intercession is prayer for others, for prayer is not a selfish enterprise but a sharing and caring ministry, and we are to pray for our spouses, children, parents, neighbours, friends, those in authority and our nation. For the preacher, intercession is an integral part of the ministry, and a preacher who does not pray for those he preaches to has an incomplete and unfulfilled ministry.

subject: LIT
topic: Background to the Date for Easter Celebration
question: Give an account of the background to the date for the celebration of Easter.
idealAnswer: Easter can be said to have an apostolic background because it derived from a time when Jewish influence was effective, that is the first century A.D., and it depended on the lunar calendar. For three centuries the church tolerated its celebration on different days. While Asia, or the Eastern Orthodox Church, celebrated it on 14 Nisan, others elsewhere had it on the Sunday after 14 Nisan, and both were accepted because they all had apostolic authenticity. Asia therefore celebrated Easter on the same day as the Jewish Passover, and those who kept Easter on the 14th Nisan were known as Quartodecimans. A great controversy, known as the Quartodeciman controversy, erupted as a result of the date of the celebration of Easter, since Asia celebrated it on the 14th Nisan whatever the day of the week, whereas other churches observed it on the Sunday following the 14th Nisan. In 155 AD Polycarp, the Bishop of Smyrna, discussed the matter in Rome with Ancietus and they agreed to differ, so the matter seemed to have rested for some thirty-five years until 190 AD, when Victor of Rome made an energetic attempt to secure uniformity. Because of the large Asiatic population in the capital, one part of the Church was still fasting when the other was feasting. Victor held a Synod and sent out requests for others to meet; though his views were accepted, the Synod of Asia under Polycrates of Ephesus refused to conform, and so Victor stopped communion with Asia. In time the celebration of Easter upon the Sunday was adopted by all, and the only question remaining was whether, in determining the date, the Jewish reckoning was to be followed, as was the custom at Antioch, or whether it should be calculated independently, as was done at Alexandria and Rome. The latter method was the one eventually agreed upon. Easter itself is the oldest and greatest festival in Christianity, falling on the Sunday on which Christ rose from the dead; according to Tertullian it was the normal occasion for converts to be initiated into the Christian faith, so that on Easter Christians commemorated the death and resurrection of Christ and celebrated both baptism and the Eucharist.

subject: LIT
question: State the liturgical colours used in the Christian year and explain the seasons and occasions on which each is used.
idealAnswer: The Christian year contains two cycles: the Christmas Cycle, which is Advent, Christmas and Epiphany, and the Easter Cycle, which is Lent, Easter and Pentecost. Within each cycle there is a preparatory season symbolized by purple and a festival season symbolized by white, and after each cycle there is an ordinary time of growth symbolized by green; thus there is a sequence of seasons using purple, white and green, in that order, twice each year. Purple is a colour of both penitence and royalty, used during the preparatory seasons of Advent and Lent, and blue, a colour of hope, may also be used during Advent. White and gold are joyous and festive colours used during the Christmas and Easter seasons, except on the Day of Pentecost, and in other seasons on festive days such as the Baptism of the Lord, Transfiguration, Trinity, All Saints and Christ the King. White may also be used at weddings and at services where the sacrament of baptism is central, and it is recommended at services of Holy Communion, where white linens on top of the Lord's table are customary, though the perimeter hanging over the sides of the table and other visuals should reflect the day or season of the year. Green is a colour of growth, used in the seasons after Epiphany and after Pentecost, except when special days call for white or red. Red is a colour of fire, symbolizing the Holy Spirit; it is used on the Day of Pentecost and at other times when the work of the Holy Spirit is emphasized, and it is also the colour of the blood of Christ and of the blood of the martyrs. Because of its intensity, red is most effective when used occasionally rather than continuously for a whole season, and it is appropriate for evangelistic services, for ordinations and consecrations, and for church anniversaries and homecomings. It may be used beside white and gold through the Easter season, and during Holy Week, beginning with Passion or Palm Sunday, to symbolize the blood of Christ. Although the use of these colours is based on broad ecumenical tradition, other colours have been and are being used in Christian churches, and creativity with colours and other signs for the days and seasons is encouraged.
keyPoints: The Christian year has two cycles: the Christmas Cycle and the Easter Cycle
Within each cycle: purple for the preparatory season, white for the festival season, green for ordinary time
Purple: penitence and royalty, used in Advent and Lent; blue, a colour of hope, may also be used in Advent
White and gold: joyous and festive, used at Christmas and Easter and on festive days
White is also used at weddings, at baptisms and at Holy Communion
Green: growth, used in the seasons after Epiphany and after Pentecost
Red: fire and the Holy Spirit, used on the Day of Pentecost, and the blood of Christ and of the martyrs
Red is also used for ordinations, consecrations, anniversaries and Holy Week

subject: LIT
chapter: THE RELEVANCE OF CULTURE TO WORSHIP
question: Explain the "unchangeables" and the "changeables" in worship, and discuss how the Church may meet the challenge of making worship culturally relevant.
idealAnswer: Cultural relevance is not about political correctness, nor about watering down the gospel and worship; it is a process by which the church, in its mission of preaching the gospel, becomes culturally sensitive and thus relevant to her context while remaining doctrinally pure. As far as our worship and the gospel are concerned there are unchangeable facts that cannot be compromised, for biblical truths and doctrinal facts are unchangeable: that Christ is the Son of God, that He died to save sinners and that He shall come again to judge the world. The unchangeables are three. The first is Jesus, for Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever, and the place of God the Father, Son and Holy Spirit in our worship does not change. The second is the Word of God, for the grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands for ever; the Word gives us our directives for worship, for our lifestyle choices, for practical instruction and for our salvation, so the prominent place of reading and interpreting the Word in our worship cannot change. The third is divine principles, for Titus 1:9 instructs those in leadership to hold firmly to the trustworthy message as it has been taught, and God's truth and the divine principles He has given do not change. The changeables are equally clear. Change comes with age, for we change physically as we age, and while younger people may want a radically different setting with opportunity for self-expression and spontaneous songs, prophecies and revelations, an older congregation may prefer a solemn, reflective and calm setting; we must be sensitive to both and in an intergenerational congregation there must be a fair balance. Ministry methods change, since worship styles, technology, outreach methods and teaching styles are always being adapted: Jesus preached from a boat but we use microphones, Paul wrote on papyrus with a quill but we use computers, the early church studied from scrolls but we have many translations and Bibles on phones, and Paul wore a toga but we wear suits and cassocks. God Himself is a God of change, for the Bible speaks of a new song, a new heaven and earth, new wine, new life, a new covenant, a new creation, a new man and a new command, so the church cannot minister to the people of this millennium with a methodology designed to reach the people of the 1950s. The challenges are met in three ways. First, obtain a biblical worldview, for a worldview is the lenses through which we see our world, and since in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, we will not base our feelings and attitudes on a person's age or social status but will love everyone as God's special creation. Secondly, embrace new methodologies, as Jesus taught in the parables of the old garment and the new wineskins; Jesus embraced what was new and effective and presented truth in the language of His culture, using objects, seeds, soil, coins, camels and fig trees. Thirdly, be creative in worship, for God wants His church to sing a new song; this does not mean we cannot continue praising God with the grand old hymns, nor that we may shut out the new songs, for it is not an either-or but a both-and situation.
keyPoints: Cultural relevance is not political correctness or watering down the gospel
The unchangeables are Jesus, the Word of God and divine principles
The place of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit and of reading the Word cannot change
The changeables: change comes with age; ministry methods change; God is a God of change
Contrasts: the boat and the microphone, papyrus and PowerPoint, scrolls and mobile phones, toga and cassock
Meeting the challenge: obtain a biblical worldview
Meeting the challenge: embrace new methodologies, as Jesus did
Meeting the challenge: be creative in worship — a "both, and" situation, not "either, or"

markingRubric.label: Cultural relevance defined
markingRubric.description: States that cultural relevance means sensitivity to context while remaining doctrinally pure.

markingRubric.label: The unchangeables
markingRubric.description: Names and explains Jesus, the Word of God and divine principles.

markingRubric.label: The changeables
markingRubric.description: Explains change with age, changing ministry methods and God as a God of change.

markingRubric.label: Meeting the challenges
markingRubric.description: Gives the three ways: a biblical worldview, new methodologies and creativity in worship.

subject: MS
question: State all the three classifications of Wesley's understanding of human nature and briefly explain each of them.
idealAnswer: Wesley's doctrine of man draws on both the Western and Eastern Christian traditions, both of which held that humanity was created in God's image, and his understanding of human nature can be classified under three main themes. The first is humanity as God's gracious creation. It was the free grace of God that formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed into him a living soul, and the state of man before the Fall was complete perfection. Man is a complex being composed of both body and spirit, and Wesley discussed man created in the image of God under three images: the natural image, a spirit endued with understanding, will and liberty; the political image, in which man is God's vice-regent with dominion over the lower creation; and the moral image, in which man was holy, merciful and perfect as God is, which for Wesley was the principal image. The second theme is humanity as fallen. Adam fell first as a result of unbelief, a lack of trust in God, and Eve believed a lie, giving more credit to the word of the Devil than to the Word of God; so for Wesley the nature of human sin is not pride but unbelief, out of which pride, self-will and every other evil disposition flow. The Fall brought not only physical death but pain, sickness and unholy tempers, and while the natural and political images were polluted or lost in part, the moral image was totally lost. The third theme is humanity as freshly restored. The beginning of the work of salvation in any human being is God's prevenient grace, which goes before any human action and enables a response; by justification we are pardoned, saved from the guilt of sin and restored to the favour of God, and by sanctification we are saved from the power and root of sin and restored to the image of God, so that the individual is renewed and grows into the whole image of God.

Three themes: humanity as God's gracious creation, humanity as fallen, humanity as freshly restored
Gracious creation: free grace formed man of dust and breathed in a living soul; before the Fall man's state was complete perfection; man is body and spirit
The image of God under three images – natural, political and moral, the moral being the principal image
Humanity as fallen: Adam fell through unbelief, not pride; Eve believed a lie
The natural and political images were polluted or lost in part, the moral image totally lost
Humanity as freshly restored: prevenient grace begins the work, justification pardons and restores to God's favour
Sanctification saves from the power and root of sin and restores the image of God
