question: Complete the syllabus definition: 'the word sinner is a technical term for common people regarded by the Pharisees as ____________'.
acceptedAnswers: untaught in the Law; who did not abide by rigid pharisaic standards
explanation: For the Pharisees a 'sinner' was one untaught in the Law who did not abide by rigid pharisaic standards - which is why Jesus' eating with such people gave offence.

manualReference.excerpt: The word sinner is a technical term for common people regarded by the Pharisees as untaught in the Law; who did not abide by rigid pharisaic standards.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 2

subject: NT
question: What distinction does the syllabus draw between the titles 'Son of Man' and 'Son of God'?

options.text: 'Son of Man' was a title used only by the Scribes
options.rationale: In this passage Jesus applies the title to Himself.

options.text: 'Son of Man' emphasises deity, while 'Son of God' emphasises His messianic office
options.rationale: The syllabus reverses this: 'Son of Man' emphasises His full humanity.

options.text: Both titles refer only to Jesus' earthly ministry
options.rationale: The syllabus links 'Son of God' expressly with His deity.

options.text: 'Son of Man' emphasises that Jesus is fully human, while 'Son of God' emphasises deity

explanation: As God's Son, Jesus has authority to forgive sin; as a man He can identify with our deepest sufferings and help us overcome sin.

manualReference.excerpt: The title "Son of man" emphasizes that Jesus is fully human, while son of God emphasizes deity, i.e. He is fully God.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 2

subject: NT
question: What did 'hardness' of heart connote to the Hebrew, as distinct from the modern sense of callousness or cruelty?

options.rationale: The syllabus speaks of stubborn resistance, not mere ignorance.

options.text: Unteachableness, a stubborn resistance to the purpose of God

options.rationale: Grief was Jesus' response to their hardness, not the meaning of the word.
The term is used morally and spiritually, not physically.

explanation: The Pharisees' refusal to debate the moral question of doing good on the Sabbath illustrates precisely this unteachable, stubborn resistance to God's purpose.

manualReference.excerpt: Hardness (hard-hearted), to us means callousness or cruel, but here (i.e. to the Hebrew) it connotes unteachableness, a stubborn resistance to the purpose of God.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 3

subject: NT
question: Which list gives the five fishermen among the Twelve as named in the syllabus?

options.text: Peter, Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew and Thaddaeus
options.rationale: Only Peter, Andrew and Philip belong to the list of fishermen.

options.text: Peter, James, John, Andrew and Philip
Peter, James, John, Levi and Judas
options.rationale: Levi was a publican and Judas hailed from Kerith in Judah.

options.text: Peter, James, John, Andrew and Thomas
options.rationale: Thomas is not named among the fishermen in the syllabus's list.

explanation: The syllabus notes that five of the Twelve were fishermen, one a publican and one a zealot, and that all were Galileans except Judas, who came from Kerith in Judah.

manualReference.excerpt: The five fishermen among the Twelve were: (1) Peter (2) James (3) John (4) Andrew (5) Philip.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 3

subject: NT
question: According to the syllabus, why did Jesus teach in parables?

options.text: Because the Scribes had forbidden direct teaching in the synagogue
options.rationale: The syllabus gives no such prohibition.

options.text: In order to conceal His messiahship from the Romans
options.rationale: No political motive is given in the syllabus.

options.text: Because the crowds could not read the written Law
options.rationale: Literacy is not the reason offered.

options.text: In order to test the spiritual responsiveness of His audience

explanation: Those provoked by the parables into intensive reflection could obtain enlightenment; those who would not reflect would be ever seeing but never perceiving.

manualReference.excerpt: The essence of His reply seems to be that He did so in order to test the spiritual responsiveness of His audience.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 4

subject: NT
question: In the parable of the mustard seed, what is the preferred view of the birds of the air which rested in the shade of the shrub?

options.text: They depict the false teachers who corrupt the church
options.rationale: This interpretation is not offered in the syllabus.
The syllabus does not identify the birds with the apostles.

options.text: They depict Satan snatching away the word
options.rationale: The birds stand for Satan in the parable of the sower, not in the parable of the mustard seed.

options.text: They depict the incorporation of the Gentiles into God's kingdom programme

explanation: Although the parable may be viewed simply as showing the expansion of the kingdom from insignificant beginnings, the syllabus states that the incorporation of the Gentiles is the preferred view.

manualReference.excerpt: The incorporation of the Gentiles into God's kingdom programme is a preferred view.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 4

subject: NT
question: When Jesus asked the demon-possessed man of the Gerasene country his name, he replied, 'My name is ____________ for we are many.'
explanation: Many evil powers controlled the man and tormented him as one combined force under the leadership of one demon as their spokesman, which explains the alternating singular and plural pronouns.

manualReference.excerpt: "my name is Legion for we are many" - the man replied.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 5

subject: NT
question: The account of the raising of Jairus' daughter is broken by the incident of the woman with the issue of blood, giving the section a 'sandwich' structure.
explanation: What appeared to be a disastrous delay in fact assured the restoration of Jairus' daughter, as if it were providentially ordered to test and strengthen Jairus' faith.

manualReference.excerpt: This section has a "sandwich" structure.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 5

subject: NT
question: For what reasons were the Twelve sent out two by two?

options.text: For legal reasons, for the sake of witness, and for fellowship
To fulfil a Roman regulation on travelling teachers
options.rationale: The legal reason given rests on Old Testament witness law, not Roman regulation.

options.text: For safety on the roads and to save expense
options.rationale: Neither safety nor economy is given as a reason in the syllabus.

options.text: So that one might preach while the other healed
options.rationale: The syllabus describes a threefold ministry shared by all of them.

explanation: The practice of going two by two was common, was required for legal purposes of testimony, and served both witness and fellowship.

manualReference.excerpt: The Twelve sent out two by two, was a common practice which was for legal reasons (cf. 11:1; 14:13; John 8;17; Dt. 17:6; 19:15) also for the sake of witness (2 Cor. 13:1), and fellowship.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 6

subject: NT
question: Mark 6:30 is the only place in this Gospel where the Twelve are called ____________.
explanation: The syllabus notes that it is here and here only in Mark that the Twelve are given the title 'apostles'.

manualReference.excerpt: It is here and here only in this Gospel that the Twelve are called apostles
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 6

subject: NT
question: By declaring his possessions 'Corban', from which commandment could a person absolve himself?

options.rationale: The syllabus links Corban with duty to parents.

options.text: The fourth commandment, on keeping the Sabbath
options.rationale: Restrictive Sabbath rules are cited as a further example, but the Corban vow concerned the fifth commandment.
Covetousness is discussed in chapter 10, not in the Corban tradition.

options.text: The fifth commandment, which enjoins respect to parents

explanation: The Corban vow is offered as one example among many of scribal traditions which distorted and obscured the Old Testament.

manualReference.excerpt: In their tradition, it was possible for a person to declare all his possessions to be Corban and thereby absolve oneself from the fifth commandment which enjoins respect to parents.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 7

subject: NT
question: The cure of the Syro-Phoenician woman's daughter is the only miracle in Mark which Jesus performed without setting eyes on the sick person and without giving any vocal command.
explanation: It was the woman's demonstration of humility and faith that moved Jesus to assure her, at a distance, that her daughter was cured.

manualReference.excerpt: This miracle is the only one in the book of Mark that Jesus performed without even setting eyes on the sick person and without giving any vocal command.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 7

subject: NT
question: Why could the seven basketfuls left over at the feeding of the four thousand hold more than the twelve basketfuls of Mark 6:43?

options.text: They were the large baskets used by Roman soldiers
options.rationale: The syllabus makes no reference to Roman baskets.

options.text: They were probably rope or mat baskets, sometimes large enough to carry an adult
They were seven times the size of an ordinary basket
options.rationale: The difference lies in the kind of basket, not in a fixed multiple.

options.text: They were temple measures used for grain offerings
options.rationale: No cultic measure is mentioned in the syllabus.

explanation: The syllabus draws attention to the different Greek words for basket, comparing the large rope or mat basket of Acts 9:25 in which a man could be carried.

manualReference.excerpt: they were probably rope or mat baskets, sometimes large enough to carry an adult.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 8

subject: NT
topic: From Galilee to Jerusalem: Jesus Concentrates on Ministry to His Disciples
question: What was the main task of Jesus in undertaking the journey from Galilee to Jerusalem?

options.text: To confront the Sanhedrin in open debate
options.rationale: The confrontations in Jerusalem follow; they are not the purpose of the journey.

options.text: To carry the gospel to the Gentile cities of the Decapolis
options.rationale: The Decapolis ministry belongs to an earlier stage.

options.text: To keep the Feast of Tabernacles at the temple
options.rationale: The syllabus makes no reference to that feast.

options.text: To prepare His disciples for His impending crucifixion

explanation: On this journey Jesus explained the nature of His messianic vocation and its implications for those who choose to follow Him, with three definite predictions of the passion.

manualReference.topicTitle: From Galilee to Jerusalem: Jesus Concentrates on Ministry to His Disciples
manualReference.excerpt: The main task of Jesus in undertaking this journey from Galilee to Jerusalem was to prepare His disciples for His impending crucifixion.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — From Galilee to Jerusalem: Jesus Concentrates on Ministry to His Disciples

subject: NT
question: Four interpretations have been suggested for the promise of Mark 9:1 that some standing there would not taste death until they saw the kingdom of God. Which does the syllabus regard as most reasonable in this context?

options.text: The destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70
options.rationale: This is listed as one of the four possibilities but is not the preferred view.

options.text: Pentecost and the beginning of missionary enterprise
options.rationale: This too is listed, but the syllabus prefers the transfiguration.
Again a listed possibility, but not the one the syllabus judges most reasonable.

explanation: The specific reference in the following account of the transfiguration (9:2a) indicates that Mark understood a definite connection between the prediction and that event.

manualReference.excerpt: The transfiguration is the most reasonable view in this context.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 9

subject: NT
question: Jesus taught that Elijah had already come in John the Baptist but had not been recognised.
explanation: The disciples were correct about Elijah, but their concept of the Son of Man was deficient because it did not include the truths of His suffering and death.

manualReference.excerpt: Christ then adds (Mk 9:13) that Elijah had already come in John the Baptist but had not been recognized.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 9

subject: NT
question: In the lessons on discipleship of Mark 9:43-50, which THREE organs does the syllabus name as symbols of various types of activity?

options.text: The eye that desires what it ought not
The hand that snatches for things it should not
The foot that goes where it ought not
The ear that listens to what it ought not
options.rationale: The ear is not among the organs mentioned in this passage.

options.text: The tongue that speaks what it ought not
options.rationale: The tongue is not listed here; it belongs to the healing of the deaf and dumb man in chapter 7.

explanation: The hyperboles are not to be pressed literally; the point is that participation in the kingdom of God is worth any sacrifice, and that a disciple must take prompt, decisive action against whatever would draw him away.

manualReference.excerpt: The organs mentioned here are really symbols for various types of activity, for example, (1) the hand that snatches for things it should not, (2) the foot that goes where it ought not; (3) the eye that desires what it ought not.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 9

subject: NT
question: What was the difference between the schools of Shammai and Hillel on the question of divorce?

options.rationale: Both permitted divorce; they differed over the grounds.

options.text: Shammai forbade divorce but permitted separation, while Hillel forbade both
options.rationale: This distinction is not made in the syllabus.

options.text: Shammai allowed divorce for almost any cause, while Hillel held the bond indissoluble
options.rationale: The positions are the other way round: Shammai was the strict school.

options.text: Shammai held the marriage bond indissoluble except for the wife's infidelity, while Hillel allowed divorce for almost any cause

explanation: Jesus replied first that Moses' legislation was a concession to human weakness, and then took the questioners back beyond Moses to God's ideal at creation.

manualReference.excerpt: The school of Shammai maintained the strict interpretation of this, that the marriage band was indissoluble except in the event of the wife's infidelity. The school of Hillel took the liberal view allowing divorce for almost any cause (v. 5).
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 10

subject: NT
question: Which command in Jesus' list to the rich man occurs only in Mark, and how is it interpreted?

options.text: 'Do not defraud', interpreted as 'Do not covet'
'Do not bear false witness', interpreted as 'Do not slander'
options.rationale: That commandment is not peculiar to Mark's list.

options.text: 'Honour your father and mother', interpreted as 'Do not use Corban'
options.rationale: Corban belongs to the discussion of tradition in chapter 7.

options.text: 'You shall have no other gods', interpreted as 'Do not love money'
options.rationale: The first commandment is invoked in the exposition, but it is not the command peculiar to Mark.

explanation: Jesus quoted commandments dealing with human relationships that are more easily verified in a person's conduct; the one necessary thing the rich man lacked was unrivalled allegiance to God, since wealth was his god.

manualReference.excerpt: The command Do not defraud occurring only in Mark is interpreted "Do not covet"
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 10

subject: NT
question: Why is Bartimaeus' use of the title 'son of David' significant in Mark?

options.text: It occurs here for the first time in Mark and designated the Messiah as David's descendant
It was a title reserved for the reigning high priest
options.rationale: The title belongs to the Messiah as David's descendant.

options.text: It showed that Bartimaeus regarded Jesus merely as a prophet
options.rationale: It shows rather that he believed Jesus of Nazareth was Israel's Messiah.

options.text: It was the customary greeting given to any rabbi in Jericho
options.rationale: The syllabus says the bystanders may have objected precisely to this address.

explanation: Despite his physical blindness Bartimaeus believed Jesus was Israel's Messiah, in contrast with the blind unbelief of most Jews; Jesus did not silence him, implying He accepted the title.

manualReference.excerpt: They might have been opposed to him addressing Jesus as son of David (occurring here for the first time in Mark) which designated the Messiah as David's descendant.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 10

subject: NT
question: By entering Jerusalem mounted on a colt, Jesus made a claim that which prophecy applied to Him?

options.rationale: Malachi 4:5 concerns the coming of Elijah.
Isaiah 53 is cited elsewhere for the suffering of the Son of Man, not for the entry.
Psalm 118:25 lies behind the crowd's cry 'Hosanna', not behind the choice of the colt.

explanation: Jesus chose an animal never ridden before, in accordance with the prophet's description of a new colt, and used a donkey rather than a horse to show that He would not fulfil His messianic office as a warrior.

manualReference.excerpt: Jesus decided to do so by an act which constituted a claim that the prophecy of Zechariah 9:9 applied to Him.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — The Entry into Jerusalem (vs. 1-11)

subject: NT
topic: The Beginnings of Conflict with the Religious Leaders (vs. 12-12:44)
question: Why was the appearance of the fig tree deceptive, and of what did Jesus make it a symbol?

options.text: It was out of season, so Jesus used it to teach patience in prayer
options.rationale: The syllabus does use the withered tree to teach faith, but the deceptive appearance points to the Temple.

options.text: Its leaves promised fruit which was absent; it became a symbol of the Temple, which had the appearance of dedication to God but fell short of doing His will
It bore fruit without leaves, so Jesus used it as a symbol of hidden faith
options.rationale: The reverse is the case: it bore leaves without fruit.

options.text: It was planted by the roadside, so Jesus used it to teach against private ownership
options.rationale: No such lesson is drawn.

explanation: In Palestine fig trees produced small edible buds in March before the large green leaves of early April; leaves without those buds meant the tree's appearance was deceptive.

manualReference.topicTitle: The Beginnings of Conflict with the Religious Leaders (vs. 12-12:44)
manualReference.excerpt: the tree's leaves promised fruit; the absence of the green fruits, therefore, meant that the tree's appearance was deceptive. It is this that Jesus uses as a symbol for the Temple.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — The Beginnings of Conflict with the Religious Leaders (vs. 12-12:44)

subject: NT
topic: The Beginnings of Conflict with the Religious Leaders (vs. 12-12:44)
question: Both the cursing of the barren fig tree and the cleansing of the Temple signify God's impending judgment on Israel for religious hypocrisy.
explanation: This is another example of Mark's sandwiching of two stories together so that each episode helps explain the other.

manualReference.topicTitle: The Beginnings of Conflict with the Religious Leaders (vs. 12-12:44)
manualReference.excerpt: Both episodes signify God's impending judgment on Israel for religious hypocrisy.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — The Beginnings of Conflict with the Religious Leaders (vs. 12-12:44)

subject: NT
question: What did the Sadducees deny, in contrast with the Pharisees?

options.text: The obligation to pay the poll tax to Caesar
options.rationale: The tax question was put by the Pharisees and Herodians.

options.text: The authority of the Pentateuch and the levirate marriage law
options.rationale: They appealed to the Pentateuch and quoted the levirate law; they did not deny them.

options.text: The resurrection, future judgment, and the existence of angels and spirits
The Davidic descent of the Messiah
options.rationale: That question is raised by Jesus Himself, not by the Sadducees.

explanation: The Sadducees, generally believed to be Jewish aristocrats, denied all three; the Pharisees acknowledged them all.

manualReference.excerpt: The Sadducees (generally believed to be Jewish aristocrats) denied the truth of the resurrection, future judgment, and existence of angels and spirits (Acts 23:6-8).
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 12

subject: NT
question: By Jesus' time the Jews had accumulated hundreds of Laws, totalling ____________.
explanation: Some religious leaders tried to distinguish between major and minor laws, and some taught that all were binding; Jesus' answer summarised them all in love for God and love for others.

manualReference.excerpt: By Jesus' time, the Jews had accumulated hundreds of Laws, totaling 613.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 12

subject: NT
question: What does Jesus' question about David's son, quoting Psalm 110:1, strongly imply about the Messiah?

options.text: That the Messiah is both God (David's Lord) and man (David's son) at the same time
That the scribes were right to expect a purely political deliverer
options.rationale: The point tells against, not for, a merely political expectation.

options.text: That David was mistaken in what he wrote
options.rationale: The syllabus says David spoke by the Holy Spirit.

options.text: That the Messiah could not be descended from David at all
options.rationale: Jesus does not deny the Davidic descent; He shows the Messiah is both son and Lord.

explanation: Jesus' rhetorical question pointed His listeners to one valid answer only: the Messiah is David's son and David's Lord at once, and He will restore the future Davidic kingdom on earth.

manualReference.excerpt: the Messiah is David's son and David's Lord at the same time.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 12

subject: NT
topic: The Last Things: Jesus Tells about the Future (vs. 1-37)
question: Which four disciples came to Jesus privately on the Mount of Olives to ask when the temple's destruction would occur?

options.rationale: Bartimaeus was not one of the Twelve.
Philip is not named among the four in this passage.
Neither Thomas nor Judas appears in this scene.

explanation: The four senior disciples asked both when the destruction would occur and what sign would indicate its imminence.

manualReference.topicTitle: The Last Things: Jesus Tells about the Future (vs. 1-37)
manualReference.excerpt: the four senior disciples, Peter, James, John and Andrew got alone with Him and asked Him when the Temple's destruction would occur.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — The Last Things: Jesus Tells about the Future (vs. 1-37)

subject: NT
topic: The Last Things: Jesus Tells about the Future (vs. 1-37)
question: Against what THREE kinds of deception or disturbance does the Olivet Discourse warn the disciples, as 'the beginning of the sufferings'?

options.text: Famine among the Christians of Judea
options.rationale: The famine relieved by the Antioch collection belongs to the Acts narrative, not to this warning.

options.text: Uprisings or disturbances in the political and international field
Divisions between Greek-speaking and Hebrew believers
options.rationale: That dispute belongs to Acts 6, not to the Olivet Discourse.

explanation: Such things are incidental to the course of the age and are not necessarily to be taken as signs of the end; they are the beginning of birth pains.

manualReference.topicTitle: The Last Things: Jesus Tells about the Future (vs. 1-37)
manualReference.excerpt: There would be imposters in the religious sphere, uprisings or disturbances in political and international field and calamities in the physical realm.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — The Last Things: Jesus Tells about the Future (vs. 1-37)

subject: NT
question: Why did the Jewish leaders resolve not to arrest Jesus during the feast?

options.text: Because it might provoke violent opposition from His supporters coming to Jerusalem from Galilee for the Passover
Because they had not yet found any witnesses against Him
options.rationale: The search for witnesses belongs to the trial itself.

options.text: Because arrests were forbidden by Roman law during festivals
options.rationale: No Roman prohibition is mentioned in the syllabus.

options.text: Because Pilate had refused to hear the case during the feast
options.rationale: Pilate does not enter the narrative until the trial.

explanation: Their desire was fulfilled through Judas Iscariot, who disclosed where Jesus might be found at night and almost alone.

manualReference.excerpt: Their reason was that it might provoke violent opposition on the part of supporters of Jesus who would be coming to Jerusalem from Galilee to observe the Passover.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — The Passion Narrative (14:1-15:52)

subject: NT
question: What was the prearranged signal by which the two disciples were to find the room for the Passover?

options.text: A palm branch laid across the doorway
options.rationale: Palm branches belong to the entry into Jerusalem.

options.text: A lamp burning in an upper window
options.rationale: No such signal is mentioned in the syllabus.

options.text: A man carrying a jar of water, since normally only women carried water jars
A servant bearing a wineskin, since only men carried wineskins
options.rationale: The syllabus says men carried wineskins; the eye-catching sight was a man with a water jar.

explanation: For security reasons the participants were not disclosed and the location kept secret, so the unusual sight of a man carrying a water jar served as a signal.

manualReference.excerpt: A man carrying a jar of water would meet the two disciples. Normally only women carried water jars (men carried wineskins). This unusual eye-catching sight suggests that it was a prearranged signal.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — The Passion Narrative (14:1-15:52)

subject: NT
question: How had the false witnesses at the trial twisted Jesus' actual words about the temple?

options.text: He had never spoken of the temple at all
options.rationale: He had spoken of it, but not in the form the witnesses alleged.

options.text: He had said the temple would stand for ever, not that it would fall
options.rationale: Jesus had predicted the temple's complete destruction in chapter 13.

options.text: He had said 'Destroy this temple and in three days I will raise it up', not 'I will destroy this temple'
He had spoken of Herod's temple, but they applied it to the tabernacle
options.rationale: The reverse is true: He was speaking of His own body, not of Herod's temple.

explanation: Jesus was speaking not about Herod's Temple but about His own death and resurrection.

manualReference.excerpt: He did not say "I will destroy this Temple," He said "Destroy this temple and in three days I will raise it up" (Jn. 2:19).
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — The Passion Narrative (14:1-15:52)

subject: NT
question: How does the syllabus explain the 'cup' from which Jesus shrank in Gethsemane?

options.text: It was the fear of desertion by His disciples
options.rationale: That desertion is predicted, but it is not the cup.

options.text: It was the cup of the Passover which Judas had defiled
options.rationale: No such interpretation is offered.

options.text: It was the physical pain of scourging and crucifixion alone
options.rationale: The syllabus says it was certainly more than physical suffering, since many a martyr has shown greater courage.

options.text: It was the alienation Jesus knew would occur when separated from God the Father at the cross

explanation: It was the agony of His sinless soul being made sin and exposed to the divine judgment of sin; the sinless Son of God took on our sins and was in that moment separated from the Father.

manualReference.excerpt: this "cup" was the alienation Jesus knew would occur when separated from God the Father, at the cross (Heb. 5:7-9).
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — The Passion Narrative (14:1-15:52)

subject: NT
question: The syllabus contrasts Peter and Judas by saying that Peter's remorse opened the way for repentance and a reaffirmation of his loyalty, whereas Judas had no faith in Jesus that could be renewed.
explanation: Peter's third denial was punctuated by the cock's second crowing, and he broke down weeping bitterly; but his remorse led to restoration.

manualReference.excerpt: Peter had faith in Jesus that could be renewed, but Judas did not.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — The Passion Narrative (14:1-15:52)

subject: NT
question: The three non-religious charges laid against Jesus before Pilate are summarised in the syllabus as which offences?

options.rationale: Those were the crimes of Barabbas, not the charges against Jesus.
Blasphemy was the religious charge which would mean nothing to Pilate.
These were earlier religious accusations, not the charges before Pilate.

explanation: Because blasphemy was a religious crime that would mean nothing to a Roman governor, the Jews accused Jesus of encouraging non-payment of taxes, of claiming to be a king, and of causing riots.

manualReference.excerpt: Tax evasion, treason, and terrorism - all of these would be cause for Pilate's concern.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 15

subject: NT
question: For what period did total darkness engulf the whole land at the crucifixion?

options.text: For the whole day from dawn to dusk
options.rationale: The syllabus specifies a three-hour period.

options.text: From sunset on Friday until sunset on Saturday
options.rationale: That is the reckoning of the Sabbath, not of the darkness.

options.text: From the sixth hour (noon) until the ninth hour (3 pm)
From the third hour (9 am) until the sixth hour (noon)
options.rationale: Jesus hung on the cross in daylight for those three hours; the darkness came afterwards.

explanation: The darkness was probably a cosmic sign of God's judgment on human sin, which was placed on Jesus, and it visualised what His cry from Psalm 22:1 expressed.

manualReference.excerpt: Jesus hanged on the cross for three hours in the daylight (9am till noon) and then at the sixth hour (noon) total darkness engulfed the whole land (Palestine and environs) until the ninth hour (3 pm).
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 15

subject: NT
question: What did the tearing of the veil before the Holy of Holies signify?

options.text: That Jesus' death for our sins had opened the way for us to approach our Holy God
That the temple would soon be destroyed by the Romans
options.rationale: The destruction of the temple is predicted separately, in the Olivet Discourse.

options.text: That the Day of Atonement had been abolished for the Jews only
options.rationale: The syllabus draws a wider conclusion about access to God.

options.text: That the office of high priest had passed to the apostles
options.rationale: No such transfer is taught here.

explanation: The veil symbolically separated the Holy God from sinful mankind, and the place was entered only once a year by the High Priest on the Day of Atonement.

manualReference.excerpt: When Jesus died, the veil was split in two, showing that Jesus' death for our sins had opened the way for us to approach our Holy God.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Chapter 15

subject: NT
topic: The Women's Visit to the Sepulchre (vs. 1-8)
question: The young man robed in white whom the women found sitting in the tomb was, according to the syllabus, clearly an angel.
explanation: The women, ignorant that the tomb had been sealed and guarded, were astonished to find him there; he told them that Jesus had risen and that they should notify the disciples and Peter.

manualReference.topicTitle: The Women's Visit to the Sepulchre (vs. 1-8)
manualReference.excerpt: The young man was clearly an angel.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — The Women's Visit to the Sepulchre (vs. 1-8)

subject: NT
question: On what evidence do nearly all scholars conclude that Mark 16:9-20 is not part of the original text of the Gospel?

options.text: Its disagreement with the resurrection accounts in the other Gospels
options.rationale: Disagreement with the other Gospels is not the ground given.

options.text: A statement to that effect by the Fathers Papias and Irenaeus
options.rationale: Papias and Irenaeus are cited concerning Mark's relation to Peter, not concerning this passage.

options.text: Its absence from every Latin and Syriac version
options.rationale: The syllabus names Sinaiticus and Vaticanus specifically.

options.text: Its dissimilarity in vocabulary and style, and its absence from the oldest and best manuscripts, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus

explanation: The syllabus adds that it is nevertheless not to be deduced that these verses are not part of the inspired Word of God.

manualReference.excerpt: The evidence for this inference being their considerable dissimilarity from the rest of this Gospel both with regards to vocabulary and style, and especially their absence from the oldest and best manuscripts of the Gospel, namely Sinaiticus and Vaticanus.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Disputed Conclusion (vs. 9:20)

subject: NT
question: Mark 16:16 teaches that baptism is a necessary requirement for salvation.
explanation: The syllabus notes that the second half of the verse shows by contrast that it is unbelief that condemns; baptism alone without faith does not save.

manualReference.excerpt: V. 16 does not mean that baptism is a necessary requirement for salvation.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK — Disputed Conclusion (vs. 9:20)

subject: NT
question: Where and when does the syllabus say the Book of Acts was written?

options.text: In Jerusalem, immediately after the Jerusalem Council
options.rationale: No such date or place is given.

options.text: In Antioch, shortly after the first missionary journey
options.rationale: Antioch was the base of Paul's missionary operations, but the syllabus places the writing of Acts in Rome.

options.text: In Rome, during the two years (AD 59-61) when Paul was a prisoner there
In Caesarea, during Paul's imprisonment under Felix
options.rationale: The syllabus names Rome and the two-year imprisonment there.

explanation: Luke, Paul's companion, is the undisputed author, and Acts appears to have been written in Rome during Paul's two-year imprisonment.

manualReference.excerpt: It seems that Acts was written in Rome during the two years (AD 59-61) when Paul was a prisoner there.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Introduction

subject: NT
question: In the forty days between His resurrection and ascension, Jesus made ____________ recorded appearances to the disciples.
explanation: The syllabus adds that He later made a special appearance to Paul, and that these appearances would free the disciples' minds of any doubt as to His continued existence as a living person.

manualReference.excerpt: In the 40 days between His Resurrection and Ascension, Jesus made 10 recorded appearances to the disciples.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 1

subject: NT
question: Pentecost is the New Testament name for which Jewish festival?

options.rationale: That feast belongs to the Passover season, not to Pentecost.
The Day of Atonement is a fast, not the wheat-harvest festival.

options.text: The Feast of Weeks, when the wheat harvest was celebrated
The Feast of Tabernacles, when the ingathering was celebrated
options.rationale: The syllabus identifies Pentecost with the Feast of Weeks.

explanation: It was a one-day festival during which special sacrifices were offered.

manualReference.excerpt: Pentecost is the New Testament name for the Feast of Weeks, when the wheat harvest was celebrated.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 2

subject: NT
question: 'The ninth hour' at which Peter and John went up to the temple - three in the afternoon - was the hour of ____________ associated with the evening sacrifice.
acceptedAnswers: national prayer associated with the evening sacrifice
explanation: The syllabus observes that the apostles still worshipped as Jews, with no sense of a need to break away from the Temple.

manualReference.excerpt: "The ninth hour" - Three in the afternoon was the hour of national prayer associated with the evening sacrifice.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 3

subject: NT
question: Luke traces the growth of the church: 3,000 converts on the first day, then ____________, then multitudes both men and women.
explanation: The arrest of Peter and John had little impact on the growth of the church, which kept growing.

manualReference.excerpt: 3,000 converts the first day (2:41) Then 5000 (4:4). Then multitudes both men and women.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 4

subject: NT
question: Which two abortive Messianic rebellions did Gamaliel cite in advising the Sanhedrin to leave the apostles alone?

options.text: Those of Herod Agrippa and Sergius Paulus
options.rationale: Both were rulers, not leaders of Messianic revolts.

options.text: Those of Theudas and Judas the Galilean

options.rationale: Barabbas belongs to the passion narrative and Bar-Jesus to Cyprus; neither is cited by Gamaliel.

options.text: Those of Simon the sorcerer and Agabus
options.rationale: Simon was a sorcerer in Samaria and Agabus a prophet; neither led a rebellion.

explanation: Gamaliel argued that if the new movement were not of God it would fail as those uprisings had, but that if God were really in it no human opposition could break it.

manualReference.excerpt: if it is not of God, it is bound to fail, as did the Messianic rebellions of Theudas and Judas the Galilean.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 5

subject: NT
question: What was the complaint of the Greek-speaking Christians which led to the appointment of the seven?

options.text: That the apostles required them to be circumcised
options.rationale: The circumcision question arises later, at the Jerusalem Council.

options.text: That the Hebrews had appointed all the elders from among themselves
options.rationale: The syllabus states the complaint concerned the neglect of their widows.

options.text: That they were not allowed to preach in the temple
options.rationale: The complaint concerned the daily distribution, not preaching rights.

options.text: That their widows were neglected in the distribution of supplies

explanation: The apostles accepted the criticism, which was in reality directed against them, but recognised that their first priority was the ministry of the word of God and prayer.

manualReference.excerpt: The Greek-speaking Christians complained against the Hebrews that their widows were neglected in the distribution of supplies.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 6

subject: NT
question: How does the syllabus best characterise Stephen's address before the Sanhedrin?

options.text: More of an apology - a statement of teaching or recital of Old Testament history climaxing in a rebuke for their murder of Jesus
An appeal to his rights as a Roman citizen
options.rationale: That appeal belongs to Paul, not to Stephen.

options.text: A formal legal defence answering each charge in turn
options.rationale: The syllabus says it is sometimes considered a defence, but that it is clearly more of an apology.

options.text: A prophecy of the destruction of Jerusalem
options.rationale: Stephen recites Israel's history; he does not predict the fall of the city.

explanation: Stephen's recital of Old Testament history climaxes in a stinging rebuke for the murder of Jesus.

manualReference.excerpt: it is clearly more of an apology - that is, a statement of teaching or a recital of Old Testament history, climaxing in a stinging rebuke for their murder of Jesus (vs. 51-53).
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 7

subject: NT
question: The Holy Spirit sent Philip to evangelise an official of an African queen on the Gaza road, and the syllabus observes that this would relay the Gospel to the heart of Africa.
explanation: After the eunuch's baptism the Spirit led Philip away, and whatever became of the Ethiopian afterwards is unknown.

manualReference.excerpt: This would relay the Gospel to the heart of Africa.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 8

subject: NT
question: When the believers in Jerusalem refused to trust the converted Saul, who became his advocate before them?

options.rationale: Peter is occupied at this point with the churches outside Jerusalem.
Philip had carried the Gospel to Samaria; he is not Saul's advocate.
James appears later as head of the church at Jerusalem, but he is not named here.

explanation: Barnabas disabused the minds of the critics of their negative thoughts on two grounds: that Saul had met the risen Lord who spoke to him, and that he had boldly preached Christ, thereby placing his own safety at risk.

manualReference.excerpt: He finds an advocate in Barnabas (v. 27), who disabused the minds of the critics of their negative thoughts on the score that,
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 9

subject: NT
topic: THE BEGINNING OF THE GENTILE MISSION - LEADERSHIP OF PETER (9:32-12:25)
question: Whom did Peter heal at Lydda, and how long had the man been bed-ridden?

options.text: Publius' father, who had fever and dysentery
options.rationale: That healing took place on Malta, through Paul.

options.text: Eutychus, who had fallen from a window
options.rationale: Eutychus was restored by Paul at Troas.

options.text: Aeneas, a paralytic who had been bed-ridden for eight years
Dorcas, a disciple who had been ill for eight years
options.rationale: Dorcas was raised at Joppa after she had died; she was not a paralytic.

explanation: The healing of Aeneas led many to come to faith in Christ, and the gospel began to attract a wider audience, Gentiles in particular.

manualReference.topicTitle: THE BEGINNING OF THE GENTILE MISSION - LEADERSHIP OF PETER (9:32-12:25)
manualReference.excerpt: Here, Peter healed one Aeneas, a paralytic who had been bed-ridden for eight years.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — THE BEGINNING OF THE GENTILE MISSION - LEADERSHIP OF PETER (9:32-12:25)

subject: NT
question: Cornelius the centurion had been circumcised as a full-fledged proselyte to Judaism before Peter came to him at Caesarea.
explanation: Cornelius, described as devout and God-fearing, followed the Old Testament way to the best of his knowledge and ability, but had not been circumcised.

manualReference.excerpt: it can be inferred he was not a full-fledged proselyte to Judaism (he had not been circumcised (11:3) but he did worship Yahweh.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 10

subject: NT
question: When Peter returned to Jerusalem, what was the primary problem the Jewish believers had with his conduct?

options.rationale: Circumcision is not the issue raised at this point.

options.text: Not his preaching to Gentiles, but his eating with them
His claim to have seen a vision
options.rationale: The vision formed part of his defence, not the charge against him.

options.text: Not his eating with Gentiles, but his baptising them
options.rationale: The syllabus states expressly that the primary problem was the eating.

explanation: Eating with someone is a mark of acceptance and fellowship, and the reaction of the Jewish Christians shows they still held to the Law of Moses.

manualReference.excerpt: The primary problem was not his preaching to Gentiles but his eating with them
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 11

subject: NT
question: Who was the first of the Twelve to suffer martyrdom, and at whose hands?

options.text: Stephen, at the hands of the Sanhedrin
options.rationale: Stephen was one of the seven, not one of the Twelve.

options.text: James the Lord's brother, at the hands of the Judaizers
options.rationale: James the Lord's brother appears later as head of the church at Jerusalem.

options.text: James, the brother of John, at the hands of Herod Agrippa I
Peter, at the hands of Herod Agrippa II
options.rationale: Peter was imprisoned but delivered; and the Herod of this chapter is Agrippa I.

explanation: Herod Agrippa I, who did everything to win favour with the Jews, found it politically expedient to arrest Christians, and afterwards attempted to execute Peter also.

manualReference.excerpt: James, brother of John, was the first of the Twelve to suffer martyrdom in the hands of "Herod the King" (v. 1).
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 12

subject: NT
question: What was the major event at Paphos on the first missionary journey?

options.text: The stoning of Paul and his recovery
options.rationale: The stoning took place at Lystra.

options.text: The conversion of the pro-consul Sergius Paulus, which the false prophet Bar-Jesus tried to prevent
The conversion of the jailer and his household
options.rationale: That took place at Philippi on the second journey.

options.text: The founding of the church at Antioch of Syria
options.rationale: Antioch was already the sending church.

explanation: It is at this point that Luke first uses the name Paul and thereafter calls him so consistently.

manualReference.excerpt: The major event here was the conversion of the pro-consul, Sergius Paulus, whiles the false prophet, Bar-Jesus, wanted to prevent this.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 13

subject: NT
question: Lystra, where Paul healed a cripple and was later stoned and left for dead, was the hometown of Timothy.
explanation: The syllabus adds that it is possible Timothy witnessed these events, citing 2 Timothy 3:11.

manualReference.excerpt: Lystra was the hometown of Timothy (16:1).
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 14

subject: NT
question: What critical question was the Jerusalem Council convened to settle for the Gentiles?

options.text: Whether Gentile churches should send financial relief to Judea
options.rationale: The relief collection was an earlier act of fellowship, not the Council's question.

options.text: Whether one has to become a 'Jew' before he could become a Christian, or whether God accepts us in Christ irrespective of our background
Whether John Mark should be received back into the mission
options.rationale: That was the contention between Paul and Barnabas, not the Council's business.

options.text: Whether Paul and Barnabas should undertake a second missionary journey
options.rationale: That dispute followed the Council.

explanation: The syllabus notes the profound implication of this for the issue of culture in relation to faith in Christ - for example, whether Africans must adopt the European cultural clothing in which the Gospel came to them.

manualReference.excerpt: This second event was crucial as it was to settle for the Gentiles the very critical question of whether one has to become a "Jew" before he could become a Christian or that God accepts us in Christ irrespective of our background.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — THE JERUSALEM COUNCIL (CHAPTER 15:1-35)

subject: NT
question: What basis did James suggest for the prohibitions laid on Gentile believers by the Jerusalem Council?

options.text: That Gentile Christians must be alert to the sensitivities of their Jewish brethren, with whom they might be worshipping
That the Roman authorities required these observances
options.rationale: Roman requirements have nothing to do with the Council's reasoning.

options.text: That the Law of Moses remained binding on all believers
options.rationale: The Council decided that Gentiles need not be circumcised or keep the Law as the Jews did.

options.text: That these were the only commandments given before the Law of Moses
options.rationale: No such argument appears in the syllabus.

explanation: Since Jews and Gentiles might be worshipping together, the Gentiles were to have fellow-feeling for the Jews and not become careless about what the Jews cared for most.

manualReference.excerpt:
The basis for this prohibition as suggested by James was that the Gentile Christians must 
be alert to the sensitivities of their Jewish brethren.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — THE JERUSALEM COUNCIL (CHAPTER 15:1-35)

subject: NT
question: What good does the syllabus say God brought out of the sharp disagreement between Paul and Barnabas over John Mark?

options.text: The Jerusalem Council was convened to settle the matter
options.rationale: The Council had already met before this dispute.

options.text: Mark was permanently excluded from the ministry
options.rationale: Paul later acknowledged Mark's worth and regarded him as a colleague.

options.text: Two missionary journeys emerged from it - Barnabas went to Cyprus with Mark, and Paul to Syria and Cilicia with Silas
Barnabas returned to Jerusalem and became an elder there
options.rationale: Barnabas went to Cyprus with Mark.

explanation: God over-ruled the dissension so that two journeys emerged, and Barnabas is commended for living up to his name, Son of Encouragement, in making Mark a useful servant of the Lord.

manualReference.excerpt: God certainly over-ruled this dissention for, two missionary journeys rather emerged from it.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — THE SECOND MISSIONARY JOURNEY (15:36-18:22)

subject: NT
question: Why did Paul have Timothy circumcised at Derbe and Lystra?

options.text: Because the Jerusalem Council had ruled that all half-Jews must be circumcised
options.rationale: The Council ruled that Gentiles need not be circumcised; Paul acted out of sensitivity, not obligation.

options.text: Because circumcision was required of all who preached in the synagogue
options.rationale: No such requirement is stated in the syllabus.

options.text: Because Timothy, though the son of a Jewess, was uncircumcised, and this would be offensive to the Jewish community
Because Timothy's Greek father demanded it
options.rationale: The father's influence is given as a possible reason why Timothy had remained uncircumcised.

explanation: F. F. Bruce holds that Paul simply regularised Timothy's status as a half-Jew; Paul was guided by the decision of the Jerusalem Council in being sensitive to issues that concerned the Jews.

manualReference.excerpt: There was a problem, however, because Timothy was uncircumcised, though the mother was a Jewess; and this would be offensive to the Jewish community.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — The Details Of Paul'S 2Nd Missionary 'Durney:

subject: NT
question: Lydia's conviction at Philippi, in which God took the initiative in her readiness to hear the word, is what theology describes as prevenient grace.
explanation: God went before, pre-disposing Lydia to give a ready acceptance to the gospel.

manualReference.excerpt: Her conviction is what is described as "prevenient grace" in theology i.e. God took
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 16

subject: NT
question: Why does Luke commend the Bereans above the Thessalonians?

options.text: They were the first Gentiles to be baptised in Macedonia
options.rationale: The first Macedonian convert named is Lydia at Philippi.

options.text: They were more open-minded, received the message with great eagerness and examined the Scriptures to see if what Paul said was true
They contributed generously to the collection for Judea
options.rationale: The Macedonian gifts are mentioned elsewhere; this is not the ground of the commendation.

options.text: They protected Paul from the Judaizers by hiding him
options.rationale: The brethren did plan his escape, but the commendation rests on their study of the Scriptures.

explanation: Paul's approach to preaching actually encouraged people to investigate the Scriptures for themselves, so it is not surprising that many believed.

manualReference.excerpt: These Jews, whom Luke calls the Bereans, were more open-minded than the Thessalonians.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 17

subject: NT
question: Athens and Corinth, though only fifty miles apart, were quite different: Athens was noted for its culture and learning, Corinth for its ____________.
explanation: Corinth was marked by profligate and licentious living and was a centre for the worship of Aphrodite, the goddess of love, who promoted immorality in the name of religion.

manualReference.excerpt: Athens was noted for its culture and learning, Corinth for its commerce and extravagance.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 18

subject: NT
question: Gallio's refusal to hear the Jews' case against Paul was crucial because it was tantamount to legitimatising Christianity in the eyes of Roman law.
explanation: Judaism was a licensed religion under Roman law, and Gallio treated Christianity as coming under the aegis of Judaism and therefore not a matter for a civil court; as proconsul of Achaia, any judgment he pronounced established legal precedent.

manualReference.excerpt: This decision was crucial for it was tantamount to legitimatizing Christianity in the eyes of Roman Law.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 18

subject: NT
question: Why did Paul move his Ephesian ministry from the synagogue to the lecture hall of Tyrannus?

options.text: Because the city clerk forbade Jewish assemblies
options.rationale: The city clerk appears later, at the riot.

options.text: Because the opposition of some Jews hardened against the message was so strong that he could no longer use the synagogue as a base for evangelism
Because the synagogue ruler had been converted and the building was sold
options.rationale: No such event is recorded in the syllabus.

options.text: Because Apollos had taken over the synagogue teaching
options.rationale: Apollos had already left Ephesus before Paul arrived.

explanation: Paul had spoken boldly in the synagogue for three months - something of a record for him without a riot - before moving to the neutral ground of Tyrannus' lecture hall, where he ministered for two years.

manualReference.excerpt: The strength of the opposition was such that Paul felt that he could no longer use the synagogue as a base for evangelism.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 19

subject: NT
question: The root cause of the riot which arose in Ephesus because of 'the Way' was a doctrinal dispute rather than an economic one.
explanation: Demetrius and his fellow silversmiths saw their business declining as more people became believers and accepted Paul's teaching that man-made gods are no gods at all.

manualReference.excerpt:
The root cause was neither doctrinal 
nor ethical, but economic.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 19

subject: NT
question: The name Eutychus, the young man restored to life at Troas, literally means ____________.
explanation: Luke the physician affirmed that Eutychus was picked up dead after falling from a third-storey window, and the syllabus observes that his restoration proved true to his name.

manualReference.excerpt: The name Eutychus, literary means "fortunate".
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 20

subject: NT
question: What did James and the elders suggest Paul do in order to allay Jewish suspicions that he was advocating a wholesale rejection of the Mosaic Law?

options.text: Take the Nazirite vow himself for thirty days
options.rationale: It was the four men who evidently had a Nazirite vow; Paul was to join in their rites and pay their costs.

options.text: Circumcise Trophimus the Ephesian before bringing him to the temple
options.rationale: Trophimus was the Gentile whose presence gave rise to the false accusation; no such proposal was made.

options.text: Deliver the collection publicly in the temple courts
options.rationale: The collection is not the action proposed at this meeting.

options.text: Join in the purification rites of four men who had taken a vow, and pay their expenses

explanation: The action was to demonstrate to the believers that Paul respected the Mosaic Law - a principle of his ministry, to become like a Jew to win the Jews - but the syllabus notes that the solution proposed by the elders did not work.

manualReference.excerpt: James and the elders suggested that Paul join in the purification rites of four men who had taken a vow and pay their expenses (vs. 22-24).
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — PAUL'S ARREST AND IMPRISONMENT (vs. 1-28:31)

subject: NT
question: The letter of Claudius Lysias which accompanied Paul to Felix at Caesarea is the only secular letter in the New Testament.
explanation: When a prisoner was forwarded to a superior, the subordinate officer was required to send a written statement; the syllabus notes that Lysias bent the truth in claiming that he rescued Paul because he was a Roman citizen.

manualReference.excerpt: It is the only secular letter in the New Testament.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — PAUL'S ARREST AND IMPRISONMENT (vs. 1-28:31)

subject: NT
question: Why did Felix leave Paul in prison even though he knew him to be innocent?

options.text: Because Paul had already appealed to Caesar
options.rationale: The appeal to Caesar was made later, before Festus.

options.text: Because Tertullus had substantiated the charges
options.rationale: The syllabus says Tertullus had not been able to substantiate his charges.

options.text: Because he hoped for a bribe, and partly because he wanted to pacify the Jews
Because Lysias had found fault in him
options.rationale: Lysias had found no fault in Paul, and neither had the Sanhedrin.

explanation: Felix was in a dilemma: he could not convict Paul, since neither Lysias nor the Sanhedrin nor Tertullus had established a case, yet he was unwilling to release him.

manualReference.excerpt: On the other hand Felix was unwilling to release Paul because he hoped for a bribe (v. 26), and partly because he wanted to pacify the Jews.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 24

subject: NT
question: What was the effect of Paul's use of the technical phrase 'I appeal to Caesar'?

options.text: It secured his immediate release from custody
options.rationale: He remained a prisoner; the appeal only moved the case to Rome.

options.text: It obliged Festus to send him back to Jerusalem for trial
options.rationale: Going up to Jerusalem was precisely what Paul avoided by the appeal.

options.text: It required Agrippa to retry the case in Caesarea
options.rationale: The syllabus says a retrial was now beyond the powers of both Festus and Agrippa.

options.text: It quashed all local proceedings and transferred his case to the imperial court in Rome

explanation: Paul was entitled to this exercise of privilege as a citizen of the empire, and by it the divine purpose that he should reach Rome was carried forward.

manualReference.excerpt: This exercise of his privilege quashed all local proceedings, and transferred his case to the imperial court in Rome (v. 12).
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 25

subject: NT
question: Who was the Agrippa before whom Paul made his defence, and who was Bernice?

options.text: Herod Antipas, who had beheaded John the Baptist; Bernice was Herodias' daughter
options.rationale: Herod Antipas belongs to the Gospel narrative.

options.text: Herod the Great's son Archelaus; Bernice was his wife
options.rationale: Neither name appears in the syllabus at this point.

options.text: Herod Agrippa II, grandson of Agrippa I; Bernice was his sister, living with him as his wife
Herod Agrippa I, who had killed James; Bernice was his daughter
options.rationale: Agrippa I had already died; this is his grandson, Agrippa II.

explanation: Agrippa was profoundly impressed by Paul's defence, but to Festus the idea of a resurrection from the dead was so unthinkable that he cried out that Paul must be crazy.

manualReference.excerpt: Agrippa was Herod Agrippa II, the grandson of Agrippa I.
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 26

subject: NT
question: The fearsome wind which swept down from the Cretan mountains and put the ship out of control was called the north-easter, also known as ____________.
explanation: The ship had set out from Fair Havens, where Paul's earlier suggestion had been ignored by the ship's captain, and headed for Crete only to be struck by this wind.

manualReference.excerpt: only to be struck suddenly by the fearsome wind called the 'north-easter' (also known as Euraquilo – v. 14)
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 27

subject: NT
question: The island on which the sailors were shipwrecked was Malta - a Phoenician word which, by a strange coincidence, means ____________.
explanation: The islanders showed the shipwrecked seafarers unusual kindness by building a fire in the cold and rain of the early morning.

manualReference.excerpt: The island on which the sailors were shipwrecked was Malta - a Phoenician word, which by a strange coincidence, means "escape".
manualReference.citation: New Testament Studies — THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES — Chapter 28

subject: NT
question: What was the one basic problem disturbing the churches in Galatia?

options.text: Division between rich and poor at the love feast
options.rationale: That problem belongs to Corinth, not to Galatia.

options.text: Denial of the resurrection of the dead
options.rationale: That error is dealt with in 2 Timothy, where Hymenaeus and Philetus are named.
The syllabus names an internal doctrinal threat, not state persecution.

subject: NT
question: Explain the parable of the sower and the interpretation which Jesus gave of it in Mark 4:1-20.
idealAnswer:
The parable of the sower stands at the head of Mark's collection of parables depicting the character of God's kingdom, and the syllabus reads it as an explanation of the opposition Jesus met. The reason why Jesus was opposed by the religious leaders and others, including His own relations, was the spiritual condition of their hearts, and in the parable He urged His hearers to give careful consideration to the nature of their own hearts. Some hearers never understood or grasped His message at all; others were discouraged through difficulties; others again were seduced through prosperity; the result was that only a limited proportion became lastingly committed to it.

Before explaining the parable Jesus answered the disciples' question as to why He employed parables. The essence of His reply is that He did so in order to test the spiritual responsiveness of His audience. Those provoked by the parables into intensive reflection could proceed to obtain enlightenment concerning them, while those who would not reflect on them could be ever seeing but never perceiving; that is, they would understand the literal meaning of the words but not the parable's deeper significance.

In the interpretation the farmer, or sower, probably represents Jesus and all who sow or proclaim the word of God, which is the seed. The kinds of soil represent four different ways in which people respond to God's word, three of them negative. The first is hard-hearted indifference, where Satan, like the birds, comes immediately and takes the word away, so that in effect there is no response. The second is a hasty, enthusiastic but shallow profession of acceptance which lasts only a short time because the word takes no root; there is a lack of spiritual depth, and when trouble or persecution comes on account of the word such hearers quickly fall away, their profession proving not to be genuine. The third are those who hear the word but are preoccupied with the cares and riches of this life, which choke the word and make it unfruitful, indicating that they are not true believers. By contrast others hear the word, accept it - welcome it for themselves - and produce a crop. These are evidently genuine disciples who bear fruitful yields of varying amounts: thirty, sixty or a hundredfold.
keyPoints: The parable explains the opposition Jesus met: the spiritual condition of the hearers' hearts
Hearers are urged to consider the nature of their own hearts
Jesus taught in parables to test the spiritual responsiveness of His audience
Those who would not reflect would be ever seeing but never perceiving
The sower represents Jesus and all who proclaim the word; the seed is the word of God
Hard-hearted indifference: Satan, like the birds, takes the word away at once
Shallow, rootless profession falls away when trouble or persecution comes

Genuine disciples hear, accept and bear fruit thirty, sixty or a hundredfold

subject: NT
question: Give an account of Jesus' teaching on marriage and divorce in Mark 10:1-12, and explain why He referred the Pharisees back to the creation.
idealAnswer:
The syllabus stresses that the question put by the Pharisees was malicious. It was put to Jesus in order to test Him, that is, to try to induce Him to incriminate Himself by contradicting the Mosaic Law. The Mosaic enactment of Deuteronomy 24:1-4 stated that a husband was allowed to divorce his wife by writing and giving to her a certificate of divorce if he had found some unseemly thing in her, and the whole question turned upon what constituted an unseemly thing.

Shammai and Hillel were the authorities in the interpretation of the Mosaic Law, and different groups took their authority from them. The school of Shammai maintained the strict interpretation, holding that the marriage band was indissoluble except in the event of the wife's infidelity. The school of Hillel took the liberal view, allowing divorce for almost any cause. To answer either school directly would have set Jesus against a recognised body of opinion, which is what His questioners intended.

In reply Jesus first pointed out that Moses' legislation was a concession to human weakness, rightly introduced to regulate divorce in a defective state of society. He quoted the words, 'Because of the hardness of your heart he wrote to you this commandment.' Moses' provision was therefore not a divine ideal but a restraint upon an existing evil.

Secondly, Jesus took the Pharisees back beyond Moses to God's ideal at the beginning of creation. From that ideal we discover that marriage was instituted as the divine ideal for man and woman, and that the bond is permanent and indissoluble. By going behind the concession to the creation ordinance Jesus set the discussion on a different footing altogether: the question is not how much divorce the Law will tolerate, but what God intended marriage to be from the beginning. The passage that follows, on receiving the kingdom in childlike trust, continues the same emphasis upon the divine order rather than upon human casuistry.

Deuteronomy 24:1-4 allowed a certificate of divorce for 'some unseemly thing'
The debate turned on what constituted an unseemly thing
Shammai held the bond indissoluble except for the wife's infidelity
Hillel allowed divorce for almost any cause
Jesus replied that Moses' legislation was a concession to human weakness
'Because of the hardness of your heart he wrote to you this commandment'
Jesus took them back beyond Moses to God's ideal at creation: the bond is permanent and indissoluble

subject: NT
question: Give an account of the trial of Jesus before the Sanhedrin as presented in Mark 14:53-65.
idealAnswer:
The syllabus explains that this trial by the Sanhedrin, the Jewish Supreme Court, had two phases: a small group met at night and the full Council met at daybreak. Jesus was tried for religious offences such as calling Himself the Son of God, which according to the Law was blasphemy. The trial was obviously fixed, because these religious leaders had already decided to kill Jesus.

The Sanhedrin began their deliberations by seeking evidence against Jesus in order to justify a death sentence, but they found none. Many witnesses testified falsely, but their testimonies did not corroborate. In Jewish trials the witnesses served as the prosecution and gave their testimonies separately, and to convict a person the Mosaic Law required precise agreement in the testimony of at least two witnesses.

The claim on which the false witnesses finally agreed twisted Jesus' actual words. He did not say, 'I will destroy this Temple'; He said, 'Destroy this temple and in three days I will raise it up', and He was speaking not about Herod's Temple but about His own death and resurrection. To this first accusation Jesus gave no response, because the evidence itself was confusing and erroneous, and not answering was wiser than trying to clarify fabricated accusations.

The high priest then asked, 'Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?' To refuse to answer this would have been taken as a denial of His mission. Jesus' answer predicted a powerful role-reversal: sitting at the right hand of God meant that He would come to judge them and that they would be answering questions. By tearing his clothes the high priest showed that he regarded this bold declaration as blasphemy; this symbolic expression of horror and indignation was required of the high priest whenever he heard blasphemy, and his reaction also expressed relief, since Jesus' self-incriminating answer removed the need for more witnesses. Without further investigation the high priest called for a verdict, and since there were no objections they all condemned Him as worthy of death. Thereafter some members showed their contempt through mockery and physical abuse, spat in His face - an act of gross personal insult - blindfolded Him on account of His messianic claims, struck Him with their fists and demanded that He prophesy who hit Him.

The charge was religious - calling Himself the Son of God, which was blasphemy

Witnesses served as the prosecution; the Law required precise agreement of at least two
The false witnesses twisted Jesus' words about destroying the temple

He answered the high priest's question about the Christ, predicting a role-reversal
The high priest tore his clothes, the required expression of horror at blasphemy

subject: NT
question: Describe the supernatural events which accompanied the death of Jesus in Mark 15 and explain the significance the syllabus attaches to them.
idealAnswer:
Mark records five supernatural events that accompanied the death of Jesus: the darkness, Jesus' cry 'My God, my God', His loud cry, the tearing of the temple curtain from top to bottom, and the confession of the Roman centurion.

Jesus hung on the cross for three hours in the daylight, from nine in the morning until noon, and then at the sixth hour total darkness engulfed the whole land, that is Palestine and its environs, until the ninth hour, three in the afternoon. The darkness was probably a cosmic sign of God's judgment on human sin, which was placed on Jesus. It visualised what His cry expressed.

That cry, 'Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani', is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew of Psalm 22:1, and means 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' The syllabus insists that this was more than a righteous sufferer affirming his faith that the Father would cause him to triumph. Jesus' cry combined abandonment by the Father in a judicial and not a relational sense, together with a genuine affirmation of His relationship to the Father. He was bearing the curse of sin and the Father's judgment upon sin, and experienced for the first time the horror of separation from God, who cannot look on sin and therefore hid His face. Although seemingly exhausted, Jesus was offered vinegar by the soldiers and then uttered a loud cry, after which He breathed His last.

The tearing of the temple curtain carries its own significance. A heavy veil hung in front of the Holy of Holies, a place reserved by God for Himself, and it symbolically separated the Holy God from sinful mankind. The place was entered only once a year, on the Day of Atonement, by the High Priest as he made a sacrifice to gain forgiveness for the sins of all the people. When Jesus died the veil was split in two, showing that His death for our sins had opened the way for us to approach our Holy God. The centurion's confession completes the list, so that a Gentile soldier bears witness to what the religious leaders had denied.
keyPoints: Five supernatural events: darkness, the cry of dereliction, the loud cry, the torn curtain, the centurion's confession
Darkness from the sixth hour (noon) to the ninth hour (3 pm) over the whole land
The darkness was probably a cosmic sign of God's judgment on human sin placed on Jesus
'Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani' - Aramaic for the Hebrew of Psalm 22:1
The cry combined judicial (not relational) abandonment with a genuine affirmation of relationship
Jesus bore the curse of sin and experienced separation from God who cannot look on sin

subject: NT
question: Give an account of the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15:1-35 and state its major conclusions.
idealAnswer:
The syllabus describes the Jerusalem Council as probably the second most significant event in the missionary advance of the Gospel to the Gentiles, the first being the experience Peter went through concerning the conversion of the household of Cornelius and the acceptance of his report by the church in Jerusalem. This second event was crucial because it was to settle for the Gentiles the very critical question of whether one has to become a Jew before he could become a Christian, or whether God accepts us in Christ irrespective of our background. The syllabus draws out the implication for culture and faith: since the Gospel came to us from Europe, must we adopt the European cultural clothing that came with it, or can we be truly African and still be accepted by God in Christ?

The proponents are then set out. Those who belonged to the party of the Pharisees presented their case that the Gentiles must be circumcised and required to obey the law of Moses. Peter spoke about the experience he went through in Cornelius' house and how the Gentiles experienced the same outpouring of the Holy Spirit as had occurred to the Jews at Pentecost. Barnabas and Paul spoke about the miraculous signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them. James, the brother of Jesus, who had become an important person among the elders in the church at Jerusalem, gave the speech which clarified the position of the church, and his proposals were accepted.

The conclusions were introduced by the words 'It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us', which means that they were based on human reasoning and conviction by the Holy Spirit, both agents being important in knowing the will of God when taking decisions. The major conclusions were that the Gentiles were not to be circumcised like the Jews before they could become Christians; that so far as the Law of Moses was concerned they were to abstain from food sacrificed to idols, from the eating of blood and from animals whose blood had not been poured out; and that they were to abstain from sexual immorality, since there were even shrine-prostitutes in some Gentile cities. The basis for the food prohibitions was that Gentile Christians must be alert to the sensitivities of their Jewish brethren with whom they might be worshipping. Judas and Silas were sent with Barnabas and Paul to authenticate the letter, and at Antioch the people were glad for its encouraging message.

The critical question: must one become a Jew before becoming a Christian?
Its implication for culture: European cultural clothing versus being truly African in Christ
The Pharisees' party demanded circumcision and obedience to the law of Moses

'It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us' - human reasoning with the Spirit's conviction
Conclusions: no circumcision; abstain from food sacrificed to idols, blood, strangled animals and sexual immorality
Judas and Silas were sent with Barnabas and Paul to authenticate the letter
