subject: NT
question: Describe Paul's ministry in Athens and the two schools of philosophy which he had to address at the Areopagus.
idealAnswer:
Athens was the capital city of the district of Attica in ancient times and the capital of modern Greece, and was named after the patron goddess Athena. In New Testament times Athens could still boast of being one of the most famous centres of wisdom, architecture and art. Though it had been surpassed economically by Corinth and intellectually by Alexandria, the city nevertheless maintained a great reputation.

Three features of the city are singled out. The rocky hill of the Acropolis, about 156 metres high, carried many temples which were centres of worship. West-north-west of the Acropolis lay the Areopagus, which was the seat of Athens' highest court of justice. There was also the Agora, or market place, a large open space surrounded by colonnades, temples, bazaars and government buildings, where the Athenians spent their time discussing political issues and exchanging goods and services.

Besides temple worship, two schools of philosophy reigned in Athens which Paul had to address. The Epicureans, founded by Epicurus (341-270 BC), held a materialistic view of life: death is the end of everything and therefore nothing is to be feared, so the pursuit of happiness was to be the goal of human existence. Paul's message of divine judgment and resurrection was therefore contrary to their beliefs. Stoicism was founded by Zeno of Citium, who taught in a building called the Stoa Poikile in the Agora, from which the school takes its name. In Stoicism the primary focus is on how life is to be lived, with the attainment of virtue stressed above all, virtuous living being living in accordance with nature. Some scholars have contended that the apostle himself was influenced by Stoicism, reflected in letters which stress self-sufficiency, contentment in all circumstances and indifference to whether one is poor or wealthy.

Paul used two approaches. In the synagogue, where there were Jews and God-fearing Gentiles, he used his normal method of proving from the Old Testament Scriptures that Jesus is the Messiah. In the market place his approach was different: his message was geared towards moving the audience from what they knew to what they did not know, and was made relevant to their needs. The idol worshippers needed to move from the Unknown God to the Known God, and the philosophers needed to know that there is a God who will judge all the affairs of men after death, which God has proved by raising Jesus from the dead. This pattern of preaching is key to good preaching. Not many converts were won at Athens, as Paul appeared to be in transition, and no church seems to have been established there.

Epicureans, founded by Epicurus (341-270 BC): materialistic, death ends everything, pursuit of happiness

In the synagogue Paul proved from the Old Testament that Jesus is the Messiah
In the market place he moved his hearers from what they knew to what they did not know
Idolaters from the Unknown God to the Known God; philosophers to a God who judges and who raised Jesus
Few converts; no church appears to have been established at Athens

subject: NT
question: Discuss the chief ideas of Stephen's speech before the Sanhedrin and give an account of his death.
idealAnswer:
Stephen's address before the Sanhedrin is sometimes considered as his defence, that is, an answer to the legal charges brought against him, but it is clearly more of an apology: a statement of teaching, or a recital of Old Testament history, climaxing in a stinging rebuke for their murder of Jesus.

Three chief ideas are designed to be emphasised by Stephen's Old Testament story. The first is that the Jewish people throughout their long history have rebelled against God and His accredited messengers. The second is that God does not live in, nor does He desire, a material and fixed shrine or temple: His presence is not confined to sacred sites but accompanies His people, who are to be always a pilgrim church on earth. A subsidiary theme is that the Jewish people have not only rebelled against God and their leaders but have consistently rejected the messengers, or saviours, whom God sent to them, the outstanding proof being their recent rejection of their Messiah.

Other commentators, especially Bruce, suggest two themes running through the speech. The first is that throughout their history God raised up men to act as deliverers of His people, but the Jews repeatedly rejected them and disobeyed the law given by God: after dealing with the establishment of the nation through God's call of Abraham, the speech treats of Joseph, who was rejected by his brothers but rescued by God, and then at greater length of Moses, who came to deliver the people but was rejected by them. The second is that the Jews had the tabernacle in the wilderness and later the temple built by Solomon, but they fell into idolatry and made the mistake of thinking that God actually dwelt in the temple. These two themes are intermingled in the speech.

Stephen's indictment of unbelieving Jews touched his hearers on a tender spot. They became furious, gnashed their teeth at him, and stoned him to death. His death looked more like a lynching than a judicial execution for blasphemy: there was no trial, and Jewish Law had an elaborate arrangement to safeguard the accused person, for if he should recant, or if a witness for the defence should suddenly appear, the stoning must be stopped. It is clear that no such precautions were made for Stephen's benefit. The most impressionable person in this violent scene seems to have been Saul, who looked after the witnesses' clothes and so agreed that Stephen should be stoned; Paul never forgot this awful sight.

subject: NT
question: Outline the factors which worked to bring to pass Paul's decision of reaching Rome with the Gospel, and describe his dealings with the Jews in Rome.
idealAnswer:
The syllabus lists four factors which brought to pass Paul's decision of reaching Rome with the Gospel. Most important of all was the overruling hand of God, which was obvious throughout the narrative. Secondly, there was the Roman system of governance, which ensured the security and rights of individuals. Thirdly, there was Paul's knowledge and use of his civil rights, seen in his appeal to Caesar and in his appeal to his Roman citizenship when he was about to be flogged. Fourthly, there was Paul's knowledge of the Jewish religion and of the fulfilment of the Jewish hope in the Messiah, Jesus Christ.

Luke traces the journey carefully: from Malta to Syracuse in Sicily, to Rhegium in Italy, to Puteoli, and finally to Rome itself. At Puteoli there were already many Christians, which is significant because it shows that the gospel had already spread from Rome to the Italian seaport. Certainly a church had been planted in Rome by Roman Jews who had gone to the Pentecost feast. Paul accepted the invitation of a Christian fellowship there to spend a week with them. By this time he had evidently become a trusted prisoner and was allowed to live by himself, with a soldier to guard him, residing in a rented house.

In Rome, following his principle of speaking first with the Jews, Paul called the Jewish leaders to meet with him because he could not go to their synagogues. He made several points: that he was innocent of damaging the Jews or their customs; that the Roman authorities in Judea thought him innocent; that his only option had been to appeal to Caesar because the Jews refused to deal with him justly; that he was not pressing charges against Israel but only wanted to be acquitted; and that his primary objective in calling them was to talk about the hope of Israel. That hope was more than the resurrection: it meant the fulfilment of the Old Testament promises to Israel, for Paul firmly believed that Jesus is the Messiah of Israel who will return and establish Himself as king of Israel and Lord of the nations.

As on many previous occasions his address divided the people into two camps. As the unconvinced Jews left in disarray Paul applied the words of Isaiah with prophetic insight: obstinate refusal to believe results in calloused hearts, deafened ears and spiritually blinded eyes. Yet while Paul was in Rome during this incarceration the gospel was never hindered. Men may bind preachers, but the gospel cannot be chained; so the kingdom message went from Jew to Gentile and from Jerusalem to Rome.

subject: NT
question: Explain the problems which had arisen in the churches of Galatia and Paul's purpose in writing the epistle.
idealAnswer:
There was one basic problem disturbing the churches in Galatia: the teaching of the Judaizers. That problem threatened the peace and spiritual welfare of the Christians on two fronts. Firstly, Paul's gospel of justification by faith was threatened by the teaching that Christians, both Gentile and Jew, must keep Moses' law. Secondly, Paul's personal authority as an apostle was attacked, a tactic used to undermine the authenticity of his teachings.

Paul represented the chief obstacle to the success of the Judaizers. As the leader of the mission to the Gentiles his voice carried great weight, and he was as relentless in opposing them as they were in pushing their teaching, saying that to them he did not yield submission even for a moment, that the truth of the gospel might be preserved. In order to prevail they therefore had to destroy his influence, and they attacked him at his Achilles heel: because he was not one of the Twelve apostles, they argued, his authority was not apostolic, and whatever he knew he got second-hand and got it garbled at that.

Paul saw clearly that the issues raised by the subversive activities of the Judaizers had wider implications than the dominant Jewish Christian element realised, and the rapidity with which the Galatians had departed from the freedom of the gospel served as a goad to him, so that he wrote, 'I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting Him who called you by the grace of Christ for a different gospel.'

His purposes may therefore be set out in three parts. He wrote to defend his place and authority as a genuine apostle of Jesus Christ, chiefly in chapters 1 and 2, establishing that his commission and gospel came directly from Jesus and that the gospel he preached had been vindicated before the other apostles. He wrote to correct the error of the Judaizers and to prove the truth of the gospel he preached, in chapters 3 and 4, which includes a demonstration that justification is by faith and not by the law. And he wrote to teach about the Spirit-controlled life that accompanies justification by faith, in chapters 5 and 6, because his detractors seemed to say that his doctrine of grace led to licentiousness; in this last section he appeals to total inward moral change, which may be seen as Paul's ethics. The key word of the epistle is faith and its theme is justification by faith.

subject: NT
question: Discuss the contrast between law and grace as Paul sets it out in Galatians 5.
idealAnswer:
The last verse of chapter 4 describes the believer's position: he is free. The first verse of chapter 5 refers to his practice: he should live as a free man. Christ leads into glorious freedom, and there is need to preserve it. It is in this setting that Paul illustrates the difference between the law and grace. The law would say, 'if you earn your freedom you will become free'; but grace says, 'you have been made free at the tremendous cost of the death of Christ, now in gratitude to God, you should stand fast in the liberty wherewith Christ has made you free.'

The essential distinction is stated thus: the Law commands but does not enable, whereas grace provides what the law demands and then enables a man to live a life consistent with his position by the power of the Holy Spirit. C. H. Mackintosh has put the same point memorably: 'The Law demands strength from one who has none and curses him if he cannot display it. The Gospel gives strength to one who has none and blesses him in the exhibition of it.'

Paul also teaches in this chapter that legalism - undue respect for the law and legal forms - makes Christ of no value. The Judaizers insisted on the necessity of Gentile believers being circumcised for salvation; Paul insists that to depend on circumcision is to make Christ of no benefit, for if observing a mere ritual could help, then Christ is unnecessary. Legalism moreover requires men to keep the whole Law: one cannot accept the easy commandments and reject the others.

The positive side follows in the teaching on walking by the Spirit. Paul teaches how we may fulfil the just requirements of the law, not by our own strength but by the saving grace which comes through faith in the atoning work of Christ. By believing in Jesus, He fills us with His Holy Spirit, and we live the Christian life controlled by God's Holy Spirit and no longer by our human desires. The Christian who walks by the Spirit therefore does not manifest the desires of the flesh but bears the fruit of the Spirit, and so fulfils the just requirement of the law summed up in the commandment to love one's neighbour as oneself. All the virtues listed constitute one fruit, singular, so that all of them must be manifested in the Christian who lives in the power of the Holy Spirit.

subject: NT
topic: Qualifications Necessary for Spiritual Oversight or the Ministry
question: State the qualifications necessary for spiritual oversight in the church, distinguishing the office of bishop from that of deacon.
idealAnswer:
The seriousness with which Paul regarded the ministry is revealed in the detailed qualifications required of those who were to be appointed to the office of bishop or deacon. His aim was to encourage respect for the congregation's leaders. In general terms, bishops must be men of integrity, sobriety and conscientiousness; and both bishop and deacon should be the husband of one wife and a model of a family head.

The office of bishop is a noble one, and the qualifications required are high and of permanent significance. The bishop must be a man of able mind and excellent character, socially adaptable and tactful, and able to teach and lead. In everything he must be above reproach, including in his marital and family relationships; he must be deeply grounded in the faith and must command the respect of all.

The word 'deacon' means servant or helper, and refers to the bishops' assistant. Deacons take care of the mundane matters of church life - mundane meaning worldly as contrasted with spiritual or heavenly - and particularly the distribution of charity. Like the bishops, deacons must also be men of quality, even though their function in the congregation is significantly different. Deacons should be proved blameless through examination before entering office. The desirable characteristics named are sincerity in speech and faith, sobriety and unselfishness, and their private life ought to manifest a true Christian home. Good service in the diaconate results in higher position and confidence, with consequent influence.

The reference to 'women' in verse 11 may imply a female order of deaconesses, or may refer to deacons' wives, who were expected to help in the charitable work of their husbands. The section closes with the statement of the purpose of the letter, how people ought to conduct themselves in God's household, and with the quotation of an early Christian hymn or creed which traces the career of Christ from incarnation to ascension.

subject: NT
question: Outline the counter-measures which Paul prescribed to Timothy in 1 Timothy 4:6-16 against the threats to the safety of the church.
idealAnswer:
It is necessary that a good minister instructs the people in sound doctrine, which is the diet of his own soul, and superstition is to be avoided; taboos should have no place in an intelligent Christian approach, in contrast to the many systems of taboos in heathen cults.

The first counter-measure is that the minister should live on his own message. A good minister is not a theorizer: he teaches the apostolic doctrine which he has made his own, both as nourishment by which to live and as a standard by which to judge himself. Secondly, superstition is to be avoided; the church at this stage was confronted with invented stories and untrue fables, and Timothy is reminded to have nothing to do with godless and silly myths but to train himself in godliness.

Thirdly comes self-training. Paul is here thinking of Christian service as a form of athletic contest, and he often used athletic analogies to drive home the need for spiritual discipline. The minister's own spiritual life does not come automatically: he must train himself in spiritual exercises, since the prize for the good fight is both here and hereafter, for while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way, holding promise for the present life and also for the life to come.

Fourthly, Timothy is to be an example. There is to be a note of authority in his teaching, and Paul's purpose is to inspire the timid young man to display firmness. Many of the Ephesian Christians, especially the elders, were almost certainly of mature years, and having served under Paul the veteran, some would look with disfavour and contempt on the youthful missionary. As a counter-balance to contempt, Timothy would have to live in an exemplary manner, so that it would become evident that in Christianity authority is contingent upon character and not age.

Fifthly, he was to give himself to his spiritual ministry, attending both to his public ministry and to his private life. The public service is to consist of at least three ministerial essentials: the public reading of Scripture, since it has always been the practice of God's people to read the Word aloud in the congregation; preaching, which is exhortation, including the exposition and application of the passages read and addressed to Christians, preaching to non-Christians being evangelism rather than exhortation; and teaching, which may refer primarily to a more catechetical treatment of the truths of the Christian faith. By faithful adherence to a godly life and to the Word of God, Timothy would save both himself and his hearers from the false teachings.

subject: NT
question: Discuss Paul's call to Timothy to faithfulness in 2 Timothy 1:3-18.
idealAnswer:
The remembrance of Timothy inspires the apostle with thanksgiving to God. He is moved by Timothy's love but dwells more on his sincere faith, his salvation and his ministry; and Paul viewed his own faith in Christ not as a break with his Jewish forefathers but in continuity with their faith. As he prayed for Timothy night and day his gratitude kept increasing, for as he sat chained in prison there was little else he could do but pray. He remembers Timothy's tears at their last parting and had longed for the companionship which was such a joy to him; it is interesting to learn that even the great apostle at times became lonely, discouraged and in need of support from fellow Christians.

Convinced that Timothy possessed true faith, Paul urged him to fan into flame his God-given ability for ministry, since God's gift must be used to reach and maintain its full potential. Timothy needed the reminder that God did not give us a spirit of timidity but a spirit of power and love and self-control, because he might have been intimidated by the opposition to Paul and to the gospel, possibly threatened and ashamed at having to defend a prisoner and at the foolishness which they both preached about a despised and crucified Jesus. Such timidity or cowardice has no place in God's service; instead God gives a spirit of power, of love and of self-discipline, and these three virtues supplied by the Holy Spirit should characterise Timothy.

In the call to courage Timothy is told that he should not be ashamed, and would not be if his ministry were marked by those virtues. He would then be able to stand against his opponents and would not be ashamed to testify about the Lord, nor ashamed of Paul His prisoner. Paul exhorted him to join in suffering for the gospel, for it is in such circumstances that the power of God is shown; and he spells out that God saved us and called us to a holy life, a salvation which had nothing to do with a believer's merits but was purely because of God's own purpose and grace.

Timothy was also to guard the truth: to view what he had heard from Paul as the essential outline of sound teaching and to maintain it with faith and love in Christ Jesus. The stewardship of the truth had passed into his hands and he was to pass it on to other faithful Christians, guarding it meanwhile through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us. Finally, examples are set side by side. All who were in Asia turned away from Paul, probably fearing for their own safety, forsaking him when he needed them most; over against them stands Onesiphorus, who supported him not only in Ephesus but also in Rome. The negative and positive examples were designed to strengthen Timothy's resolve to stand shoulder to shoulder with Paul.

The call to guard the truth: the pattern of sound teaching, kept through the Holy Spirit and passed on

subject: NT
question: What are the marks of a good workman according to 2 Timothy 2:14-26?
idealAnswer:
The instruction of the previous verses was not for Timothy only: he was to keep reminding others of these things and to charge his people solemnly before the Lord to avoid disputing about words, which does no good but only ruins the hearers.

As for Timothy himself, he was to do his best to be sure he would meet with God's approval, a workman or labourer who does not need to be ashamed. Paul had spoken of shame before men, but shame before God is worse; and Timothy need not fear such shame if he would correctly handle the word of truth. He was also to avoid godless chatter - literally, to shun profane empty utterances - which only advances ungodliness like gangrene, gangrene being the mortification of a part of the body caused when it is cut off from its normal supply of blood and nutrition. Two men are named whose teachings were corrupting the local church, Hymenaeus and Philetus, whom Paul had already delivered over to Satan; these two had wandered away from the truth regarding the crucial doctrine of the resurrection, and according to Paul they destroy the faith of some.

The next mark is that of a clean instrument. Paul uses the metaphor of a household: in a large household are all sorts of containers, some made of gold and silver and others of wood and clay, and more importantly some are for noble purposes and some for ignoble - a reference to the faithful and the unfaithful within the church. The metaphor shows how one can be an instrument for noble purposes by cleansing himself from the ignoble vessels. Timothy was to have nothing to do with the false teachers, and in this way he would be a vessel for noble use, made holy, useful to the master and prepared for any good work. What is clean and set apart for special use can easily get contaminated and rendered unusable through contact with the corrupt, and Paul was concerned that Timothy keep himself in a usable condition for the Lord.

The last mark is faithfulness in conduct. Timothy was to shun youthful passion and aim at righteousness, faith, love and peace. Probably Paul did not have sexual passions primarily in mind: the evil desires of youth would include all the unholy desires that characterise young people, such as self-assertion, love of argument, partiality, intolerance and impatience. The Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kindly to everyone, correcting his opponents with gentleness, so that God may perhaps grant that they will repent and come to know the truth. When brethren fall into false teaching they must be treated with gentleness and Christian love in the hope that they will come to their senses and escape from the trap of the devil who has taken them captive; for false teaching is always the handiwork of Satan, but God in His grace often salvages the situation through the Christ-like ministry of His servants.

A workman who does not need to be ashamed - shame before God is worse than shame before men
Correctly handling the word of truth
Avoiding godless chatter, which advances ungodliness like gangrene
Hymenaeus and Philetus wandered from the truth about the resurrection and destroy the faith of some
The metaphor of the household: vessels of gold and silver, wood and clay, for noble and ignoble use
By cleansing himself Timothy would be a vessel for noble use, made holy, useful to the master, prepared for every good work
Shun youthful passions - self-assertion, love of argument, partiality, intolerance, impatience
The Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but correct opponents with gentleness, that they may repent

subject: OT
question: List 3 economic policies of Jeroboam.
idealAnswer: The military success of Jeroboam II brought with it improved economic development, and Israel built a close relationship with Phoenicia, the dominant commercial power of the Middle East. Three economic policies of Jeroboam may be listed. First, he imposed tolls upon all caravans passing through Israel, which brought a great deal of revenue into the treasury. Secondly, he created increased opportunities for international trade, so that many people became very rich. Thirdly, he developed Samaria into a strong commercial centre, whose splendid buildings demonstrated well enough the prosperity of the Northern State.

subject: OT
topic: Brief Survey of the Former Prophets
question: List five (5) military achievements of Joshua the Son of Nun.
idealAnswer: The book of Joshua deals with the conquest and settlement of the Promised Land after the death of Moses, and at every step Joshua was successful. His military achievements include the invasion of the land (chapters 1–5) and the crossing of the River Jordan; the capture and fall of Jericho (chapter 6); the conquest of the south (chapter 10); the conquest of the north (chapters 11–12); and the quick military operations against the important cities of Canaan, which all illustrate his successes. To these may be added the division of the conquered land among the tribes and the appointment of cities of refuge (chapters 13–22). His one failure was at Ai, because Achan coveted some of the spoils from Jericho.

subject: OT
topic: Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos
question: Describe the Vision of the Basket of the Summer Fruit in Amos 8:1-14. Outline the activities of the cruel and materialistic merchants of the Northern Kingdom and the result after the judgments.
idealAnswer: In the fourth of Amos' five visions of doom the Lord showed the prophet a basket filled with ripe summer fruit, and then explained to him that it symbolised Israel, which was now ripe for judgment. The vision is directed against the cruel and materialistic merchants of the Northern Kingdom, whose activities Amos sets out. They robbed the poor by selling them mouldy food and trampled upon the needy. They longed for the Sabbath to end and for the various religious holidays to be over, so that they might once again start cheating, using their weighted scales and undersized measures. And they made slaves of the poor, buying them for a debt of a piece of silver or for a pair of shoes. Amos then declares the results that would follow when this judgment took place: the sound of singing in the Temple would be turned to weeping; dead bodies would be scattered everywhere; fearful heavenly signs would occur (8:9); and there would be no comforting words from God (8:11-12). The vision thus belongs with the other visions – the locusts, the fire, the plumb line and the Lord at the altar – in which Amos declares that God would no longer turn away from punishing his people.

God explained that it symbolised Israel, now ripe for judgment
The merchants robbed the poor by selling them mouldy food and trampled upon the needy
They longed for the Sabbath and religious holidays to end so they could resume cheating
They used weighted scales and undersized measures
They made slaves of the poor, buying them for a debt of a piece of silver or a pair of shoes

subject: OT
topic: Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos
question: Amos ends his prophecy on a positive note concerning the future restoration of Israel. List any four of these areas and explain how this is going to happen.
idealAnswer: Amos ends his prophecy on a positive note concerning the future restoration of Israel, and five areas of restoration are named. The first is the restoration of the Davidic dynasty (9:11a). God had made a covenant with David that there would always be a descendant to sit on his throne, and though the exile made that promise seem impossible, “in that day” God would raise up and restore the kingdom to its promised glory – a promise fulfilled not by an earthly political leader but by the promised Messiah, who would renew the spiritual Kingdom and reign for ever. The second is the restoration of unity in the nation (9:11b-12). The kingdom had been divided in 931 B.C. in the reign of Rehoboam, and Amos declares that the fallen tent will be rebuilt as it used to be, referring to a restored united kingdom: “I will restore the fortunes of my people Israel”. The third is the restoration of agriculture (9:13). The soil will be so fertile that the reaper will be overtaken by the ploughman and the planter by the one treading grapes, so that seedtime and harvest follow in rapid succession without interruption by drought or plague, and new wine will drip from the mountains and flow from all the hills. The fourth is the restoration of the people (9:14a): during the exile the Jews would be scattered all over the world, and this promise refers to the bringing back of the captives from everywhere they had been scattered. The fifth is the restoration of liberty (9:14b): they will plant vineyards and gardens and will eat their crop and drink their wine, being in control of their own produce instead of growing crops as tribute for other nations. Amos adds that this restoration would be permanent (9:15): “I will plant Israel in their own land, never again to be uprooted from the land I have given them.”
keyPoints: The restoration of the Davidic dynasty (9:11a) – a descendant to sit on David's throne, fulfilled by the promised Messiah
The restoration of unity in the nation (9:11b-12) – the divided kingdom rebuilt as it used to be
The restoration of agriculture (9:13) – reaper overtaken by the ploughman, new wine dripping from the mountains
The restoration of the people (9:14a) – the scattered captives brought back from all over the world
The restoration of liberty (9:14b) – they will plant, eat their crop and drink their wine, in control of their own produce
The restoration would be permanent (9:15) – never again to be uprooted

subject: OT
question: Although Amos was from the Southern Kingdom – Judah, he was commissioned by God to preach in the Northern Kingdom city of Bethel. Historically describe Bethel.
idealAnswer: Bethel was historically one of the places where significant events had taken place in the life of Israel. Abraham had encamped there (Genesis 12:8). It was there that Jacob had his famous dream (Genesis 28:10-22), and the dream so moved him that he gave the place the name “Bethel”, which means “House of God”; before that the place had been known as Luz (Genesis 28:19). The history of the town changed when the United Kingdom was divided in 931 B.C. (1 Kings 12). Bethel then became one of the two major religious sites of the Northern Kingdom, and it was there that the idolatrous worship of the golden calf was instituted, a worship that continued to the end of the Northern Kingdom. Thus Bethel, the house of God, became the house of iniquity. It was about this place that Amos prophesied (Amos 7:10-13), and it was to Bethel that God commissioned him, a man of Judah, to go and preach.

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
question: What is divorce? How does God view divorce according to Malachi chapter two?
idealAnswer: Divorce, as Malachi 2:14-16 presents it, is the putting away of a wife – and not merely the putting away of a woman, but the putting away of a woman who is a man's companion and the wife of his covenant. In Malachi's day the men of Israel were marrying pagan women who were idolaters, which God had expressly forbidden, and were making the offence worse by divorcing the Jewish wives of their youth: the older men were cruelly divorcing their ageing wives and marrying attractive young foreigners, so that family life suffered. God views divorce in four ways. First, it is an act of cruelty (2:14), because the woman put away is “his companion”, one who has shared her life and life's experiences with her husband, and he writes her off as if it were nothing; that is cruelty and callousness. Secondly, it is an act of disloyalty (2:14), because she is not only his companion but “the wife of thy covenant”: he vowed his life to her, left father and mother to cleave to his wife and vowed never to let her go, but his vow has turned out to be empty words. Thirdly, it is an act which frustrates God's design of a godly seed (2:15): when a man divorces the wife of his youth and gets involved in a mixed marriage the future of the children is placed in jeopardy, for it is only when parents remain faithful to their marriage vows that God's desire for godly children will be fulfilled. Fourthly, it is an act which God hates: “I HATE DIVORCE” (2:16). God hates evil, and his children are to have the same attitude toward it, as Paul says, “abhor what is evil” (Romans 12:9). Divorce therefore shows a failure of the faithfulness God requires of his people, faithfulness to himself and faithfulness in human relationships.
keyPoints: Divorce is the putting away of a wife who is the husband's companion and the wife of his covenant
In Malachi's day men married pagan women and divorced the Jewish wives of their youth
It is an act of cruelty (2:14) – putting away a companion who has shared his life
It is an act of disloyalty (2:14) – she is the wife of his covenant, to whom he vowed his life
It is an act which frustrates God's design of a godly seed (2:15)
It is an act which God hates – “I hate divorce” (2:16)
God requires faithfulness to himself and in human relationships

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
question: The church has intensified her teaching on tithe, and you have been called upon to give a teaching on tithing in your society as a lay preacher. Write down your thoughts on the topic.
idealAnswer: The Hebrew word for tithe is ma'aser, and it means a “tenth”. Its origin is difficult to trace, but it is known to have existed in ancient Babylon and also in Persia, Egypt and China, and it is quite certain that Abraham knew of it when he migrated from Ur, for he gave a tenth to Melchizedek, priest of the Most High, so that in Abraham's day the giving of tithes had already been recognised as a holy deed. When Jacob made his covenant with God at Bethel the payment of tithe was included (Genesis 28:16-22). The legal requirement of tithing developed late and customs varied. At first the one who paid the tithe was entitled to share it with the Levites (Deuteronomy 14:22-23); after the Levitical code was completed the tithes belonged exclusively to the Levites (Numbers 18:21), who in turn gave a tenth of what they received to provide for the priests (Numbers 18:25-32). A Hebrew who lived too far from the temple could sell his animals and buy substitutes at the temple with the money (Deuteronomy 14:24-26), a permission which eventually led to gross abuses by the priests, which our Lord rebuked when he cleansed the temple. Leviticus 27:30 makes it clear that a tithe of everything belongs to the Lord and is holy to the Lord, and Deuteronomy 12:5-12 instructs that the tithe is to be brought to the house of God, not partaken of at home, while each Hebrew had to make a declaration of honesty before the Lord so that no deceit would be practised (Deuteronomy 26:13-15). Tithing was thus God's way in Old Testament days of providing the means to sustain his work and to provide for his ministers, the priests. In Malachi's day there had been a total disregard for this rule: the people disobeyed the clear instructions of God's word and were therefore robbing God, being greedy and self-centred in spite of God's goodness to them, and they were now experiencing God's chastisement and being deprived of his blessing (Malachi 3:7-9). What should they do? The answer is simple: they must repent and “bring the whole tithe into the storehouse”. If they are willing to do this, God will open the windows of heaven and pour out a blessing on them, and will also remove the chastisement they were experiencing in their agriculture (Malachi 3:10-12). It is believed that by the time of Jesus this injunction was being obeyed, so that teaching on it was hardly necessary; in Matthew 23:23 and Luke 11:42 Jesus encouraged his hearers to continue to pay their tithes but to be mindful also of the weightier matters of the law – justice, mercy and faithfulness. That is the balance our own teaching on tithing must keep.
keyPoints: The Hebrew word for tithe is ma'aser, meaning a tenth
Tithing was known in Babylon, Persia, Egypt and China, and Abraham knew of it (Genesis 14; Hebrews 7:4)
Jacob included the payment of tithe in his covenant with God at Bethel (Genesis 28:16-22)
At first the tithe was shared with the Levites (Deuteronomy 14:22-23); later it belonged exclusively to them (Numbers 18:21)
The Levites gave a tenth of the tithe to provide for the priests (Numbers 18:25-32)
A tithe of everything belongs to the Lord and is holy to the Lord (Leviticus 27:30)
The tithe is to be brought to the house of God (Deuteronomy 12:5-12), with a declaration of honesty (Deuteronomy 26:13-15)
Tithing sustains God's work and provides for his ministers
In Malachi's day the people robbed God and were deprived of his blessing (Malachi 3:7-9)
They must repent and bring the whole tithe into the storehouse; God will open the windows of heaven (Malachi 3:10-12)
Jesus urged the payment of tithes together with justice, mercy and faithfulness (Matthew 23:23; Luke 11:42)

markingRubric.label: Meaning and origin of the tithe
markingRubric.description: Ma'aser means a tenth; the practice was ancient and widespread, and Abraham and Jacob knew of it.

markingRubric.label: The Old Testament regulation of tithing
markingRubric.description: Tithes shared with and later belonging to the Levites, the Levites' own tenth for the priests, the tithe holy to the Lord, brought to the house of God with a declaration of honesty.

markingRubric.label: The purpose of tithing
markingRubric.description: God's way of providing the means to sustain his work and to provide for his ministers.

markingRubric.label: Israel's disregard of tithes in Malachi's day
markingRubric.description: The people disobeyed God's clear instructions and were robbing God, and so were under chastisement and deprived of blessing.

markingRubric.label: The remedy and the promise
markingRubric.description: Repent and bring the whole tithe into the storehouse; God will open the windows of heaven, pour out a blessing and remove the chastisement on their agriculture.

explanation: It tests whether the candidate can teach the biblical basis, purpose and practice of tithing as set out in the section on Malachi 3:7-12.

subject: OT
question: In discussing the date for the Ministry of Malachi, it is argued that he worked after the return from the Babylonian Exile. Give five reasons to either support or refute this claim by Bible scholars.
idealAnswer: The exact time of Malachi's ministry is not given in the book, but several indications place it after the return from the Babylonian Exile, in the period of Ezra and Nehemiah. First, the prophet mentions a “governor” as being over the land (1:8); this was the political condition that existed when the Jews returned from Babylon, whereas before the exile the political leader of the nation was a king, and Haggai likewise used the word governor of Zerubbabel. Secondly, he must have prophesied after the ministry of Haggai and Zechariah, who prophesied during the building of the temple (520–516 B.C.), for there is no reference in Malachi to the rebuilding of the temple. Thirdly, the impression of a drift into a casual attitude towards worship shows that some time had passed since the rebuilding: the temple services had been resumed long enough for the priests to become weary with the regular performance of them (1:13), and irregularities had crept in (1:7-8, 12-14; 3:8-9). Fourthly, there are details which link the prophet to the time of Nehemiah, especially the latter years of his governorship over Judah; Nehemiah came to Jerusalem as governor in 445 B.C., served some years and returned temporarily to Persia in 433 B.C. Fifthly, on his return to Jerusalem Nehemiah found gross sin and violation of the Law (Nehemiah 13), and there is a very close agreement between Nehemiah 13 and the book of Malachi, from which we may infer that Malachi prophesied during the return of Nehemiah, probably a few years after 433 B.C. The claim of the scholars is therefore to be supported: Malachi is a post-exilic prophet, indeed the last prophet of the Old Testament, after whom came the four hundred years of silence.
keyPoints: The exact date of Malachi's ministry is not given in the book
He mentions a “governor” over the land (1:8) – a post-exilic condition; before the exile the leader was a king
Haggai used the word governor of Zerubbabel
He prophesied after Haggai and Zechariah, who prophesied during the temple building (520–516 B.C.)
There is no reference to the rebuilding of the temple
Temple services had been resumed long enough for the priests to grow weary and for irregularities to creep in
Details link him to the time of Nehemiah, especially the latter years of his governorship
Nehemiah came as governor in 445 B.C. and returned to Persia in 433 B.C.
The close agreement between Nehemiah 13 and Malachi suggests he prophesied a few years after 433 B.C.

subject: OT
topic: Brief Survey of the Former Prophets
question: Write a brief introduction to the book of Judges and, using the prophetic interpretation of the pattern of history, give the five stages of the analysis of the book.
idealAnswer: Judges covers the period in Israel's history between Joshua's death and the rise of Samuel, roughly 1220 to 1050 B.C. It was a time of transition in which the only thing that held the scattered tribes together was their common faith: loyalty to God meant a strong united nation, while turning to the gods around brought weakness and division. The story in Judges chapter 1 gives the impression that Israel under Joshua could not drive out the Canaanites as the book of Joshua portrays, and this failure leads on to a story of increasing chaos and confusion; one thing that comes out clearly is that history continually repeated itself through the period, a pattern of failure repeated later in Samuel and Kings. The prophetic interpretation of this pattern is described carefully in Judges 2:11-23, in five stages. First, the people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the Lord; they forsook the Lord and served the Baals, the gods of the Canaanites. Secondly, the Lord's anger came upon Israel and he gave them up into the hands of foreign powers – the Moabites, Midianites, Amorites and Philistines. Thirdly, they cried to the Lord, and he had pity on his people's sufferings and raised up judges to deliver them, among them Othniel, Ehud, Deborah, Gideon, Abimelech, Tola, Jair and Jephthah. Fourthly, the judges were given military victory and success by God against their enemies. Fifthly, when the judges died the people returned to their old sinful and idolatrous ways, and so the pattern of failure started all over again. The book ends with an appendix (chapters 17–21) illustrating the moral and religious decline of those times, and the explanation given for the state of affairs is that “there was no king in Israel and every man did what was right in his own eyes” (Judges 17:6; 21:25).
keyPoints: Judges covers Joshua's death to the rise of Samuel, roughly 1220–1050 B.C.
A time of transition held together only by common faith; loyalty to God meant a strong united nation
Israel could not drive out the Canaanites, leading to increasing chaos and confusion
Stage 1: the people did evil, forsook the Lord and served the Baals
Stage 2: the Lord's anger gave them into the hands of foreign powers – Moabites, Midianites, Amorites, Philistines
Stage 3: they cried to the Lord and he raised up judges (Othniel, Ehud, Deborah, Gideon, Abimelech, Tola, Jair, Jephthah)
Stage 4: the judges were given military victory and success by God
Stage 5: when the judges died the people returned to their idolatrous ways and the cycle began again
The appendix (17–21) shows the moral decline: there was no king in Israel

subject: OT
chapter: INTRODUCTION TO PROPHETS AND PROPHECY IN ISRAEL
question: Write a note on any two of the following: a. The role of the Prophets in Israel. b. The prophetic Word. c. The Prophetic Action. d. Prophecy and the Future.
idealAnswer:
a. The role of the prophets in Israel. The prophets played a variety of roles in the life of Israel. They gave oracles, which was generally consultative; they preached and taught during worship; they interceded on behalf of the people, as Amos prayed that the judgment of God should not come upon his people, and they also spoke of the needs of the people to God; and they declared the will and the purpose of God even when this was not requested and in other contexts than the cultic services. Their ministry was unpredictable, for the prophet was free to act as and when the Spirit of God directed. They were feared in society and free from all constraints, so that Jeremiah, who would otherwise have been persecuted as a traitor after his first utterance, had the sovereign freedom to say what he was directed to say, as Nathan did to David (2 Samuel 12:1-12).

b. The prophetic Word. In ancient Israel the WORD was something very important. A man's spoken word had great significance, and the written word was not as important as the spoken word, since few could read and write. It was your spoken word that testified against you in court; the blessing was a powerful word, and when Jacob stole the blessing it could not be taken back, so that when Esau asked “what is left for me?” his father answered “nothing”. The word had an independent power and was an instrument of effective power. That is why the word of the prophet was very important; and the prophetic word was the very word of God, not the prophet's own words, and the same word was to be proclaimed by the prophet.

c. The Prophetic Action. The prophets do not only speak but act, and this is what is termed the prophetic action or prophetic symbolism. The prophetic action is itself creative of what it depicts: Ezekiel, for example, builds a city on sand with mud and makes a toy soldier (Ezekiel 4), by which he meant that he was helping to bring about the siege and destruction of Jerusalem. These actions were not just illustrations but depicted what was likely to happen, and the performing of the action was in itself a contribution to bringing about what was conveyed, for the prophetic actions were believed to contain power to shape the future.

d. Prophecy and the Future. A commonly held meaning of the word prophecy is “to predict the future”, but that is not its proper meaning. In the Old Testament the word means to speak the word of God. Prophecy therefore takes many forms: sometimes it is an explanation of past events, sometimes a warning, an admonition or appeal, a piece of advice or exhortation in the present, and sometimes it is directed to the future. Prophecy in the Old Testament has a past reference occasionally, a future reference occasionally and the present most often, for the prophets were primarily religious commentators on the life they saw around them, including its social, economic and political life. Very often the future reference was to the immediate future and was conditional – “if you do not repent, then …” – though the writing prophets also foretold the certainty of God's future plans and occasionally referred to the coming of Christ.
keyPoints: Roles: giving oracles (consultative); preaching and teaching during worship; interceding for the people; declaring God's will unasked
The prophets were free and unpredictable, feared in society, e.g. Nathan and David
The spoken word had great significance in Israel and was more important than the written word
The word had independent power; the prophetic word was the very word of God, not the prophet's own
Prophetic action or symbolism: the prophets act as well as speak, e.g. Ezekiel's city of mud (Ezekiel 4)
Prophetic actions were not mere illustrations but were believed to contain power to shape the future
Prophecy does not properly mean to predict the future but to speak the word of God
Prophecy has a past reference occasionally, a future reference occasionally and the present most often
Future references were often to the immediate future and conditional on repentance

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
question: Discuss this statement in the view of Malachi 3:13-4:6: “It is vain to serve God; and what profit is there to serve God?”
idealAnswer: This complaint belongs to the last of the six charges of the book, that Israel had discredited God's service. The majority of the people said that it does not pay to serve the Lord (3:13-15). They complained that they were religious, that they had kept the law of God and his charge and had walked in mourning before him, but that it had not been profitable to them and God had not rewarded them; God, they said, let the “real sinners” get away with their sin and even blessed them. In reality the statement was untrue, and the ones who complained were themselves the ungodly sinners: although they were religious and went through the motions of religious rites, it was superficial and external, they were hypocrites and had no heart for God, and their arrogant complaining was a discrediting of God's service. Over against them stood the remnant or minority in the nation, who believed that it does pay to serve the Lord (3:16-4:3). Among those who profess to know God there is always a remnant who truly are godly; though blessing may be delayed they do not complain, but wait patiently for him. Three things are said about the godly: they feared or reverenced the Lord and served him faithfully; they spoke to one another, defending God's actions and exhorting one another not to lose heart in spite of their hard conditions; and they esteemed his name, in contrast to the rest of the nation, who by their life-style despised God's name. God admires the faith of the humble and meek: he paid attention and heard them, and a book of remembrance was written before him of those who feared the Lord (3:16). His future response will make this plain, for in that day of the Lord he will honour the believing remnant – “they will be mine, says the Lord of hosts, on that day that I prepare my own possession, and I will spare them as a man spares his own son who serves him” (3:17). It is therefore not vain to serve the Lord: the Lord sees our service and remembers our labours, and though his reward may be delayed it will not be denied, whereas for the godless it will be denied, as Malachi 4:1-3 shows in the awful judgment awaiting those who have been superficial and not genuine God-fearers.
keyPoints: The complaint belongs to the charge that Israel has discredited God's service (3:13-4:6)
The majority said it does not pay to serve the Lord (3:13-15)
They claimed to have kept God's law and charge and walked in mourning, without reward
They complained that the real sinners got away with sin and were blessed
In reality the complainers were the ungodly – religious but superficial, hypocrites with no heart for God
The remnant believed that it does pay to serve the Lord (3:16-4:3)
The godly feared the Lord and served him faithfully, spoke to one another, and esteemed his name
A book of remembrance was written before him of those who feared the Lord (3:16)
In that day God will spare them as a man spares his own son who serves him (3:17)
It is not vain to serve the Lord: the reward may be delayed but will not be denied; for the godless it will be denied (4:1-3)
